One impression,
three different ledgers.

Follow a single ad purchase from contract to settlement: what the advertiser pays, what the publisher receives, and what the platform keeps, and how prediction, auctions, budgets, real-time systems, and causal measurement determine each number.

On this page

    A one-day learning roadmap

    In this chapter

    • Name the five layers of an ad system and what each one decides.
    • Know the day's schedule and the six questions you should be able to answer by 17:00.
    • Derive the running example's per-impression numbers: q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005, a $0.015 expected bill, $0.020 attributed and $0.008 incremental contribution.
    • Write the advertiser, network and publisher ledgers per 1,000 impressions, and see why the attribution report shows a $5 gain while the causal ledger shows a $7 loss.
    • State the advertiser's break-even lift, Δq∗=qa/g=0.000375\Delta q^{*}=qa/g=0.000375Δq∗=qa/g=0.000375.

    Computational advertising prices, allocates and settles heterogeneous impression opportunities when feedback is constrained, delayed and incomplete. An impression opportunity is one chance to show one ad to one user in one slot at one moment. Five layers interact:

    • A model estimates a conditional expectation, such as the probability that this impression leads to a purchase.
    • The product contract decides who pays whom for which event.
    • Auctions and budgets decide which opportunities can be bought, and at what price.
    • Systems decide whether a decision executes before its deadline and is recorded correctly.
    • Experiments are the only layer that tests whether the advertising creates value customers will keep paying for.

    Calling any single layer “the ad engine” ignores the constraints that actually drive profit.

    This reader assumes your background in theoretical CS, distributed systems, ML platforms and trading. It does not re-teach gradient descent, indexing or consensus. What you lack is the domain's own models: what each party optimizes, what each logged event means, what can and cannot be observed, and how the money is split. By the end of the day you should be able to derive a simplified bidding policy on your own, review the design of an ad system, and spot where claims about Axon's moat run ahead of their evidence. One day will not substitute for years of running campaigns.

    Company and product names used throughout: AppLovin is the ad-tech company under discussion. Axon is its ad prediction and bidding engine. MAX is its mediation product for publishers: for each ad slot in a publisher's app, it runs an auction across many demand sources (ad networks and other buyers) and returns the winning ad. Adjust is AppLovin's MMP (mobile measurement partner): a third party that records app installs and in-app events and attributes them to the ads that preceded them. The public facts about these products, and the limits on how their data may be used, are checked in AppLovin and Axon.

    An eight-hour schedule and six acceptance outcomes

    The day is 390 minutes of study plus 90 minutes of breaks, 480 minutes (8 hours) in total (study blocks: 20 + 50 + 100 + 60 + 70 + 40 + 50 min; breaks: 10 + 60 + 10 + 10 min). Each block ends with a deliverable. The main text is enough for the whole track; external links are for later verification, not for today.

    Terms used above: ROAS (return on ad spend) is attributed revenue divided by ad spend; it ignores the cost of goods and ignores whether the ad caused the sale. In a first-price auction the winner pays its own bid; in a second-price auction the winner pays the highest competing bid (or the seller's floor price, if that is higher). Settlement is the final, contractually checked computation of who owes whom.

    When you finish, you should be able to answer six questions:

    1. How much is a given opportunity worth, and to whom?
    2. Which contract makes the platform bear conversion risk? (Under per-conversion billing the platform pays publishers for impressions but is paid only when a conversion occurs, so it absorbs the variance.)
    3. How should you bid under a budget?
    4. Why does a model that improves offline (on held-out logs) not necessarily make more money online?
    5. How do you keep auction wins, billing and attribution from being conflated in the books?
    6. What evidence would suffice to support the claim that “the model creates a durable commercial advantage”?

    Expanding acronyms is not the goal. If all you can say is that DSP means demand-side platform (software that bids for impressions on behalf of advertisers), CTR means click-through rate (clicks per impression) and RTB means real-time bidding (a separate auction for each individual impression, run while the page or app loads), you have not met the day's goal.

    A fictional campaign used throughout

    Two explicitly separate contracts. The CPA campaign below is used to study billing and conflicting incentives. Its advertiser economics are negative at the stated defaults. Chapter 3 first checks that outcome, then separately teaches advertiser bidding under direct/pass-through auction buying with no fees. Its main-line $4 CPM first-price optimum uses advertiser value w=Δqg=$0.008w=\Delta qg=\$0.008w=Δqg=$0.008; the $7.50 CPM network-spread optimum is confined to the optional appendix. Both use the same causal-value inputs but different payment contracts.

    Roles. The advertiser is a merchant that sells goods and pays for advertising. The publisher owns the app or website that provides ad slots. The ad network sits between them: it buys impressions from publishers and bills advertisers. Later chapters call it the platform; both words mean the same party here. (Products and cash flow splits the network into its functional roles.)

    Events, in the order they occur.

    • A bid request is the publisher's invitation to bid on one ad opportunity.
    • A win means the network won that auction.
    • An impression means the ad was actually displayed. In general a win does not guarantee one (the ad can fail to load); this example assumes it does.
    • A click means the user tapped the ad.
    • A conversion is the agreed target action; here, a purchase.
    • Attribution credits an order to an ad according to fixed rules. Here only post-click orders count: an order is attributed only if the user clicked the ad first, within the contract's attribution window. The window's length is left unspecified; it does not change any number below.
    • A billable attributed conversion is an attributed order that also passes the contract's checks (attribution window, deduplication, refunds, chargebacks) and can therefore be billed. In this example each one is billed exactly once.

    Attribution is a crediting rule, not a measurement of causal effect. An attributed order may have happened without the ad.

    Conventions. Pre-advertising contribution per order is sales revenue minus the cost of goods, fulfillment and other variable non-advertising costs, before ad spend and fixed costs. “Expected” means the average over many repetitions of the same campaign. The budget derivations in later chapters constrain expected spend; that alone does not guarantee that realized spend stays under the cap (hard budgets are covered in Real-time advertising systems). All amounts are in US dollars; all counts and budgets are per day. Each chapter defines its own symbols; where a letter changes meaning between chapters, the local definition governs.

    The campaign. The network charges the advertiser $30 per billable attributed conversion. This is a CPA (cost per action) contract: the price is per action, not per impression. The network buys impressions from publishers through auctions and pays for each one at the price the auction rule sets (first price by default; see Prediction and bidding). Each order is worth $40 of pre-advertising contribution to the advertiser. The network sees 1,000,000 similar bid opportunities per day and has a daily media budget of $2,000 for buying impressions.

    Symbol Value Meaning
    NNN 1,000,000 per day Bid opportunities received; not the number of impressions bought
    BBB $2,000 per day Network's cap on expected media spend (paid to publishers); not a cap on the advertiser's bill
    pclickp_{\text{click}}pclick​ 0.01 Probability of a click given an impression
    pconvp_{\text{conv}}pconv​ 0.05 Probability of a billable attributed conversion given a click
    qqq 0.0005 Probability of a billable attributed conversion per impression; the denominator is impressions, not clicks
    aaa $30 per conversion CPA price the advertiser pays the network; not the product's selling price
    ggg $40 per order Advertiser's pre-advertising contribution per order
    vvv $0.015 per impression Network's expected revenue per impression, v=qav=qav=qa
    Δq\Delta qΔq 0.0002 Causal lift in purchase probability per impression from showing the ad (a given teaching parameter)

    Simplifying assumptions (later chapters relax some of them):

    • Opportunities are homogeneous: every one has the same qqq and Δq\Delta qΔq.
    • Every win produces a successful impression, so paying per win and paying per impression coincide. Real-time advertising systems drops this assumption.
    • Conversion probability does not depend on the bid or on the competitive threshold (the highest competing bid). Winning a more contested auction does not change who the user is.
    • Opportunities are independent, and repeated exposure of the same user has no interaction effects.
    Worked example

    What one impression is worth, and to whom

    Given: pclick=0.01p_{\text{click}}=0.01pclick​=0.01 clicks per impression, pconv=0.05p_{\text{conv}}=0.05pconv​=0.05 billable conversions per click, a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable conversion, g=$40g=\$40g=$40 per order, Δq=0.0002\Delta q=0.0002Δq=0.0002 incremental purchases per impression.

    1. Billable conversions per impression (only post-click orders are attributed, so there is no no-click term): q=pclick pconv=0.01×0.05=0.0005.q=p_{\text{click}}\,p_{\text{conv}}=0.01\times0.05=0.0005.q=pclick​pconv​=0.01×0.05=0.0005.
    2. Network's expected revenue per impression: v=qa=0.0005×$30=$0.015.v=qa=0.0005\times\$30=\$0.015.v=qa=0.0005×$30=$0.015. Per 1,000 impressions this is $15, the network's eCPM (effective revenue per thousand impressions; CPM, cost per mille, is a price per 1,000 impressions).
    3. Contribution the attribution report credits to the ad, per impression: qg=0.0005×$40=$0.020,qg=0.0005\times\$40=\$0.020,qg=0.0005×$40=$0.020, or $20 per 1,000 impressions.
    4. Contribution the ad actually adds, per impression: Δq g=0.0002×$40=$0.008,\Delta q\,g=0.0002\times\$40=\$0.008,Δqg=0.0002×$40=$0.008, or $8 per 1,000 impressions.
    5. Expected counts per 1,000 impressions: 1,000×0.01=101{,}000\times0.01=101,000×0.01=10 clicks and 1,000×0.0005=0.51{,}000\times0.0005=0.51,000×0.0005=0.5 billable conversions.

    Result: one impression carries three values: $0.015 billed, $0.020 attributed, $0.008 incremental. Per 1,000 impressions: $15, $20 and $8.

    Check: count first, then price. 10 clicks × 0.05 = 0.5 conversions; 0.5 × $30 = $15 billed and 0.5 × $40 = $20 attributed, matching steps 2–3. The attributed-to-billed ratio is g/a=40/30=4/3g/a=40/30=4/3g/a=40/30=4/3, and $20/$15 = 4/3.

    About Δq\Delta qΔq. For each eligible opportunity, Δq\Delta qΔq is the difference in purchase probability between showing the ad and not showing it for that same opportunity. We set it by assumption. Attribution reports cannot reveal it: they credit every post-click order, whether or not the ad caused it. Estimating it needs a randomized experiment, and even then a per-user lift divided by impressions per user equals Δq\Delta qΔq only under extra conditions. The lift must be scaled from assigned users to exposed users; the control group sees the next-best ad, not no ad; and effects must add up across a user's impressions (assumed here, rarely true in practice). Attribution, experiments and data covers the first two. That Δq<q\Delta q < qΔq<q here means attribution over-credits the ad. The gap q−Δqq-\Delta qq−Δq need not equal the rate of attributed-but-non-incremental orders, because attribution rules can also miss orders the ad did cause (here, any purchase without a prior click).

    Worked example

    Three ledgers per 1,000 impressions

    Given: the per-1,000 values above ($15 billed, $20 attributed, $8 incremental) and a publisher payment of PPP dollars per 1,000 impressions (the network's media cost). PPP comes from the auction and is left symbolic here.

    1. Advertiser, as the attribution report shows it: attributed contribution minus bill. 1,000 (qg−qa)=$20−$15=+$5.1{,}000\,(qg-qa)=\$20-\$15=+\$5.1,000(qg−qa)=$20−$15=+$5.
    2. Advertiser, causal ledger: incremental contribution minus bill. 1,000 (Δq g−qa)=$8−$15=−$7.1{,}000\,(\Delta q\,g-qa)=\$8-\$15=-\$7.1,000(Δqg−qa)=$8−$15=−$7.
    3. Network: bill collected minus media cost, $15−P\$15-P$15−P. It is positive only if P<$15P<\$15P<$15, i.e. the network pays publishers less per 1,000 impressions than its eCPM.
    4. Publisher: receives PPP (before its own costs and any loss of user experience).
    5. Advertiser break-even on the causal ledger: Δq g≥qa  ⟺  Δq≥Δq∗=qag,Δq∗=0.0005×3040=0.000375.\begin{aligned}\Delta q\,g\ge qa&\iff\Delta q\ge\Delta q^{*}=\frac{qa}{g},\\ \Delta q^{*}&=\frac{0.0005\times30}{40}=0.000375.\end{aligned}Δqg≥qaΔq∗​⟺Δq≥Δq∗=gqa​,=400.0005×30​=0.000375.​

    Result: the report says the advertiser gains $5 per 1,000 impressions; it actually loses $7. The campaign pays for itself only if Δq≥0.000375\Delta q\ge0.000375Δq≥0.000375, almost twice the assumed 0.0002. Prediction and bidding derives the same threshold.

    Check: payments are transfers, so they cancel when the three causal ledgers are summed: ($8−$15)+($15−P)+P=$8(\$8-\$15)+(\$15-P)+P=\$8($8−$15)+($15−P)+P=$8, exactly the incremental contribution, for any PPP. Summed on the attributed view, the ledgers show $20; the $12 difference is the over-credit 1,000 (q−Δq) g=1,000×0.0003×$401{,}000\,(q-\Delta q)\,g=1{,}000\times0.0003\times\$401,000(q−Δq)g=1,000×0.0003×$40.

    What changes if Δq\Delta qΔq doubles to 0.0004? Incremental contribution becomes 0.0004×$40=$0.0160.0004\times\$40=\$0.0160.0004×$40=$0.016 per impression, $16 per 1,000, so the causal net turns to $16−$15=+$1\$16-\$15=+\$1$16−$15=+$1 per 1,000; 0.0004 clears the 0.000375 break-even. Nothing else moves: the bill stays $15, the attribution report still shows +$5, and the network's ledger is unchanged. Attribution is blind to the one parameter that decides whether the advertiser keeps paying.

    All figures in the running example are teaching assumptions, not AppLovin's rates or industry benchmarks. Fractional conversion counts are expected values.

    Pitfall

    $2,000 caps the network's media spend, not the advertiser's bill. The advertiser pays a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable conversion regardless of what the network paid for the impressions, so its bill can exceed $2,000. An advertiser budget would be a second, independent constraint.

    Products and cash flow

    In this chapter

    • Specify any ad product on five independent dimensions: context, creative, transaction type, billing event, objective.
    • Price one campaign as CPM, CPC or CPA with the same expected payment, and say who absorbs click risk and conversion risk under each.
    • Trace $100 of advertiser spend through net and gross revenue recognition, and see why an 80% and a 20% gross margin can hide identical gross profit.
    • Decide whether to scale a budget by comparing the return on the additional spend with the break-even return (one over the contribution margin), and correct attribution-based ROAS for over- or under-crediting.

    Specify an ad product along five independent dimensions

    People often list “search, feed, RTB, CPC, performance advertising” as if they were categories of one kind. They are not. Search names the user context (a results page for a typed query); a feed is another context, a scrolling stream of content with ads inserted between items. RTB (real-time bidding) names a transaction mechanism: each individual ad opportunity is auctioned in milliseconds while the page or app loads. CPC (cost per click) names the billing event. Performance advertising names the optimization goal: the advertiser pays for, and judges results by, measurable downstream actions such as installs or purchases, as opposed to brand advertising, which buys reach and awareness. If you force these into one mutually exclusive taxonomy, the objective function you build downstream will be wrong.

    Dimension Typical values Impact on product and technology
    User context Search, content feed, web pages, in-game interstitials (full-screen ads shown at natural breaks, e.g. between levels) How the user reveals intent, and how much the ad disrupts the core product
    Creative and interaction Text, images, video, native cards (ads styled to match surrounding content), playable ads (a short interactive demo of a game) How creatives are produced, reviewed, displayed and measured
    Transaction type Direct deals (negotiated by hand, fixed price and volume); programmatic guaranteed (fixed price, reserved volume, executed through automated buying systems); preferred deals (fixed price, first look at inventory, no volume commitment); private auctions (invitation-only); open auctions (any qualified buyer, via RTB) Who commits to volume, and who bears the risk of under-delivery (delivering fewer impressions than promised)
    Billing event Impressions, clicks, installs, purchases and other actions When money is owed, and who bears response risk (the risk that a paid-for impression produces no click or conversion)
    Optimization objective Clicks, installs, revenue, contribution profit, incremental profit Model labels, observation windows and control constraints

    The dimensions combine freely. Take a rewarded video: an ad the user opts into inside a game in exchange for an in-game reward such as extra lives. The publisher can sell that slot through a first-price auction (the winner pays its own bid; see Prediction and bidding) and be paid per impression, while the advertiser's goal is a target D7 ROAS. ROAS (return on ad spend) is revenue divided by ad spend, defined precisely below; the D7 version counts revenue from the first seven days after a user is acquired. These descriptions do not conflict, because each belongs to a different dimension. Note also that the reward does not require the user to install the advertised app, so a user who is willing to finish the video does not necessarily intend to buy anything. Google AdMob rewarded ads documentation

    Contexts differ in how intent becomes visible. In search, the query states part of the user's current need. A feed has to infer opportunities from context, past behavior, and how users have responded to creatives. Open-web and in-app advertising must additionally join supply, user identity and conversion events across companies. These differences change how hard prediction is and what the product can do. They do not show that any context inherently earns a higher incremental return.

    Advertisers buy a delivery service under constraints

    A campaign is the advertiser's unit of purchase. To run one, the platform needs at least six groups of inputs:

    • business goals and the conversion events that measure them;
    • budget and flight dates (the start and end of delivery);
    • permitted audiences and geographies;
    • creatives and landing pages;
    • attribution rules and value postbacks (server-to-server messages that report each conversion, and its value, back to the ad platform);
    • billing and settlement terms.

    Below the campaign, ad groups usually carry finer targeting, bidding or creative combinations, but the hierarchy differs across platforms. Do not treat one platform's menu structure as a universal data model.

    “Optimize for purchases” is still underspecified. Does a purchase mean an order placed, a payment completed, or an order still valid after the refund period? Is value the merchandise revenue, the merchant's commission, or contribution profit? Does D7 revenue mean revenue accumulated over the first seven days, or revenue on day seven only? In this reader, D7 ROAS uses the half-open window [t0, t0+168 h)[t_0,\ t_0+168\text{ h})[t0​, t0​+168 h), where t0t_0t0​ is the moment of acquisition (for app campaigns, the install). It equals the cohort's cumulative attributed revenue in that window divided by the ad spend that acquired the cohort. The metric is only valid once the window has fully elapsed for every user in the cohort. Other platforms draw the day boundaries differently, so redefine the metric for each interface.

    Changing one field definition can change offline training labels, delivery behavior and reports without any change to the model. Advertiser onboarding is therefore more than a configuration form. Events, currency, time zone, deduplication keys, attribution windows, refunds and target constraints together must form an executable contract.

    Creative is a decision variable too. The same user can click and retain very differently depending on the creative shown. A pure “user value model” ignores creative supply, review latency, creative fatigue (response decays as the same audience sees a creative repeatedly) and landing-page quality. A platform that reliably finds high-CTR creatives may simply be rewarding clickbait, so the product needs user-experience and downstream-quality metrics as guardrails: constraints that must not degrade while the primary metric is optimized.

    Publishers sell attention and pay for it with product quality

    Publishers and app developers track revenue per thousand ad requests (often called RPM or request eCPM). They also track fill rate (the share of ad requests that receive an ad), ad latency, ad load (how many ads are shown per session or per unit of content) and user retention. If every filled request renders exactly one impression, request RPM equals fill rate times impression eCPM, where eCPM is revenue per thousand impressions (defined below). Raising revenue per ad at the cost of users opening the app less often erodes future supply. The seller therefore optimizes a combination of ad revenue, user experience and future usage, not each auction in isolation.

    Guaranteed contracts add a further layer. Suppose a publisher has committed to deliver one million qualifying impressions this month. Each qualifying opportunity can either count toward the contract or be sold on the spot market (the real-time auction). The comparison is between spot revenue and the shadow value of the opportunity: the Lagrange multiplier on the contract's delivery constraint, i.e. the marginal value of one more qualifying impression toward avoiding an under-delivery penalty. Supply forecasting, admission control (deciding whether to accept a new guaranteed contract given forecast supply), under-delivery penalties and allocation across overlapping contracts all enter this decision. Google Ad Manager draws exactly this line: programmatic guaranteed reserves and commits inventory, while a preferred deal carries no volume guarantee. Google Ad Manager deal types, Difference between guaranteed and preferred deals

    Roles and money flows

    The main functional roles are:

    • DSP (demand-side platform): buys inventory and optimizes delivery on behalf of advertisers.
    • SSP (supply-side platform): manages and sells a publisher's inventory.
    • Ad exchange: the marketplace that runs auctions matching buyers to sellers.
    • Ad server: selects which ad to show for a request, delivers it and logs the result.
    • Ad network: a company that bundles several of these roles, typically buying from publishers and selling to advertisers.
    • Mobile ad mediation: software in the app that decides which of several demand sources fills each ad request. Each demand source usually ships an SDK (software development kit, a library embedded in the app). Mediation either runs a bidding auction, in which all sources bid simultaneously, or a waterfall, which calls demand sources one at a time in a configured priority order until one fills.
    • MMP (mobile measurement partner), e.g. Adjust or AppsFlyer: sits in the feedback loop and provides measurement and attribution (crediting an install or purchase to an ad; see Attribution, experiments and data). Money does not pass through the MMP.

    Sources: IAB (Interactive Advertising Bureau) 2025 commerce media white paper, glossary appendix, Adjust integration documentation.

    The diagram below is organized by function. A real company may merge several boxes, and not every intermediary exists in every transaction.

    You cannot read a company's revenue off this diagram. Buying on a client's behalf, buying and reselling, charging a service fee, revenue sharing and acting as a settlement agent are different contracts, and they change both how revenue is recognized and who bears risk. Establish the company's transaction role first, then read its financial statements (worked example below).

    Keep billing events and optimization objectives apart

    The common pricing units are:

    • CPM (cost per mille): price per thousand impressions. An impression is one successful display of an ad.
    • CPC (cost per click): price per click.
    • CPI (cost per install): price per app install.
    • CPA (cost per action, or per acquisition): price per contractually defined action, such as a purchase.
    • CTR (click-through rate): clicks divided by impressions.
    • CVR (conversion rate): conversions divided by a denominator you must state. CVR per click and conversion probability per impression are different quantities; the second equals CTR times the first for post-click conversions.
    • eCPM (effective CPM): some revenue or value restated per thousand impressions, eCPM=1000×amount/impressions\text{eCPM}=1000\times\text{amount}/\text{impressions}eCPM=1000×amount/impressions. It is a unit conversion for comparing across contracts, not necessarily the price on any invoice.

    Use the running example from the roadmap chapter. An ad network buys impressions in auctions and charges the advertiser a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable conversion. An impression is clicked with probability pclick=0.01p_{\text{click}}=0.01pclick​=0.01 (the CTR), and a click converts with probability pconv=0.05p_{\text{conv}}=0.05pconv​=0.05 (post-click CVR), so a billable conversion follows an impression with probability q=0.01×0.05=0.0005q=0.01\times0.05=0.0005q=0.01×0.05=0.0005. The network's expected revenue per impression is v=q a=0.0005×$30=$0.015v=q\,a=0.0005\times\$30=\$0.015v=qa=0.0005×$30=$0.015, an eCPM of $15. That does not mean the network bids $15 CPM. The optional network-spread appendix derives bids for a network maximizing its own spread. Those bids use its CPA receipts and are not advertiser recommendations. The main bidding lesson instead uses the advertiser’s incremental contribution and an explicitly different direct-buying contract. Nor is the advertiser billed per impression: it still pays $30 per conversion. Valuation, bid and payment are three separate quantities.

    The billing event decides who bears response risk: the risk that paid-for impressions yield fewer clicks or conversions than forecast. The network's media cost is set in the auction regardless of how it bills, so any shortfall the advertiser does not pay for comes out of the network's margin.

    2. Expected campaign payment, identical by construction: CPM 1,000×$151{,}000\times\$151,000×$15; CPC 10,000 clicks×$1.5010{,}000\text{ clicks}\times\$1.5010,000 clicks×$1.50; CPA 500 conversions×$30500\text{ conversions}\times\$30500 conversions×$30; each $15,000\$15{,}000$15,000.
    3. Sampling noise with the forecast rates correct. CPM: payment is fixed once impressions are delivered, standard deviation $0. CPC: $1.50Ipclick(1−pclick)=$1.509,900≈$149.25\$1.50\sqrt{I p_{\text{click}}(1-p_{\text{click}})}=\$1.50\sqrt{9{,}900}\approx\$149.25$1.50Ipclick​(1−pclick​)​=$1.509,900​≈$149.25 (1.0% of the mean). CPA: $30Iq(1−q)=$30499.75≈$670.65\$30\sqrt{I q(1-q)}=\$30\sqrt{499.75}\approx\$670.65$30Iq(1−q)​=$30499.75​≈$670.65 (4.5% of the mean).
    4. Forecast error, which dominates sampling noise at this scale. If the true CTR is 0.005, there are 5,000 clicks and 250 conversions: the advertiser pays $15,000 under CPM, $7,500 under CPC, $7,500 under CPA. If instead the true CVR is 0.025, there are 10,000 clicks and 250 conversions: it pays $15,000, $15,000 and $7,500.
    5. Advertiser's realized cost per conversion in those two scenarios: CPM $60 and $60; CPC $30 and $60; CPA $30 and $30.

    Result: same expected payment, different risk bearer. Under CPM the advertiser bears both click and conversion risk; under CPC the network bears click risk and the advertiser conversion risk; under CPA the network bears both.

    Check: the advertiser's payment scales with the ratio of true to forecast rates for exactly the events it pays for: CPC payment = $15,000 × (true CTR ÷ 0.01); CPA payment = $15,000 × (true qqq ÷ 0.0005). Both scenarios halve qqq, so CPA pays $7,500 in both.

    Equal expected payments are a modelling convenience. A party that absorbs variance and forecast error charges for it, so in practice CPA and CPC prices carry a risk premium relative to the CPM equivalent. Shifting the billing event also shifts incentives: under CPA the network's revenue depends on the advertiser's conversion definition and reporting; under CPM the advertiser must police impression quality itself.

    Define the return metrics precisely:

    • ROAS (return on ad spend) = revenue under an agreed definition (usually attributed revenue, i.e. revenue credited to ads by the attribution rules) ÷ ad spend. It is often quoted as a percentage: 300% means 3.0.
    • iROAS (incremental ROAS) = incremental revenue ÷ ad spend, where incremental revenue is the revenue that would not have occurred without the ads. Keep the two numerators distinct.
    • tCPA (target CPA): the average cost per conversion that an automated bidding algorithm tries to achieve across a campaign.
    • tROAS (target ROAS): the ROAS that an automated bidding algorithm tries to achieve.

    Optimizing toward a CPA target does not mean being billed per conversion, and it does not guarantee that every conversion costs less than the target. Google's tCPA, for example, sets bids automatically to hit an average conversion-cost target, while the advertiser is typically still billed per click. Google tCPA documentation

    LTV (lifetime value: the total value a customer generates over a horizon) also needs a definition before use. State at least: the horizon; whether it measures revenue or contribution profit; whether refunds are deducted; whether it is discounted; and whether acquisition ad spend has already been subtracted. Treating revenue LTV as a profit valuation systematically overstates what you can afford to bid.

    Three ledgers and the limits of scaling

    Each party keeps its own ledger. The advertiser's ledger records the business value gained and what was paid for it. The network's ledger records what it collects from advertisers and what it pays publishers and service providers. The publisher's ledger records what it earns from selling inventory and what it loses in user experience and future usage. All three reports can show growth while total real economic value does not rise.

    The platform's gross margin, the advertiser's campaign return and the payoff from further scaling are three different questions. A platform can hold an 80% gross margin while the advertiser earns less with every extra dollar it spends. Below, one ad budget is entered into two income statements, and then we examine how scaling changes each side's returns. Throughout, amounts are for one fixed period, “spend” means the amount billed to the advertiser in that period, and refunds, credits and taxes are ignored.

    1. What is the denominator of the platform's 80% gross margin?

    Four accounting terms first.

    • Take rate: the amount the platform keeps after paying the publisher, divided by total advertiser spend (sometimes called gross billings).
    • Gross vs net revenue recognition: a platform that recognizes revenue gross books the full advertiser spend as revenue and the publisher payout as a cost. One that recognizes revenue net books only the amount it keeps.
    • Cost of revenue: costs directly incurred to deliver the service, such as serving infrastructure, data and payment processing. Under gross recognition it also includes the publisher payout, often called TAC (traffic acquisition cost).
    • Gross profit = recognized revenue − cost of revenue. Gross margin = gross profit ÷ recognized revenue.
    Worked example

    $100 of spend under net and gross recognition

    Given, for one period: advertiser spend S=$100S=\$100S=$100; publisher payout P=$75P=\$75P=$75; the platform's direct service costs D=$5D=\$5D=$5 (serving, data, payment processing), all classified as cost of revenue. Compare two platforms with identical cash flows, one that qualifies for net recognition and one that qualifies for gross recognition (the control test below decides which; neither chooses).

    1. Take rate, a cash-flow ratio identical for both: (S−P)/S=($100−$75)/$100=25%(S-P)/S=(\$100-\$75)/\$100=25\%(S−P)/S=($100−$75)/$100=25%.
    2. Net recognition: revenue =S−P=$25=S-P=\$25=S−P=$25; cost of revenue =D=$5=D=\$5=D=$5; gross profit =$25−$5=$20=\$25-\$5=\$20=$25−$5=$20; gross margin =$20/$25=80%=\$20/\$25=80\%=$20/$25=80%. The $75 payout appears in neither line.
    3. Gross recognition: revenue =S=$100=S=\$100=S=$100; cost of revenue =P+D=$75+$5=$80=P+D=\$75+\$5=\$80=P+D=$75+$5=$80 (the $75 is TAC); gross profit =$100−$80=$20=\$100-\$80=\$20=$100−$80=$20; gross margin =$20/$100=20%=\$20/\$100=20\%=$20/$100=20%.
    4. Gross profit per dollar of advertiser spend, under both: $20/$100=20%\$20/\$100=20\%$20/$100=20%.

    Result: same cash, same $20 gross profit; reported gross margin is 80% under net recognition and 20% under gross.

    Check: the two margins share the numerator and their denominators are S−PS-PS−P and SSS, so gross margin (gross) = take rate × gross margin (net) =0.25×0.80=0.20=0.25\times0.80=0.20=0.25×0.80=0.20.

    The 80% is measured against the $25 the platform recognizes: each recognized dollar leaves $0.80 after cost of revenue. It does not mean the platform keeps 80% of the ad budget, nor that 80% is final profit; R&D, sales, taxes and the cost of capital still come out. Before comparing two ad companies' gross margins, align their revenue recognition and cost classification. Here 80% versus 20% reflects no difference in efficiency at all.

    Calling the platform an “agent” in the contract does not by itself justify net recognition. IFRS 15, the international revenue standard, and ASC 606, its US GAAP counterpart, apply the same test. The entity identifies each specified good or service promised to the customer (for an ad platform, typically the ad placement) and asks whether it controls that good or service before it is transferred to the customer. If it does, it is a principal and recognizes revenue at the gross amount of consideration; if not, it is an agent and recognizes only its fee or commission, i.e. the consideration net of what it passes to the other party. Three indicators support, but do not replace, the control assessment: primary responsibility for fulfilling the promise; inventory risk before or after transfer (for example, buying impressions up front with no matching advertiser order); and discretion in setting the price. One company can be a principal for some offerings and an agent for others. IFRS Interpretations Committee on principal versus agent, Summary of IFRS 15 principal-versus-agent requirements

    2. Why does the advertiser's profit fall while its sales rise?

    Switch to the advertiser's ledger. Its revenue, such as the $300 of incremental sales in the table below, is what consumers pay the advertiser for goods or services. It has nothing to do with the $25 of revenue the platform recognizes.

    Let mmm be the advertiser's contribution margin before advertising: the fraction of each incremental sales dollar left after goods, fulfillment and other variable non-advertising costs, before ad spend and fixed costs. Take m=40%m=40\%m=40%, so each additional $100 of sales leaves $40 to pay for advertising and contribute to profit. Assume mmm is constant across volume (variable costs are linear in sales).

    Below, “profit” always means incremental contribution profit after ad spend (incremental sales × mmm − ad spend), not the company's net income. Each column's revenue is assumed to be truly incremental, measured over the same observation period with the same revenue definition.

    Advertiser's ledgerFirst $100Additional $50Cumulative $150
    Incremental sales revenue$300$75$375
    Variable non-advertising costs (60% of sales)$180$45$225
    Contribution before ad spend (40% of sales)$120$30$150
    Ad spend$100$50$150
    Contribution profit after ad spend$20−$20$0
    iROAS (incremental sales ÷ ad spend in that column)3.01.52.5

    The first $100 of spend generates $120 of contribution and so earns $20 after paying for itself. The additional $50 generates only $30 of contribution and so loses $20 on its own. The new orders are real, but what they leave after fulfillment does not cover the extra acquisition cost. Sales rise from $300 to $375 while contribution profit falls from $20 to zero.

    3. Average iROAS hides the loss on the additional budget

    Let CCC be ad spend, RRR the incremental sales revenue it generates, and mmm the contribution margin defined above. Let ΔC\Delta CΔC be additional spend and ΔR\Delta RΔR the additional incremental revenue it generates. Here “marginal iROAS” means the finite-increment ratio ΔR/ΔC\Delta R/\Delta CΔR/ΔC; only in the limit ΔC→0\Delta C\to0ΔC→0 does it become a derivative.

    Contribution profit is mR−CmR-CmR−C, which for C>0C>0C>0 and m>0m>0m>0 is non-negative exactly when R/C≥1/mR/C\ge 1/mR/C≥1/m. So the break-even iROAS is 1/m1/m1/m: 2.5 at m=40%m=40\%m=40%, 5 at m=20%m=20\%m=20%, 1.25 at m=80%m=80\%m=80%. If m≤0m\le0m≤0, no iROAS breaks even.

    Should the advertiser add the extra $50?

    The cumulative 2.5 sits at break-even only because the early high-return spend subsidizes the late low-return spend. The trading analogue: a scaled-up strategy's marginal capacity may not cover its costs while the book's average return hides the loss from the scale-up itself.

    4. Platform gross profit can grow while customer profit falls

    Now combine the two ledgers. Assume additionally that the platform always keeps 25% of the budget, that its direct service costs are always 5% of the budget, and that it keeps recognizing revenue net.

    MetricAd budget $100Ad budget $150
    Platform net revenue$25$37.50
    Platform direct service costs$5$7.50
    Platform gross profit$20$30
    Platform gross margin80%80%
    Advertiser contribution profit$20$0

    Scaling up raises platform gross profit by $10 and cuts the advertiser's contribution profit by $20. This does not prove the platform harms customers deliberately; customer retention, competition and the prospect of future budgets all constrain it. It does prove that growth in the platform's current-period revenue, a high platform gross margin and growth in customer profit do not automatically move together.

    Suppose the system objective is “maximize sales subject to cumulative iROAS ≥ 2.5.” The $150 plan satisfies the constraint, exactly at the boundary (the constraint is inclusive), and has higher sales, so the system chooses it. Maximizing advertiser contribution profit would choose the $100 plan instead. An algorithm can execute its objective flawlessly and still produce a commercially bad outcome.

    5. The strongest assumption: revenue must be truly incremental

    “The platform attributes the order to the ad” and “the order would not have happened without the ad” are different claims. Google's documentation likewise separates standard attributed conversions from incremental conversions measured in experiments. Google Conversion Lift measurement definition

    Suppose attributed revenue is $300 but the revenue the ads actually caused is only $200. Then the first $100 of spend already loses money:

    incremental contribution profit=$200×0.4−$100=−$20.\text{incremental contribution profit} = \$200\times0.4-\$100 = -\$20.incremental contribution profit=$200×0.4−$100=−$20.

    The κ\kappaκ formula gives the same verdict: κ=200/300=2/3\kappa=200/300=2/3κ=200/300=2/3, so the break-even attributed ROAS is 1/(0.4×2/3)=3.751/(0.4\times2/3)=3.751/(0.4×2/3)=3.75, above the reported 3.0.

    To judge a platform like AppLovin's Axon (see the Axon chapter), the useful question is: under the same measurement definition, contribution margin and budget, how much does it raise the customer's true incremental contribution profit, and how much of that advantage survives as the budget grows? The platform's accounting gross margin cannot answer it.

    Your trading experience transfers directly to auditable P&L, risk limits and capacity curves. One intuition does not transfer: that an impression is a homogeneous asset you can store and resell without loss. An impression perishes the instant it is served, its value depends on the advertiser and the creative, feedback arrives with a delay, and the counterfactual (what would have happened without the ad) is never directly observed. What gets called statistical arbitrage in advertising usually carries unhedged behavioral, attribution and settlement risk.

    From advertiser value to bidding and budgets

    In this chapter

    • Choose the decision-maker, payment contract and objective before choosing a bid.
    • Compute the advertiser's incremental contribution per impression, and distinguish it from a network's expected receipts.
    • Derive advertiser-profit-maximizing bids: $4 CPM in first price and $8 CPM in ideal second price for the direct-buying example.
    • See why a $2,000 budget can remain partly unspent, and how a $500 budget changes the answer.
    • Keep response prediction, causal value and auction-price learning separate. An optional appendix studies a network maximizing its own spread.

    Start with whose money and whose objective

    The main decision-maker is the advertiser, or a buying agent instructed to act for it. The objective here is to maximize expected incremental contribution after advertising costs: contribution from sales caused by advertising, minus the advertiser's entire ad bill. Contribution is sales revenue less goods, fulfillment and other variable non-advertising costs; company fixed costs are outside this model. Spending the budget is a constraint, not a separate goal.

    Advertiser objective=incremental sales contribution−total advertising bill.\text{Advertiser objective}=\text{incremental sales contribution}-\text{total advertising bill}.Advertiser objective=incremental sales contribution−total advertising bill.

    An ad network's spread is a different ledger: advertiser payments collected minus publisher payments made, before the network's other costs. Optimizing that ledger does not automatically optimize the advertiser's outcome. The optional network-spread appendix explains the $7.50 and $6.3246 CPM network-spread examples, including the calculator. Those are network-optimal bids under a particular contract, not general advertiser recommendations or claims about Axon's internal objective.

    The existing CPA contract: first check whether buying anything makes sense

    Keep the contract from Chapter 1: the advertiser pays a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable attributed order. Let q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005 be the probability of such an order per successful impression; let Δq=0.0002\Delta q=0.0002Δq=0.0002 be the true increase in purchase probability caused by showing the ad; and let g=$40g=\$40g=$40 be contribution per additional order. These probabilities and contribution are teaching inputs, held constant as the bid changes. Attribution assigns billing credit; it does not establish causation.

    Incremental contribution per impression=Δq g=0.0002×40=$0.008,Advertiser bill per impression, in expectation=q a=0.0005×30=$0.015,Advertiser gain per impression=0.008−0.015=−$0.007.\begin{aligned} \text{Incremental contribution per impression}&=\Delta q\,g=0.0002\times40=\$0.008,\\ \text{Advertiser bill per impression, in expectation}&=q\,a=0.0005\times30=\$0.015,\\ \text{Advertiser gain per impression}&=0.008-0.015=-\$0.007. \end{aligned}Incremental contribution per impressionAdvertiser bill per impression, in expectationAdvertiser gain per impression​=Δqg=0.0002×40=$0.008,=qa=0.0005×30=$0.015,=0.008−0.015=−$0.007.​

    Let DDD be the expected number of successful impressions. Under this fixed-CPA contract the advertiser's expected incremental contribution after its bill is D(Δqg−qa)=−0.007DD(\Delta qg-qa)=-0.007DD(Δqg−qa)=−0.007D. If it can stop the campaign, the advertiser's optimum is zero impressions. Lowering the network's publisher payments does not lower the advertiser's fixed $30 CPA price. No derivative of network spread can turn this contract into a profitable one for the advertiser. Renegotiating the price, improving causal lift or stopping are economic choices that precede bid optimization.

    A separate worked contract: the advertiser pays the auction cost

    To study a useful positive-value bidding decision, we now explicitly change the payment arrangement. The advertiser buys impressions directly, or its agent passes through the exact auction cost with no service fee, markup or other charge. It does not pay the $30 CPA invoice in this worked example. The causal lift and per-order contribution stay the same. This is an analytical baseline, not a description of AppLovin's contracts.

    All prices below are US dollars per impression unless marked CPM (price per 1,000 impressions). Assume each auction win displays successfully, no floor or extra fees, risk-neutral decisions based on expected contribution, and fixed competition. Each opportunity has the same causal lift and value, independent of its competitive threshold and our bid. There are no cross-impression interactions. We assume causal lift is known; Chapter 4 explains the measurement problem.

    Why does a $6 CPM bid win 30% of opportunities?

    Two questions are separate: what price must we beat in one auction? and how often does a fixed bid beat it across many auctions? The first defines the competitive threshold; the second needs a probability model.

    1. One auction: our bid against the highest competing bid

    Assume every opportunity has at least one competing bid, and let ZZZ be the highest of them. A floor price (reserve price) is the seller's minimum acceptable price; this model has none. ZZZ is then the competitive threshold. We choose our bid bbb. If competitors bid $3, $5 and $9 CPM, then ZZZ = $9 CPM: a $6 CPM bid loses and a $10 CPM bid wins. Our own bid is not part of the maximum that defines ZZZ.

    Z=max⁡{competing bids},win  ⟺  b≥Z.Z=\max\{\text{competing bids}\},\qquad \text{win}\iff b\ge Z.Z=max{competing bids},win⟺b≥Z.

    Ties go to us (b≥Zb\ge Zb≥Z wins). Under the continuous distribution below an exact tie has probability zero, so the convention affects no result; with discrete price increments, real tie-breaking rules can matter. The threshold decides whether we win, not necessarily what we pay: in the default first-price auction the winner pays its own bid.

    2. Many auctions: treat the unknown threshold as random

    Different opportunities draw different competitors and bids, so ZZZ varies across auctions, and the bidder does not know the next value in advance. The teaching model assumes Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L) (∼\sim∼ reads “is distributed as”): price intervals of equal length are equally likely. We further assume every opportunity's threshold has this same distribution and that our own bidding does not move it (we are a price taker). The assumption concerns the highest competing bid, not each competitor's bid.

    On the $0–20 CPM range, each $2-wide interval has probability 2/20 = 10%; the intervals $0–2 and $12–14 are equally likely.

    3. We win exactly when the threshold falls below our bid

    For a fixed bbb we win exactly when Z∈[0,b]Z\in[0,b]Z∈[0,b], an interval of length bbb inside a range of length LLL. Let FFF be the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of ZZZ, so F(b)F(b)F(b) is the win probability at bid bbb:

    F(b)=P(Z≤b)=b−0L−0=bL,0≤b≤L.F(b)=P(Z\le b)=\frac{b-0}{L-0}=\frac{b}{L},\qquad 0\le b\le L.F(b)=P(Z≤b)=L−0b−0​=Lb​,0≤b≤L.

    The denominator is the whole price range, not our bid. A $6 CPM bid wins against thresholds in $0–6 (length 6) and loses against thresholds in $6–20 (length 14): probabilities 6/20 = 30% and 14/20 = 70%.

    $0$5$10$15$20 CPM

    Win: thresholds $0–6.0 CPM → 6 / 20 = 30%. Lose: thresholds above $6.0 CPM → 70%.

    This explorer chooses a bid only to illustrate its win probability. The advertiser calculator below chooses a bid to maximize advertiser incremental contribution after ad spend.

    Outside the range, F(b)=0F(b)=0F(b)=0 for b<0b<0b<0 and F(b)=1F(b)=1F(b)=1 for b≥Lb\ge Lb≥L. Bidding above LLL buys no extra win probability and, under first-price, only raises the payment, so such bids are dominated.

    4. CPM and per-event prices give the same probability

    Every price in a comparison must use the same unit. Internally bbb, ZZZ and LLL are in dollars per impression (the billable event in this direct-buying contract); a CPM quote is 1,000 times that. The subscript CPM marks a quote, not a different quantity:

    bCPM=1000 b,LCPM=1000 L,bL=$0.006$0.02=$6 CPM$20 CPM=0.30.\begin{aligned} b_{\text{CPM}}&=1000\,b,\qquad L_{\text{CPM}}=1000\,L,\\ \frac{b}{L}&=\frac{\$0.006}{\$0.02}=\frac{\$6\ \text{CPM}}{\$20\ \text{CPM}}=0.30. \end{aligned}bCPM​Lb​​=1000b,LCPM​=1000L,=$0.02$0.006​=$20 CPM$6 CPM​=0.30.​

    The factor 1,000 cancels. Dividing a $6 CPM quote by $0.02 per event mixes units and gives 300, which is not a probability.

    The seller’s billing terms fix what a billable event is: a win under win-based billing, a successful impression under display-based billing. Here every win displays successfully, so the two counts coincide. Switching the billing basis changes ad spend; it does not change the win event Z≤bZ\le bZ≤b.

    5. From win probability to expected wins

    Let WWW be the number of opportunities won. With the same bid and the same marginal threshold distribution on every opportunity, linearity of expectation gives

    E[W]=N F(b)=1,000,000×0.30=300,000 wins.\mathbb E[W]=N\,F(b)=1{,}000{,}000\times0.30=300{,}000\ \text{wins}.E[W]=NF(b)=1,000,000×0.30=300,000 wins.

    Linearity needs no independence. Dependence across opportunities (for example, one competitor bidding on correlated traffic) changes only how widely the realized count fluctuates around 300,000. With successful display on every win, these wins are also 300,000 expected impressions.

    Optional: the density derivation, and what changes outside this model

    The uniform threshold has density f(z)=1/Lf(z)=1/Lf(z)=1/L on [0,L][0,L][0,L] and 0 elsewhere, where zzz denotes a possible value of ZZZ. The total area is L⋅(1/L)=1L\cdot(1/L)=1L⋅(1/L)=1. Integrating the density over the winning interval recovers the CDF:

    F(b)=∫0bf(z) dz=∫0b1L dz=bL,0≤b≤L.F(b)=\int_0^b f(z)\,dz=\int_0^b\frac{1}{L}\,dz=\frac{b}{L},\qquad 0\le b\le L.F(b)=∫0b​f(z)dz=∫0b​L1​dz=Lb​,0≤b≤L.

    In a non-uniform market the win probability is still F(b)=P(Z≤b)F(b)=P(Z\le b)F(b)=P(Z≤b), but not b/Lb/Lb/L: if 80% of thresholds lie below $6 CPM, a $6 CPM bid wins 80%, not 30%. Floor prices, discrete bids, heterogeneous opportunity types and competitors that react to our bids each need a different model. Note also that the maximum of nnn independent Uniform(0,L)\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Uniform(0,L) competing bids has CDF (b/L)n(b/L)^n(b/L)n, so uniform individual bids do not produce a uniform threshold.

    First-price bidding: maximize the advertiser's contribution after cost

    In first price, a winner pays its own bid bbb. Define J1(b)J_1(b)J1​(b) as the advertiser's expected incremental contribution after ad spend across all NNN opportunities, and C1(b)C_1(b)C1​(b) as its expected ad spend. A loss creates neither contribution nor cost in this model.

    Expected impressions=NF(b),Expected incremental contribution=NF(b)w,C1(b)=NF(b)b,J1(b)=NF(b)(w−b).\begin{aligned} \text{Expected impressions}&=NF(b),\\ \text{Expected incremental contribution}&=NF(b)w,\\ C_1(b)&=NF(b)b,\\ J_1(b)&=NF(b)(w-b). \end{aligned}Expected impressionsExpected incremental contributionC1​(b)J1​(b)​=NF(b),=NF(b)w,=NF(b)b,=NF(b)(w−b).​

    The factor w−bw-bw−b is the advertiser's expected gain on one won impression. The factor NF(b)NF(b)NF(b) is how many impressions it expects to buy. A larger bid buys more impressions but raises the price on every first-price win. We optimize their product because we have explicitly chosen advertiser contribution after cost as the objective.

    What a real objective still needs

    This example maximizes contribution, rather than revenue, attributed conversions or full budget use. A business may instead maximize conversion volume subject to a return target, or impose minimum scale and other obligations; those are different optimization problems. A real buying agent must include its actual fees in the advertiser's bill and use values that vary by opportunity. A negative estimated incremental value calls for not bidding when no delivery obligation forces participation. The calculations above are a transparent benchmark, not evidence of how Axon or any particular platform chooses its internal objective.

    For heterogeneous opportunities, write wiw_iwi​ for incremental contribution per successful impression on request iii, Fi(bi)F_i(b_i)Fi​(bi​) for its win probability, and Ci(bi)C_i(b_i)Ci​(bi​) for its unconditional expected all-in advertiser cost. With the same display-success and separability assumptions, the advertiser problem is:

    max⁡{bi≥0}∑i[wiFi(bi)−Ci(bi)]subject to∑iCi(bi)≤B.\max_{\{b_i\ge0\}}\sum_i\bigl[w_iF_i(b_i)-C_i(b_i)\bigr]\quad\text{subject to}\quad\sum_i C_i(b_i)\le B.{bi​≥0}max​i∑​[wi​Fi​(bi​)−Ci​(bi​)]subject toi∑​Ci​(bi​)≤B.

    A budget controller (pacing) adjusts participation or bids as spend and opportunity value evolve. It should preserve the stated advertiser objective, and need not force full spend when profitable opportunities run out. The next section gives the advertiser's multiplier and pacing rule. The appendix's numerical network multipliers cannot be copied into this advertiser contract.

    Beyond uniform prices: advertiser bidding and pacing

    The $4 CPM result uses a particular distribution. For a general continuous competitive threshold, let F(b)=P(Z≤b)F(b)=P(Z\le b)F(b)=P(Z≤b) be the win-probability function and f(b)=F′(b)f(b)=F'(b)f(b)=F′(b) its density. Define j1(b)j_1(b)j1​(b) and j2(b)j_2(b)j2​(b) as advertiser incremental contribution after cost per request, under first and ideal second price.

    j1(b)=(w−b)F(b),j1′(b)=(w−b)f(b)−F(b),j2(b)=∫0b(w−z)f(z) dz,j2′(b)=(w−b)f(b).\begin{aligned} j_1(b)&=(w-b)F(b),& j_1'(b)&=(w-b)f(b)-F(b),\\ j_2(b)&=\int_0^b(w-z)f(z)\,dz,& j_2'(b)&=(w-b)f(b). \end{aligned}j1​(b)j2​(b)​=(w−b)F(b),=∫0b​(w−z)f(z)dz,​j1′​(b)j2′​(b)​=(w−b)f(b)−F(b),=(w−b)f(b).​

    The integration variable zzz is a possible competing price. In first price, an interior candidate with f(b)>0f(b)>0f(b)>0 satisfies b=w−F(b)/f(b)b=w-F(b)/f(b)b=w−F(b)/f(b); boundaries and the global objective still need checking. The reduction from value to bid is bid shading: accepting fewer wins to pay less per win. It depends on the price distribution. For uniform thresholds F/f=bF/f=bF/f=b, giving b=w/2b=w/2b=w/2. If the threshold is instead the maximum of two independent uniform bids on [0,L][0,L][0,L], then F=(b/L)2F=(b/L)^2F=(b/L)2 and F/f=b/2F/f=b/2F/f=b/2, so the first-price optimum for our w=0.008w=0.008w=0.008 is 2w/3=$0.0053333…2w/3=\$0.0053333\ldots2w/3=$0.0053333… ($5.3333 CPM). The objective rises then falls around this point.

Thus bidding www is optimal if that bid is allowed; it need not be uniquely optimal when the threshold distribution has gaps. This argument assumes one slot and the stated payment rule. Auctions with multiple ranked slots, quality weights, extra fees or other constraints need their own model.

    The advertiser's budget multiplier

    Let μA≥0\mu_A\ge0μA​≥0 be the advertiser's budget multiplier; subscript AAA identifies this advertiser contract. For a request with unconditional expected ad cost c(b)c(b)c(b), adding the spend constraint to the contribution objective gives the per-request expression wF(b)−(1+μA)c(b)wF(b)-(1+\mu_A)c(b)wF(b)−(1+μA​)c(b). The 1 accounts for the cash cost itself; μA\mu_AμA​ adds the cost of scarce budget. At a regular optimum, this dimensionless multiplier is the marginal gain in advertiser contribution-after-cost per extra dollar of budget.

    First price, interior candidate:b=w1+μA−F(b)f(b),Ideal second price:b=w1+μA.\begin{aligned} \text{First price, interior candidate:}\quad b&=\frac{w}{1+\mu_A}-\frac{F(b)}{f(b)},\\ \text{Ideal second price:}\quad b&=\frac{w}{1+\mu_A}. \end{aligned}First price, interior candidate:bIdeal second price:b​=1+μA​w​−f(b)F(b)​,=1+μA​w​.​

    These are interior conditions under the same density and boundary qualifications. For uniform first price the expression reduces to b=w/[2(1+μA)]b=w/[2(1+\mu_A)]b=w/[2(1+μA​)]. At our binding $500 cap, first price gives μA=w/(2b1∗)−1≈0.2649\mu_A=w/(2b_1^*)-1\approx0.2649μA​=w/(2b1∗​)−1≈0.2649, while ideal second price gives μA=w/b2∗−1≈0.7889\mu_A=w/b_2^*-1\approx0.7889μA​=w/b2∗​−1≈0.7889. At $2,000 both caps are slack and μA=0\mu_A=0μA​=0. These are advertiser multipliers, distinct from the appendix's network multipliers.

    Pacing keeps the objective while controlling spend over time

    Pacing is online control of how quickly money is spent. Let ttt index control periods, ctc_tct​ be actual advertiser spend in that period, sts_tst​ its desired spend trajectory, and η>0\eta>0η>0 a step size in 1/dollar. A simple illustrative update is:

    μA,t+1=max⁡{0,μA,t+η(ct−st)}.\mu_{A,t+1}=\max\{0,\mu_{A,t}+\eta(c_t-s_t)\}.μA,t+1​=max{0,μA,t​+η(ct​−st​)}.

    Overspending raises the multiplier and lowers bids; underspending lowers it, but never below zero. The zero boundary matters: bids can return to the advertiser-profit optimum without being forced beyond it just to spend money. For example, split our million opportunities into ten equal periods. At the $2,000 cap, a flat target is $200 per period, while the $4 CPM first-price optimum spends only $80 per period. Starting at zero, the multiplier stays at zero and the day spends $800, preserving the advertiser's optimum.

    This update illustrates control direction, not a stability or hard-budget guarantee. Delayed bills, traffic changes and interactions can produce oscillations; target trajectories should adapt to remaining budget and opportunity value. Actual hard spending caps require the reservation and settlement mechanisms in Chapter 5. The appendix retains a longer pacing simulation for the network's different objective as an optional extension.

    Define the event the model predicts

    Let xxx be the information available when the bid is placed (user, context, ad slot and ad). Define three indicators: S=1S=1S=1 if the impression succeeds; K=1K=1K=1 if the user clicks; Y=1Y=1Y=1 if a qualifying conversion occurs within the agreed observation window (the period after the ad in which a conversion counts, for example 7 days); each is 0 otherwise. The Chapter 1 CPA contract (checked above and used in the appendix) bills post-click attributed purchases, so a billable event requires K=1K=1K=1 and Y=1Y=1Y=1. The billable conversion probability per successful impression is

    q(x)=P(K=1,Y=1∣x,S=1)=P(K=1∣x,S=1)⋅P(Y=1∣K=1,x,S=1).q(x)=P(K=1,Y=1\mid x,S=1)=P(K=1\mid x,S=1)\cdot P(Y=1\mid K=1,x,S=1).q(x)=P(K=1,Y=1∣x,S=1)=P(K=1∣x,S=1)⋅P(Y=1∣K=1,x,S=1).

    This is the chain rule; it does not assume clicks and conversions are independent. If the contract also counts view-through conversions (conversions after an impression without a click), add the qualifying K=0K=0K=0 branch. CTR (click-through rate) is clicks per impression, and pCTR is a model's predicted CTR. CVR (conversion rate) and pCVR are the observed and predicted conversion rates (Chapter 2). Always state the denominator: P(Y=1∣K=1,x,S=1)P(Y=1\mid K=1,x,S=1)P(Y=1∣K=1,x,S=1) is per click, while q(x)q(x)q(x) is per successful impression. If a model already predicts conversions per impression, do not multiply by CTR again.

    When q(x)q(x)q(x) feeds the CPA billing model in the appendix, we also assume that, given xxx and a successful impression, response probabilities do not depend on the bid bbb or the competitive threshold ZZZ (defined in the threshold section). Failed displays produce no conversions. The expected number of billable conversions from one bid request, before we know whether we win, is therefore F(b) ρ q(x)F(b)\,\rho\,q(x)F(b)ρq(x), where F(b)F(b)F(b) is the win probability and ρ=P(S=1∣win)\rho=P(S=1\mid\text{win})ρ=P(S=1∣win) the display success rate. q(x)q(x)q(x) itself is not a per-request probability.

    For a network paid per billable conversion at settlement price aaa, v(x)=q(x) av(x)=q(x)\,av(x)=q(x)a is the expected revenue per successful impression. With this chapter's teaching values q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005 and a=$30a=\$30a=$30, v=$0.015v=\$0.015v=$0.015. For the advertiser's direct-buying objective, the value is instead w(x)=Δq(x)gw(x)=\Delta q(x)gw(x)=Δq(x)g, where Δq(x)\Delta q(x)Δq(x) is causal purchase-probability lift per successful display at information xxx and ggg is contribution per additional order. Attribution probability q(x)q(x)q(x) alone does not identify that lift. Response prediction, value prediction and incrementality (uplift) prediction have different targets.

    Model metrics. Positives are samples in which the target event occurred; negatives are samples in which it did not. AUC (area under the ROC curve) is the probability that a randomly drawn positive scores higher than a randomly drawn negative, with ties counting one half. It measures ranking, not whether the probability values are right. A model is calibrated if, among samples predicted at probability ppp, the observed frequency is ppp once their labels have matured, i.e., once the observation window has closed and late conversions are counted.

    Log loss scores probabilistic predictions. For a label y∈{0,1}y\in\{0,1\}y∈{0,1} and predicted probability p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1)p∈(0,1), the per-sample loss is −[yln⁡p+(1−y)ln⁡(1−p)]-\bigl[y\ln p+(1-y)\ln(1-p)\bigr]−[ylnp+(1−y)ln(1−p)]; a lower average over a fixed evaluation set is better. The score depends on the evaluation sample, the label definition and any sample weights, and it does not substitute for delivery profit.

    What each stage of the model pipeline does

    Candidate retrieval narrows the eligible ads to the few worth scoring; ranking then estimates response and value for that smaller set; finally, value estimates, budgets, eligibility rules and the auction rules produce the decision. If retrieval drops a high-value ad, no downstream model can recover it, so improving ranking AUC alone may never touch the system's main bottleneck. Meta's Andromeda, described publicly in 2024, shows staged retrieval followed by ranking. It is one industrial example, not a claim about every platform or about Axon's current architecture (Chapter 6). Meta 2024 Andromeda

    Ad features typically describe the advertiser and campaign (an advertiser's unit of budget, targeting and goal), the creative (the actual image, video or text shown), the ad slot, the user or context, past interactions and time. What matters is not the feature list but whether each feature is available at decision time, permitted for use, stably covered, and identical in meaning in training and serving. New ads and creatives have no feedback history, so the model must rely on transferable content and context features, and a controlled exploration budget must buy them impressions. Otherwise past winners keep accumulating labels and new candidates never get the chance to prove themselves.

    For post-click conversion, ESMM (Entire Space Multi-Task Model) trains on all impressions using the chain impression → click → conversion: it is supervised on click labels (pCTR) and click-and-convert labels (pCTCVR = pCTR × pCVR), so its pCVR tower is fitted over all impressions without ever dividing one estimate by another. This addresses sample selection bias: a CVR model trained only on clicked samples is applied to all impressions. ESMM does not by itself fix selection bias created by the serving policy (data logged under one policy used to learn or evaluate another), delayed feedback (conversions that arrive after the label is read), or causal identification. Original ESMM paper

    Accept a model only after checking ranking, calibration, stability across segments and business outcomes together. AUC measures one property of ranking, but bidding needs absolute probabilities, because value is a probability times a price. Doubling every predicted probability (while staying at or below 1) leaves ranking and AUC unchanged; under linear value bidding with a fixed coefficient and no cap, it also doubles every bid. Good overall calibration does not imply calibration on slices such as expensive publishers, new users or one country. Google's 2013 industrial paper already treated sampling, calibration and confidence as system problems; a larger model does not make them disappear. If negatives were downsampled for training, predicted probabilities must be corrected back to the true base rate (Chapter 4 gives the formula). Google click prediction paper

    Learning the auction prices needed by the bidder

    The main advertiser model assumed the threshold distribution was known. The following explains how auction feedback constrains learning it. A censored price is only known to lie in an interval. A likelihood is the probability or density the model assigns to the observed data; independent log-likelihood terms add.

    Why price feedback cannot be used directly as a regression label

    In ideal second-price, let ZZZ be the competitive threshold, bbb the logged bid and xxx the decision-time information, with conditional CDF F(z∣x)F(z\mid x)F(z∣x) and density f(z∣x)f(z\mid x)f(z∣x). Assume a win reveals ZZZ (it is the price paid), while a loss reveals only Z>bZ>bZ>b. Winning prices are selected by the policy: they are exactly the thresholds that fell below our bids. A regression fitted directly to winning prices therefore misses the high-price tail and underestimates the threshold. Let ℓ\ellℓ be the log-likelihood (natural log) and “win” and “loss” the sets of won and lost requests; each term uses that request's own ZZZ, bbb and xxx. For conditionally independent requests the censored log-likelihood is

    ℓ=∑winlog⁡f(Z∣x)+∑losslog⁡(1−F(b∣x)).\ell= \sum_{\mathrm{win}}\log f(Z\mid x) +\sum_{\mathrm{loss}}\log\bigl(1-F(b\mid x)\bigr).ℓ=win∑​logf(Z∣x)+loss∑​log(1−F(b∣x)).

    Each won request contributes the density at its observed threshold; each lost request contributes the probability that the threshold exceeded its bid. This is valid only if wins and losses are determined purely by the price comparison, and if, once the price-relevant policy history used for bidding is included in the logged xxx, the bid carries no further information about the threshold: P(Z≤z∣x,b)=F(z∣x)P(Z\le z\mid x,b)=F(z\mid x)P(Z≤z∣x,b)=F(z∣x) (non-informative censoring). If the policy used unlogged, price-relevant information, the observation model must be extended. Timeouts, creative rejections, budget filtering and users leaving the page are not “the market price exceeded the bid” and must not be coded as such losses. The price-distribution chapter of the RTB monograph is a good entry point to the censoring problem. RTB monograph, Chapter 3

    In first-price, our payment bbb is not the competitive threshold; on a win it is only an upper bound on it. With win/loss feedback alone, a win tells us Z≤bZ\le bZ≤b and a loss tells us Z>bZ>bZ>b, so every observation is censored and the log-likelihood becomes

    ℓ=∑winlog⁡F(b∣x)+∑losslog⁡(1−F(b∣x)).\ell= \sum_{\mathrm{win}}\log F(b\mid x) +\sum_{\mathrm{loss}}\log\bigl(1-F(b\mid x)\bigr).ℓ=win∑​logF(b∣x)+loss∑​log(1−F(b∣x)).

    This is a binary-response likelihood for the win probability. Without a parametric model it identifies FFF only at the bids actually placed, so learning the whole distribution requires variation in bbb. It is never valid to label your own winning bid as the competitors' price. Some exchanges return extra signals (for example, the minimum bid that would have won), so check the actual interface.

    Optional appendix: network spread and conflicting incentives

    Optional appendix: a network maximizing spread under CPA billing

    Different decision-maker and contract

    This appendix asks how an intermediary maximizes its own media spread. It charges the advertiser $30 per billable attributed conversion and buys publisher impressions. Its per-impression value is v=qa=$0.015v=qa=\$0.015v=qa=$0.015, not the advertiser's w=Δqg=$0.008w=\Delta qg=\$0.008w=Δqg=$0.008. Its $2,000 budget limits publisher payments, not the advertiser's bill. Network-optimal bids of $7.50 or $6.3246 CPM below can coexist with advertiser losses. These values and objectives are not a description of Axon. Skip this appendix when first learning advertiser bidding.

    Follow the money through three ledgers

    Take the position of an ad network: a company that buys opportunities to show ads from publishers (owners of apps and websites with ad slots) and resells them to advertisers (businesses that want their ads shown). Three amounts are easy to conflate: what the network collects from advertisers, what it pays publishers, and what the advertiser earns from the sales the ads produce. Two published examples pin down the first two; then we add the advertiser's ledger. The billing units below are defined in Chapter 2 and restated here at first use.

    Step 1 · Who pays how much per 1,000 impressions?

    An impression is one display of an ad. CPM (cost per mille) quotes a price per 1,000 impressions, so $2 CPM means $0.002 per impression. In Epom's example the network buys publisher inventory (the publisher's supply of ad impressions) at $2 CPM and sells it to advertisers at $5 CPM, keeping a $3 CPM spread. Both sides are billed per impression. Source: Epom, “Ad arbitrage” section

    For every 1,000 impressions the network receives $5 and pays the publisher $2. The remaining $3 is the media spread, before servers, sales staff and other operating costs. The example says nothing about whether the advertiser's $5 bought enough business.

    Step 2 · What if the advertiser pays only per conversion?

    A conversion is an action the advertiser values, such as a purchase or an app install. CPC (cost per click) and CPA (cost per action) contracts bill the advertiser only when that click or action occurs, not per impression. Kevel's documentation uses 9,000 impressions, 18 billable events and $5 per event. Kevel allows the billable event to be a click or another action; we take the CPA reading and treat each event as a conversion that the contract recognizes. Source: Kevel, CPC/CPA worked example under “What Is eCPM?”

    eCPM (effective CPM) restates revenue earned under any contract as revenue per 1,000 impressions:

    QuestionCalculationAnswer
    How much does the advertiser pay in total?18 conversions × $5$90
    How much is collected per 1,000 impressions?$90 ÷ 9,000 × 1,000$10 eCPM

    The contract is still $5 per conversion. The $10 eCPM converts revenue already earned into a per-1,000-impression figure so it can be compared with the price paid for impressions. It does not turn the contract into a CPM contract, and it does not guarantee that the next 9,000 impressions will earn the same.

    Step 3 · Collect per conversion, pay per impression

    The following combined example is constructed for this reader; neither source describes this transaction. Keep Kevel's 9,000 impressions, 18 conversions and $5 CPA, and assume the network bought those impressions at Epom's $2 CPM.

    Whose ledgerCalculationAmount
    Advertiser's ad bill18 conversions × $5 CPAPays $90
    Publisher's ad revenue9,000 impressions ÷ 1,000 × $2 CPMReceives $18
    Network's media spread$90 collected − $18 paid to the publisherKeeps $72

    This is “buy per impression, sell per conversion.” The network pays for every impression it buys but is paid only when a contractual conversion occurs. If the same $18 of impressions yields only 2 conversions, the network collects $10 and loses $8. Conversion prediction tells the network which impressions are worth buying; it cannot make conversions happen.

    Step 4 · The network kept $72. Did the advertiser make money?

    We cannot tell yet. We know only that the advertiser spent $90. We do not know what each extra order is worth to the advertiser, or how many of the 18 recorded conversions the ad actually caused.

    Two terms separate these questions. A conversion is attributed to an ad when an agreed rule (for example, “purchase within 7 days of a click”) credits it to that ad; attribution decides what gets billed. A conversion is incremental if it would not have happened without the ad; incrementality decides what the advertiser actually gained. Teaching assumption: each incremental order leaves $8 of contribution, meaning revenue minus cost of goods, fulfillment and other variable costs, before ad spend. The bill and media cost stay as above:

    Assumed scenarioAdvertiser's calculationIncremental contribution after ad spend
    All 18 are incremental18 × $8 − $90+$54
    Only 9 are incremental9 × $8 − $90−$18

    In both scenarios the network bills $90 for 18 contractual conversions, pays the publisher $18 and keeps $72, yet the advertiser's outcomes have opposite signs. The attributed conversions used for billing are not the incremental conversions. Measuring the latter requires causal methods, covered in Chapter 4.

    The three ledgers are now separate. The publisher counts revenue from selling impressions; the network counts collections minus media cost; the advertiser counts incremental contribution minus the ad bill. That sets up the bidding question: for impressions not yet bought, how would the network bid if it maximized its own spread, and how could this differ from the advertiser’s choice?

    Appendix calculator: network spread, two contracts and delivery failures

    Network-spread derivation: the appendix calculator's default values

    These numbers are set by this reader, not taken from a published case. The closest published derivation is Section 3.2.1 of Zhang and Wang, “Statistical Arbitrage Mining for Display Advertising” (hereafter SAM; PDF page 4, printed page 1468). SAM derives optimal bids when competing prices are uniformly distributed, but it does not build the three-party ledger below. The model here is independent, and every line can be recomputed by hand.

    Reading order: who pays whom → try a $6 CPM bid → why the optimum is $6.3246 CPM → does the advertiser make money. The tables use the default parameters and do not respond to the sliders; the interactive calculator follows the derivation.

    1. Two contracts before any algorithm

    There are three parties: a merchant selling goods, an app that shows ads, and an ad network between them. “Platform” below means this ad network. Other intermediaries (exchanges and supply-side platforms, see Chapter 2) and their fees are left out so the money flows stay visible.

    RoleWhat it doesHow money is settled
    AdvertiserSells goods and wants ads to bring more ordersPays the platform $30 for each order the contract recognizes
    PublisherOwns the app's ad slots and sells opportunities to show adsAuctions each opportunity and receives media payments from the platform
    Ad network / platformBuys opportunities from the publisher and delivers the advertiser's adsCollects from the advertiser, pays the publisher, and keeps the difference, positive or negative

    Contract A: advertiser → platform, billed per order. In this example a conversion means placing an order and nothing else. A billable attributed conversion is an order that the attribution rule credits to one of the platform's impressions and that passes the contract's checks. We assume each such order is billed exactly once, in full.

    This is a CPA contract with settlement price a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per order. That is a fixed payment price. It differs from a target CPA (tCPA), where the system tries to keep the average acquisition cost near a target (Chapter 2). An order being attributed to an ad does not prove the ad caused it; step 5 quantifies the gap.

    Contract B: platform → publisher, impressions bought one auction at a time. An ad opportunity is one slot at one moment in which an ad could be shown. A bid request is the message in which the publisher (directly or through an exchange) invites bids on that opportunity. Each request is auctioned separately within milliseconds; that is what real-time bidding (RTB) means. To win is to be selected by the auction. A successful impression is the ad actually completing the display event defined in the contract. An ad can fail to load after a win, so the two events are kept separate.

    Bids are quoted in CPM: $6 CPM means $6 ÷ 1,000 = $0.006 per impression. Each auction still sells a single opportunity; a CPM quote does not buy 1,000 impressions at once. The default is a first-price auction: the winner pays its own bid. By default every win also yields a successful impression.

    Bid request → platform bids → win → successful impression
    → user may place an order → attribution rule confirms a billable order
    The publisher is paid under the procurement contract (B); the advertiser is billed separately under the order contract (A).

    2. Inputs and derived quantities

    Every row below is a given assumption. The calculator does not train a prediction model and does not infer the ad's causal effect from attributed orders.
