    Opportunities NNN1,000,000Bid requests received in one day. None has been won yet, so this is not the number of impressions bought.
    Platform media budget BBB$2,000Cap on the platform's expected spend on media (payments to the publisher). It does not limit the advertiser's bill.
    Billable conversion probability per impression qqq0.0005 = 0.05%Probability that one successful impression produces a billable order: 5 orders per 10,000 successful impressions. The denominator is impressions, not clicks.
    Settlement price aaa$30 per orderPaid by the advertiser to the platform. Not the product's selling price, and not the price paid to the publisher.
    Display success rate ρ\rhoρ (rho)1 = 100%Probability that a win becomes a successful impression. Display failures are switched off by default.
    Competitive threshold ZZZ, upper bound LLLZZZ between $0 and $20 CPM
    LLL = $20 CPM = $0.02 per billable event    		ZZZ is the highest competing bid in one auction, the price to beat. It varies across opportunities; its distribution is specified next. A billable event is whatever the publisher contract charges for: a successful impression by default, which equals a win when ρ=1\rho=1ρ=1.

    The main lesson derives the competitive-threshold win probability. We use the same distribution in this appendix.

    One more derived quantity is needed: the platform's expected revenue per successful impression, vvv. It follows from Contract A and is not a separate input:

    v=q a=0.0005×$30=$0.015 per impression.v=q\,a=0.0005\times\$30=\$0.015\ \text{per impression}.v=qa=0.0005×$30=$0.015 per impression.

    “Expected” means the average over many repetitions under the same conditions; orders come in whole numbers, but their expected count can be fractional. $0.015 per impression is $15 per 1,000 impressions, the platform's revenue eCPM. This is only a change of units; the contract still bills per order.

    One simplification holds throughout: qqq is the same for every opportunity and does not depend on ZZZ or bbb. If qqq and ZZZ were correlated (for example, because competitors also bid more for likely buyers), a higher bid would buy a different mix of users and a single qqq would no longer apply.

    Convert to b=$0.006b=\$0.006b=$0.006 per impression and multiply count × probability × price:

    4. Why the calculator bids $6.3246 CPM

    Now the optimization problem: the platform chooses one bid, used on every opportunity, to maximize expected media gross spread, subject to expected media cost of at most $2,000. The platform is risk-neutral: it maximizes the expectation and ignores variance. “Optimal” is relative to this objective; the advertiser's profit is not in it. Because all opportunities are identical, spread is concave and cost convex in the bid (shown below), a single common bid is optimal; varying bids across identical opportunities cannot help.

    Extension A: why does the formula change under “ideal second-price”?

    An ideal second-price auction charges the winner the competitive threshold ZZZ instead of its own bid bbb; floor prices, bid increments and fees are ignored. If you bid $6 CPM and the highest competing bid is $4 CPM, first-price charges $6 CPM and ideal second-price charges $4 CPM. You win either way; only the payment differs.

    For a fixed bbb the win rate is still b/Lb/Lb/L. Conditional on winning, Z∼Uniform(0,b)Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,b)Z∼Uniform(0,b), so the expected payment per win is E[Z∣Z≤b]=b/2\mathbb E[Z\mid Z\le b]=b/2E[Z∣Z≤b]=b/2. With the default ρ=1\rho=1ρ=1:

    C(b)=N⋅bL⋅b2=Nb22L,M(b)=NL(vb−b22),M′(b)=NL (v−b),M′′(b)=−NL<0.\begin{aligned} C(b)&=N\cdot\frac{b}{L}\cdot\frac{b}{2}=\frac{Nb^2}{2L},\\ M(b)&=\frac{N}{L}\Bigl(vb-\frac{b^2}{2}\Bigr),\qquad M'(b)=\frac{N}{L}\,(v-b),\qquad M''(b)=-\frac{N}{L}<0. \end{aligned}C(b)M(b)​=N⋅Lb​⋅2b​=2LNb2​,=LN​(vb−2b2​),M′(b)=LN​(v−b),M′′(b)=−LN​<0.​

    Ignoring the budget, the best bid is b0=vb_0=vb0​=v: bid your value, the familiar truthful-bidding result for second-price auctions. Then apply the budget and the price range:

    b∗=min⁡{v, 2BLN, L}=min⁡{0.015, 0.0089443…, 0.02} → $8.9443 CPM.b^*=\min\Bigl\{v,\ \sqrt{\frac{2BL}{N}},\ L\Bigr\}=\min\{0.015,\ 0.0089443\ldots,\ 0.02\}\ \to\ \$8.9443\ \text{CPM}.b∗=min{v, N2BL​​, L}=min{0.015, 0.0089443…, 0.02} → $8.9443 CPM.

    With the same $2,000 budget, the win rate is about 44.72%, the advertiser bill $6,708.20, the platform gross spread $4,708.20 and the advertiser incremental contribution profit −$3,130.50. The Lagrangian condition is now b=v/(1+μ)b=v/(1+\mu)b=v/(1+μ), so the budget's shadow price rises to μ=v/b∗−1≈0.677\mu=v/b^*-1\approx0.677μ=v/b∗−1≈0.677. More impressions mean more attributed orders billed; with these loss-making parameters the advertiser loses more.

    The comparison holds the threshold distribution and the other inputs fixed, not the advertiser bill. In reality a change of auction rule also changes competitors' bids, so this is not a prediction of market-level outcomes.

    Extension B: are failed displays billed? Compute a 50% success rate first, then the full formula

    ρ\rhoρ is the probability that a win becomes a successful impression. At ρ\rhoρ = 50%, on average 50 of every 100 wins produce an impression. Revenue comes only from orders after successful impressions; media cost depends on the publisher contract.

    Fix a first-price bid of $6 CPM without re-optimizing. It still wins 300,000 times, but only 150,000 impressions succeed, so collections are 150,000 × 0.0005 × $30 = $2,250.

    Publisher contractMedia costPlatform gross spread
    Display-based: billed only for successful impressions150,000 × $0.006 = $900$2,250 − $900 = $1,350
    Win-based: billed on every win300,000 × $0.006 = $1,800$2,250 − $1,800 = $450

    Under win-based billing, failed displays also cost money, so the re-optimized bid is lower. Both contracts are teaching settings for this calculator.

    To cover all four combinations with one formula, introduce two pieces of notation; they are not new parameters to estimate:

    • α\alphaα (alpha), the media billing coefficient: the probability that a win is billed. α=ρ\alpha=\rhoα=ρ under display-based billing; α=1\alpha=1α=1 under win-based billing.
    • kkk, the auction payment coefficient: k=1k=1k=1 for first-price and k=2k=2k=2 for ideal second-price, so the expected price per billed event is b/kb/kb/k. It is not a fee rate, and it is unrelated to the click indicator KKK defined earlier in “Define the event the model predicts”.

    Assume display success is independent of ZZZ, so conditioning on a successful display does not change the expected payment per win. Then

    D=N bL ρ,C=N bL α bk=Nαb2kL,A=D q a=D v,M=NL(ρvb−αb2k).\begin{aligned} D&=N\,\frac{b}{L}\,\rho, & C&=N\,\frac{b}{L}\,\alpha\,\frac{b}{k}=\frac{N\alpha b^2}{kL},\\ A&=D\,q\,a=D\,v, & M&=\frac{N}{L}\Bigl(\rho vb-\frac{\alpha b^2}{k}\Bigr). \end{aligned}DA​=NLb​ρ,=Dqa=Dv,​CM​=NLb​αkb​=kLNαb2​,=LN​(ρvb−kαb2​).​

    Setting M′(b)=NL(ρv−2αb/k)=0M'(b)=\frac{N}{L}\bigl(\rho v-2\alpha b/k\bigr)=0M′(b)=LN​(ρv−2αb/k)=0 gives the budget-free bid b0=kρv/(2α)b_0=k\rho v/(2\alpha)b0​=kρv/(2α), a maximum because M′′(b)=−2Nα/(kL)<0M''(b)=-2N\alpha/(kL)<0M′′(b)=−2Nα/(kL)<0. Solving C≤BC\le BC≤B gives the budget cap. Together they form the calculator's complete formula:

    b∗=min⁡{kρv2α, kBLNα, L},advertiser incremental contribution profit=D (Δq g−q a).\begin{aligned} b^*&=\min\Bigl\{\frac{k\rho v}{2\alpha},\ \sqrt{\frac{kBL}{N\alpha}},\ L\Bigr\},\\ \text{advertiser incremental contribution profit}&=D\,(\Delta q\,g-q\,a). \end{aligned}b∗advertiser incremental contribution profit​=min{2αkρv​, NαkBL​​, L},=D(Δqg−qa).​

    The ρ\rhoρ slider covers 50%–100%, so α>0\alpha>0α>0. At ρ\rhoρ = 50% with the $2,000 budget and first-price, re-optimizing gives: under display-based billing (α=ρ\alpha=\rhoα=ρ, so ρ\rhoρ cancels in b0b_0b0​), b∗b^*b∗ = $7.50 CPM and media cost $1,406.25; under win-based billing (α=1\alpha=1α=1), b∗b^*b∗ = $3.75 CPM and media cost $703.13 (exactly $703.125). Neither budget binds. These are re-optimized bids, a different exercise from the fixed-$6 comparison above.

    Sources: what comes from the paper, and what this reader added

    SAM, Section 3.2.1, Equations 15–20 analyzes uniformly distributed competing prices and the resulting optimal bids. SAM's rrr (reward per conversion), θ\thetaθ (conversion probability) and lll (price upper bound) correspond to aaa, qqq and LLL here. SAM's symbols are not used anywhere else in this chapter.

    One difference matters. SAM's Equation 2 (Section 3) is set in a second-price auction and uses the bid as an upper bound on cost. This reader's default is first-price, where the winner pays exactly its bid; Extension A computes the actual expected second-price payment. The expressions look alike, but the models differ.

    Section 5.4 of Wang, Zhang and Yuan, “Display Advertising with Real-Time Bidding and Behavioural Targeting” (hereafter the RTB monograph), frames this class of optimization across billing schemes. The single advertiser, fixed conversion probability, specific numbers, display-failure contracts, incrementality and advertiser ledger here are assumptions this reader added to expose the mechanism, not experimental results from the literature.

    The model shows how contracts can pull the parties' objectives apart. It ignores differences in value across users and the fall in conversion probability as volume scales, so it cannot be used to judge a real platform's take rate, profitability or scaling limits.

    First-price and second-price auctions cost different amounts

    This restates the main-line auction argument for a different objective: the network uses its CPA receipts vvv in place of advertiser incremental contribution www.

    The following simplified decision model is original to this reader; by default every win yields a successful impression. Let Z≥0Z\ge0Z≥0 be the competitive threshold, the highest competing bid, which we must meet or beat to win; b≥0b\ge0b≥0 our bid; and v≥0v\ge0v≥0 the expected monetary value of winning and being shown. We win if and only if b≥Zb\ge Zb≥Z; ties have probability zero in this continuous model. For fixed xxx, F(b∣x)=P(Z≤b∣x)F(b\mid x)=P(Z\le b\mid x)F(b∣x)=P(Z≤b∣x) is the conditional CDF of the threshold, i.e., the win rate at bid bbb, and f(z∣x)=∂F(z∣x)/∂zf(z\mid x)=\partial F(z\mid x)/\partial zf(z∣x)=∂F(z∣x)/∂z is its density. From here on we fix xxx and drop it, writing F(b)F(b)F(b) and f(b)f(b)f(b); in integrals zzz denotes a value of ZZZ and dF(z)=f(z) dzdF(z)=f(z)\,dzdF(z)=f(z)dz.

    Bids, values and payments are in dollars per won-and-displayed opportunity; multiply by 1,000 for a CPM interface. Assumptions: the bidder is risk-neutral, maximizing expected net profit; given xxx, vvv does not depend on ZZZ; one bid does not change later responses; there are no fees, ties or dynamic feedback; and there is no budget yet. Let π1(b)\pi_1(b)π1​(b) and π2(b)\pi_2(b)π2​(b) be the expected net profit per request under first-price and second-price, counting zero revenue and zero cost on a loss; primes denote derivatives in bbb. Formulas containing F/fF/fF/f apply only to interior candidates with f(b)>0f(b)>0f(b)>0; the allowed bid range, its boundaries and the global optimum must still be checked.

    In a first-price auction the winner pays its own bid. Expected net profit per request is

    π1(b)=(v−b)F(b),π1′(b)=(v−b)f(b)−F(b).\pi_1(b)=(v-b)F(b),\qquad \pi_1'(b)=(v-b)f(b)-F(b).π1​(b)=(v−b)F(b),π1′​(b)=(v−b)f(b)−F(b).

    An interior optimum therefore satisfies

    b=v−F(b)f(b).b=v-\frac{F(b)}{f(b)}.b=v−f(b)F(b)​.

    This is an implicit equation, not a fixed discount. The gap F(b)/f(b)F(b)/f(b)F(b)/f(b) is the bid shading: bidding below value trades a lower payment per win against fewer wins. The second-order condition is π1′′(b)=−2f(b)+(v−b)f′(b)<0\pi_1''(b)=-2f(b)+(v-b)f'(b)<0π1′′​(b)=−2f(b)+(v−b)f′(b)<0 at the candidate. A convenient sufficient condition for a unique global maximum is that F/fF/fF/f is nondecreasing (FFF log-concave): then π1′(b)=f(b)[(v−b)−F(b)/f(b)]\pi_1'(b)=f(b)\bigl[(v-b)-F(b)/f(b)\bigr]π1′​(b)=f(b)[(v−b)−F(b)/f(b)] changes sign once, from positive to negative. The optimum always lies in [0,v][0,v][0,v], because any b>vb>vb>v earns π1(b)≤0≤π1(0)\pi_1(b)\le0\le\pi_1(0)π1​(b)≤0≤π1​(0). For uniform thresholds F(b)/f(b)=bF(b)/f(b)=bF(b)/f(b)=b, so b=v/2b=v/2b=v/2. That halving is a property of the uniform, not of first price:

    Worked example

    First-price bid when the threshold is the higher of two bids

    Given: value v=$0.015v=\$0.015v=$0.015 per impression ($15 CPM); two competitors whose bids are independent and each Uniform(0,L)\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Uniform(0,L) with L=$0.02L=\$0.02L=$0.02 per impression, so the threshold ZZZ is the larger of the two; first price; no budget.

    1. Threshold distribution. We win when both competing bids are at most bbb, so F(b)=(b/L)2F(b)=(b/L)^2F(b)=(b/L)2, f(b)=2b/L2f(b)=2b/L^2f(b)=2b/L2 and F(b)/f(b)=b/2F(b)/f(b)=b/2F(b)/f(b)=b/2 (uniform: bbb). log⁡F=2log⁡b−2log⁡L\log F=2\log b-2\log LlogF=2logb−2logL is concave, so the first-order condition has one root and it is the global maximum.
    2. First-order condition: b=v−F(b)f(b)=v−b2 ⟹ b=2v3,b=v-\frac{F(b)}{f(b)}=v-\frac{b}{2}\ \Longrightarrow\ b=\frac{2v}{3},b=v−f(b)F(b)​=v−2b​ ⟹ b=32v​, so b=2×0.015/3=$0.010b=2\times0.015/3=\$0.010b=2×0.015/3=$0.010 per impression.
    3. Win rate F(0.010)=(0.010/0.02)2=0.25F(0.010)=(0.010/0.02)^2=0.25F(0.010)=(0.010/0.02)2=0.25; expected profit per request π1=(0.015−0.010)×0.25=$0.00125\pi_1=(0.015-0.010)\times0.25=\$0.00125π1​=(0.015−0.010)×0.25=$0.00125.
    4. The uniform rule b=v/2b=v/2b=v/2 applied to this market instead: F(0.0075)=(0.0075/0.02)2=0.140625F(0.0075)=(0.0075/0.02)^2=0.140625F(0.0075)=(0.0075/0.02)2=0.140625 and π1=0.0075×0.140625=$0.00105469\pi_1=0.0075\times0.140625=\$0.00105469π1​=0.0075×0.140625=$0.00105469.

    Result: bid $10 CPM, shading one third of value instead of one half. Over 1,000,000 requests that earns $1,250; bidding $7.50 CPM earns $1,054.69, 15.6% less.

    Check: neighbouring bids do worse: $9 CPM gives 0.006 × 0.2025 = $0.001215 and $11 CPM gives 0.004 × 0.3025 = $0.00121 per request. With JJJ such competitors F=(b/L)JF=(b/L)^JF=(b/L)J and b=Jv/(J+1)b=Jv/(J+1)b=Jv/(J+1): more competition, less shading. Under ideal second price the optimum stays b=vb=vb=v whatever FFF is.

    In an ideal second-price auction the winner pays the threshold. Expected net profit per request is

    π2(b)=∫0b(v−z) dF(z),π2′(b)=(v−b)f(b).\pi_2(b)=\int_0^b(v-z)\,dF(z),\qquad \pi_2'(b)=(v-b)f(b).π2​(b)=∫0b​(v−z)dF(z),π2′​(b)=(v−b)f(b).

    π2′≥0\pi_2'\ge0π2′​≥0 for b<vb<vb<v and π2′≤0\pi_2'\le0π2′​≤0 for b>vb>vb>v, so under the assumptions above b=vb=vb=v is optimal (truthful bidding) whenever bidding vvv is allowed. If the threshold has no probability mass near vvv, nearby bids do equally well and the optimum is not unique. This does not mean every ad system should bid truthfully. GSP (generalized second-price auction) sells several ranked slots with different position values, and mechanisms with quality scores (multipliers that weight bids by predicted ad quality) must be modeled under their own rules. Real transactions also involve floor prices, fees, discrete bid increments and internal auctions (an intermediary first runs its own auction among its advertisers, then bids externally with the winner). Google Ad Exchange announced its move to first-price auctions in 2019, which is enough to show that second-price textbooks are not an operating manual for current markets. Google first-price migration announcement

    The budget-free optimum in the shared example

    Let the threshold be Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L), independent of response probabilities and identically distributed across requests, so F(b)=b/LF(b)=b/LF(b)=b/L for 0≤b≤L0\le b\le L0≤b≤L.

    Worked example

    Budget-free first-price bid

    Given: NNN = 1,000,000 bid requests; L=$0.02L=\$0.02L=$0.02 per impression; billable conversion probability q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005 per impression; settlement price a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per conversion; first price; every win is displayed; no budget.

    1. Value per impression: v=q a=0.0005×$30=$0.015v=q\,a=0.0005\times\$30=\$0.015v=qa=0.0005×$30=$0.015.
    2. Expected profit per request and its maximizer: π1(b)=(v−b)bL,π1′(b)=v−2bL.\pi_1(b)=(v-b)\frac{b}{L},\quad \pi_1'(b)=\frac{v-2b}{L}.π1​(b)=(v−b)Lb​,π1′​(b)=Lv−2b​. Setting π1′=0\pi_1'=0π1′​=0 gives b0=v/2=$0.0075b_0=v/2=\$0.0075b0​=v/2=$0.0075 per impression, a maximum since π1′′=−2/L<0\pi_1''=-2/L<0π1′′​=−2/L<0.
    3. Volume: F(b0)=0.0075/0.02=0.375F(b_0)=0.0075/0.02=0.375F(b0​)=0.0075/0.02=0.375, so 1,000,000 × 0.375 = 375,000 expected wins and 375,000 × 0.0005 = 187.5 attributed conversions.
    4. Ledgers: collections 187.5 × $30 = $5,625; media cost 375,000 × $0.0075 = $2,812.50; gross spread $5,625 − $2,812.50 = $2,812.50.

    Result: bid $7.50 CPM; expected gross spread $2,812.50, before infrastructure, channel fees, operations, bad debt and cost of capital.

    Check: closed form Nπ1(v/2)=Nv2/(4L)=106×0.0152/0.08=$2,812.50N\pi_1(v/2)=Nv^2/(4L)=10^6\times0.015^2/0.08=\$2{,}812.50Nπ1​(v/2)=Nv2/(4L)=106×0.0152/0.08=$2,812.50. Cost equals spread at the optimum because v−b=bv-b=bv−b=b at b=v/2b=v/2b=v/2, a uniform-specific coincidence.

    The advertiser's ledger is more revealing. Assume, as in the optional derivation, a contribution of g=$40g=\$40g=$40 per order and a true incremental conversion probability of Δq=0.0002\Delta q=0.0002Δq=0.0002 per impression (the order probability with the ad minus without it). Counting every attributed conversion as worth $40 gives 187.5 × $40 − $5,625 = $1,875, which looks profitable. Counting only incremental orders gives 375,000 × 0.0002 = 75 orders and 75 × $40 − $5,625 = −$2,625. The intermediary can make money while its customer loses money. If the gap persists, it eventually erodes the customer's budgets, renewals and the intermediary's pricing power.

    Write the two budget objectives separately

    Index the bid requests in the planning period by iii. For request iii, bib_ibi​ is the bid, viv_ivi​ the expected value of winning and being shown, FiF_iFi​ the threshold CDF, and Ci(bi)C_i(b_i)Ci​(bi​) the expected media cost of the request, counting zero spend on a loss. BBB is the total media budget for the period. Sums run over all requests; “s.t.” means “subject to.” Note that Ci(b)C_i(b)Ci​(b) is a per-request cost, whereas CCC in the optional calculator is the total over requests.

    Per request, expected cost is C(b)=b F(b)C(b)=b\,F(b)C(b)=bF(b) under first-price and C(b)=∫0bz dF(z)C(b)=\int_0^b z\,dF(z)C(b)=∫0b​zdF(z) under ideal second-price. To maximize total value within the budget:

    max⁡bi∑iviFi(bi)s.t.∑iCi(bi)≤B.\max_{b_i}\sum_i v_iF_i(b_i) \quad\text{s.t.}\quad \sum_i C_i(b_i)\le B.bi​max​i∑​vi​Fi​(bi​)s.t.i∑​Ci​(bi​)≤B.

    Attach a multiplier λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0 to the budget constraint. The Lagrangian separates across requests, with per-request term v F(b)−λ C(b)v\,F(b)-\lambda\,C(b)vF(b)−λC(b) (subscript dropped). λ\lambdaλ is measured in value dollars per budget dollar. Under the usual regularity conditions it is the shadow price of the budget: the increase in optimal total value per extra budget dollar. Using C′(b)=F(b)+b f(b)C'(b)=F(b)+b\,f(b)C′(b)=F(b)+bf(b) for first-price and C′(b)=b f(b)C'(b)=b\,f(b)C′(b)=bf(b) for second-price, the interior first-order conditions with λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 and f(b)>0f(b)>0f(b)>0 are

    Second-price:b=vλ,First-price:b=vλ−F(b)f(b).\text{Second-price:}\quad b=\frac{v}{\lambda}, \qquad \text{First-price:}\quad b=\frac{v}{\lambda}-\frac{F(b)}{f(b)}.Second-price:b=λv​,First-price:b=λv​−f(b)F(b)​.

    To maximize net profit under the same budget instead, solve max⁡bi∑i[viFi(bi)−Ci(bi)]\max_{b_i}\sum_i\bigl[v_iF_i(b_i)-C_i(b_i)\bigr]maxbi​​∑i​[vi​Fi​(bi​)−Ci​(bi​)] s.t. ∑iCi(bi)≤B\sum_i C_i(b_i)\le B∑i​Ci​(bi​)≤B. The per-request term becomes v F(b)−(1+μ) C(b)v\,F(b)-(1+\mu)\,C(b)vF(b)−(1+μ)C(b), where μ≥0\mu\ge0μ≥0 is the budget multiplier for this objective: the 1 stands for the cost itself and μ\muμ for the extra cost of budget scarcity. Under the same interior conditions:

    Second-price:b=v1+μ,First-price:b=v1+μ−F(b)f(b).\text{Second-price:}\quad b=\frac{v}{1+\mu}, \qquad \text{First-price:}\quad b=\frac{v}{1+\mu}-\frac{F(b)}{f(b)}.Second-price:b=1+μv​,First-price:b=1+μv​−f(b)F(b)​.

    Complementary slackness, μ(∑iCi(bi)−B)=0\mu\bigl(\sum_i C_i(b_i)-B\bigr)=0μ(∑i​Ci​(bi​)−B)=0, pins down μ\muμ. A slack budget gives μ=0\mu=0μ=0, which recovers the budget-free profit optimum; otherwise μ\muμ is set so that expected spend equals BBB. In the uniform example with BBB = $2,000, μ≈0.186\mu\approx0.186μ≈0.186 under first-price and μ≈0.677\mu\approx0.677μ≈0.677 under second-price (worked examples in the next section).

    The difference between the objectives is economic, not notational. If both objectives exhaust the budget at the same bids, comparing the conditions gives λ=1+μ≥1\lambda=1+\mu\ge1λ=1+μ≥1. But a total-value bidder can end up with λ<1\lambda<1λ<1; its second-price bid v/λv/\lambdav/λ then exceeds vvv, so it knowingly buys impressions that cost more than they are worth, because its objective counts value, not profit. With a slack budget the total-value objective has no reason to economize at all: it buys every opportunity with positive value, and “set λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 in the division formula” is not a valid step. Budget constraints, ROAS constraints (a floor on return on ad spend; see Chapter 2) and CPA constraints (a cap on average cost per action) are also different problems. Transplanting multipliers between papers often produces strategies that look alike but mean different things.

    All of this optimizes expectations under a known threshold distribution. If the distribution is unknown, it must be learned; if only win/loss outcomes are observed, the problem changes again (see Learning the auction prices). Recent research on first-price bidding with budgets distinguishes these feedback regimes, and its guarantees do not automatically transfer to production markets. ICML 2023 first-price budget research

    How a $2,000 media budget changes the bid

    Keep the homogeneous teaching parameters (NNN = 1,000,000 requests, L=$0.02L=\$0.02L=$0.02, v=q a=$0.015v=q\,a=\$0.015v=qa=$0.015 per impression, every win displayed) and cap expected media spend at BBB = $2,000. The objective is still expected collections minus media cost. Both budget-free optima cost more than $2,000, so the budget binds under either rule:

The $2,000 media budget is not the denominator of the advertiser's ROAS; the advertiser's spend is its bill. When the table switches auction format, it holds the threshold distribution fixed only to compare payment rules. Real bidders would respond, so the table does not predict equilibrium outcomes under the two mechanisms.

    With the $2,000 budget the total-value objective also bids up to the cap, so the two objectives yield the same bid. More generally, suppose both objectives' optima exhaust the same budget BBB on the same feasible set. On the boundary ∑iCi=B\sum_i C_i=B∑i​Ci​=B, net profit equals total value minus the constant BBB, so both objectives select the same point on that boundary, even with heterogeneous opportunities. We make no claim about other tied optima off the boundary. This is not a general equivalence: a net-profit objective may deliberately underspend while a total-value objective keeps buying, and any change to the feasible set or the constraints requires solving again. The budget here also constrains expected spend only; realized requests and payments are random, and enforcing a hard cap on every realized path is a separate system responsibility.

    Budget pacing is online control, not even spending

    Pacing controls the rate of spend over time. The simplest illustrative update is

    μt+1=max⁡{0, μt+η (ct−st)}.\mu_{t+1}=\max\{0,\ \mu_t+\eta\,(c_t-s_t)\}.μt+1​=max{0, μt​+η(ct​−st​)}.

    Here ttt indexes control periods (for example, minutes). μt≥0\mu_t\ge0μt​≥0 is the budget multiplier in period ttt, not the bid; the bid is derived from it, for example b=v/(1+μt)b=v/(1+\mu_t)b=v/(1+μt​) under ideal second-price, or b=v/(1+μt)−F(b)/f(b)b=v/(1+\mu_t)-F(b)/f(b)b=v/(1+μt​)−F(b)/f(b) under first-price, which is v/(2(1+μt))v/\bigl(2(1+\mu_t)\bigr)v/(2(1+μt​)) for uniform thresholds. ctc_tct​ is actual spend and sts_tst​ target spend in period ttt. The step size η>0\eta>0η>0, in units of 1/dollar, converts a spend error into a multiplier change, and max⁡{0,⋅}\max\{0,\cdot\}max{0,⋅} keeps the multiplier nonnegative. Overspending raises μ\muμ and lowers bids; underspending does the reverse. The update is projected subgradient descent on the Lagrangian dual: by the envelope theorem the dual objective's derivative in μ\muμ is budget minus spend, so a step against it moves μ\muμ by +η (ct−st)+\eta\,(c_t-s_t)+η(ct​−st​). It sets the direction of control, not stability: delayed billing data, traffic cycles and interacting control loops can make it oscillate. Feedback control in RTB advertising

    The target trajectory sts_tst​ need not be flat over the day. If evening opportunities are worth more, hold budget back for the evening; if high-value supply is scarce, an unspent budget is not necessarily a fault. Distinguish under-delivery caused by a system failure while profitable opportunities exist from stopping because no opportunity meets the economic constraints. Forcing full spend through bid multipliers quietly turns value maximization into budget-consumption maximization.

    Allocating across many campaigns adds more dimensions: which advertiser gets a given opportunity, how much budget each campaign has left, whether there are guaranteed-delivery obligations (contracts that promise a fixed number of impressions), and whether the platform earns a service fee, a per-impression price or a per-conversion price. Statistical arbitrage research links CPA revenue to CPM procurement cost, but the arbitrageur still carries user-response, attribution and payment risk; “arbitrage” here does not mean risk-free profit. Statistical Arbitrage Mining

    Attribution, experiments, and data

    In this chapter

    • Undo negative downsampling: a sampled-data prediction of 4.76% is really 0.05%, and skipping the correction overvalues the impression about 95×.
    • Evaluate a new policy offline with inverse propensity scoring (IPS), and spot when one small logging probability makes the estimate worthless.
    • Read a holdout experiment end to end: attributed ROAS 5, incremental ROAS 2, and a −$1,000 profit estimate whose 95% interval, [−$2,830, +$830], spans zero.
    • Separate the intent-to-treat effect, the effect on exposed users, and the biased exposed-versus-control comparison, and see what ghost ads add.
    • Know what ATT, SKAdNetwork and AdAttributionKit let you observe, and when.

    The delivery policy determines what training data looks like

    Ad logs are not a passive sample of the world. Every stage of delivery filters what you later get to see. Eligibility filtering (targeting, budget, frequency-cap and content-policy rules) decides which ads may compete for an opportunity. Retrieval (cheap candidate generation; see Chapter 3) decides which candidates get scored. Bidding decides which opportunities are bought. Rendering success and privacy mechanisms decide which outcomes are observed. The labels you train on are therefore conditioned on the logging policy's own choices. A conversion-rate (CVR) model fitted on won impressions estimates P(Y=1∣X,shown by the old policy)P(Y=1 \mid X, \text{shown by the old policy})P(Y=1∣X,shown by the old policy), not P(Y=1∣X)P(Y=1 \mid X)P(Y=1∣X) on traffic the old policy never bought. This is selection bias, and no model, however clever, can recover conversion labels for actions that were never taken.

    Exploration buys two things: knowledge of regions the current policy avoids, and support overlap, meaning that every action a new policy might choose also had nonzero probability of being taken by the logging policy. It costs real money and user experience. If the logging policy is stochastic and you record the probability of each action it took, you can evaluate a new policy offline with inverse propensity scoring (IPS). Let xix_ixi​ be the context of logged opportunity iii (user, placement, time), aia_iai​ the action taken (which ad, what bid; here aaa is an action, not the CPA of the running example), rir_iri​ the observed reward, μ(a∣x)\mu(a \mid x)μ(a∣x) the logging policy (not a budget multiplier here) and π(a∣x)\pi(a \mid x)π(a∣x) the policy to evaluate. The IPS estimate of the new policy's value V(π)=Ex Ea∼π(⋅∣x)[r]V(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_x\,\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)}[r]V(π)=Ex​Ea∼π(⋅∣x)​[r] is

    V^IPS(π)=1n∑i=1nπ(ai∣xi)μ(ai∣xi) ri.\hat V_{\text{IPS}}(\pi)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\pi(a_i\mid x_i)}{\mu(a_i\mid x_i)}\,r_i .V^IPS​(π)=n1​i=1∑n​μ(ai​∣xi​)π(ai​∣xi​)​ri​.

    It is unbiased under four assumptions. (1) Support: μ(a∣x)>0\mu(a\mid x)>0μ(a∣x)>0 wherever π(a∣x)>0\pi(a\mid x)>0π(a∣x)>0. (2) The logged μ(ai∣xi)\mu(a_i\mid x_i)μ(ai​∣xi​) is the probability actually used, not a reconstruction. (3) The reward is defined and observed the same way under both policies (same conversion event, attribution window and postback mechanism). (4) The new policy does not change the context distribution or the environment; in an auction this fails when the new policy's bids move clearing prices or competitors' behavior. Small logging probabilities produce large weights and high variance: for a deterministic π\piπ, the second moment of one term is E[r2∣x,π(x)]/μ(π(x)∣x)\mathbb{E}[r^2\mid x,\pi(x)]/\mu(\pi(x)\mid x)E[r2∣x,π(x)]/μ(π(x)∣x), so it grows like 1/μ1/\mu1/μ. Clipping the weight at some MMM, i.e. using min⁡{M,π/μ}\min\{M,\pi/\mu\}min{M,π/μ}, cuts variance at the cost of a downward bias (for r≥0r\ge 0r≥0). Offline replay reweights outcomes you logged; it cannot manufacture counterfactuals you never logged. Swaminathan and Joachims, counterfactual risk minimization

    Negative downsampling also shifts absolute probabilities. Fix a feature value, so the label is binary: a positive is a sample where the target event occurred, a negative one where it did not. Let ppp be the event probability in the population before sampling, sss (0<s≤10<s\le 10<s≤1) the probability that a negative is retained, and psp_sps​ the event probability among retained samples, which is what a model trained on the sampled data without weights learns. If every positive is kept and each negative is kept independently with the same probability sss, then ps=p/(p+s(1−p))p_s = p/(p+s(1-p))ps​=p/(p+s(1−p)), so

    p=s ps1−ps+s ps,equivalentlyp1−p=s⋅ps1−ps.p=\frac{s\,p_s}{1-p_s+s\,p_s},\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \frac{p}{1-p}=s\cdot\frac{p_s}{1-p_s}.p=1−ps​+sps​sps​​,equivalently1−pp​=s⋅1−ps​ps​​.

    In logit terms the correction is a constant shift of ln⁡s\ln slns. For example, with s=0.1s=0.1s=0.1 and ps=0.5p_s=0.5ps​=0.5 the true probability is 0.05/0.55=1/11≈0.09090.05/0.55=1/11\approx 0.09090.05/0.55=1/11≈0.0909, not 50%. Apply the correction once. If training already weighted each retained negative by 1/s1/s1/s, the model is already calibrated to ppp and correcting again is wrong. If the retention rate depends on features, you need the per-sample retention probability; a single constant no longer works.

    Delayed labels and time leakage

    Clicks usually precede purchases, and purchases precede long-run contribution profit. An impression that has not converted yet is not a permanent negative, but waiting for every label to mature costs the model freshness. A production pipeline therefore needs four explicit choices: an observation window (how long after the impression or click a conversion still counts), maturity cohorts (groups of events old enough that their labels are, say, 95% final), a delay model (an estimate of P(conversion arrives after t∣eventual conversion)P(\text{conversion arrives after } t \mid \text{eventual conversion})P(conversion arrives after t∣eventual conversion) used to correct immature labels), and a backfill policy (how late-arriving labels overwrite earlier negatives). Several papers address this freshness-versus-maturity tension in streaming CVR training. Delayed feedback and elapsed-time sampling

    To make the stakes concrete, assume the delay from impression to conversion is exponential with mean 3 days, so the share of eventual conversions visible at label age ttt days is H(t)=1−e−t/3H(t)=1-e^{-t/3}H(t)=1−e−t/3 (here HHH is the delay CDF, not the competing-bid CDF FFF of Chapter 3). Labels are 95% final only at t=3ln⁡20≈9.0t=3\ln 20\approx 9.0t=3ln20≈9.0 days. Compare experiment arms only at equal label maturity: two arms with the same true CVR of 1.0%, read when their impressions are 7 and 5 days old, show 0.903% and 0.811%, so the later arm looks 10.2% worse with no real difference. Nor is a young non-converted impression a negative: with eventual conversion probability ppp, P(converts eventually∣not yet at age t)=p (1−H(t))/(1−p H(t))P(\text{converts eventually}\mid\text{not yet at age }t)=p\,(1-H(t))/(1-p\,H(t))P(converts eventually∣not yet at age t)=p(1−H(t))/(1−pH(t)), which for p=1%p=1\%p=1% at t=1t=1t=1 day is 0.72%, still 72% of the base rate.

    Each training example must contain only information that was available at decision time. Account state after the purchase, conversion counters already incremented by this purchase, and attribution outcomes decided later must not leak into the features. Correct table-update timestamps are not enough for a correct point-in-time join: you must track event time, processing time and the feature-pipeline version separately. A model that wins offline through leakage does not degrade slightly online; it loses the very inputs its predictions depended on.

    Attribution allocates credit; experiments identify causation

    Attribution is a bookkeeping rule that assigns each conversion to an ad touchpoint (a click or an impression), usually because billing or optimization needs a single owner; in mobile app advertising the winner takes all, while multi-touch rules split credit fractionally but answer the same bookkeeping question. The common rule is last-touch: credit goes to the last qualifying click within a lookback window before the conversion. A click-through window bounds the gap between click and conversion; a view-through window, usually much shorter, lets an impression with no click claim the conversion when no qualifying click exists. Typical defaults for app installs are 7 days for clicks and 24 hours for views, but contracts and measurement settings vary. For mobile apps the matching is done by an MMP (Mobile Measurement Partner; see Chapter 2): the advertiser's app embeds the MMP's SDK, which reports installs and in-app events; ad networks send the MMP their click and impression claims; the MMP picks the winner under the configured rules and sends postbacks (server-to-server notifications of the attributed event) to the winning network.

    1. t = 0
      Impression. The ad renders; the network sends the MMP an impression claim (device identifier where permitted, otherwise coarser signals).
    2. ≤ 24 h
      View-through window. If no qualifying click exists, an install within 24 hours of the impression can be credited to it.
    3. click
      Click. The user taps; the network sends a click claim and opens the app store.
    4. ≤ 7 d
      Install = first open. The MMP SDK reports the first launch (not the download). The MMP looks back 7 days for clicks and credits the last one.
    5. minutes
      Install postback to the winning network; losing networks typically receive nothing about this install.
    6. later
      In-app events. Purchases inherit the install's attribution and trigger further postbacks; the cohort cutoff (e.g. day-7 revenue) is a reporting choice.

    Incrementality is a different question: how do business outcomes with the advertising intervention compare with outcomes without it? The two can disagree in both directions. A real conversion can be credited to the wrong touchpoint, and a correctly credited conversion may have happened anyway. Last-touch and view-through rules systematically reward ads placed close to purchases users were already going to make: retargeting existing customers, or spraying cheap impressions to collect view-through credit.

    Attribution answers

    Which touchpoint gets credit for this conversion? Per-conversion, deterministic, available within minutes, never negative. It drives CPA and CPI (cost per install) billing and daily optimization signals. It is silent on whether the conversion would have happened anyway.

    Incrementality answers

    How many conversions exist because the ad ran? Defined only for a population against a counterfactual, needs randomization or strong assumptions, arrives after the window matures, can be negative, and comes with a confidence interval. It decides whether spend is profitable.

    Field evidence shows that rich observational data does not reliably recover the effects that randomized experiments identify. Observational models are not useless, but predictive accuracy does not supply the identifying assumptions a causal claim needs. For example, observational IPS for the effect of exposure DDD with propensity e(x)=P(D=1∣X=x)e(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)e(x)=P(D=1∣X=x) is τ^=1n∑i[DiYi/e(xi)−(1−Di)Yi/(1−e(xi))]\hat\tau=\frac1n\sum_i\big[D_iY_i/e(x_i)-(1-D_i)Y_i/(1-e(x_i))\big]τ^=n1​∑i​[Di​Yi​/e(xi​)−(1−Di​)Yi​/(1−e(xi​))]. It is unbiased only if eee is known (or correctly modeled), 0<e(x)<10<e(x)<10<e(x)<1, and, conditional on the logged features, exposure is independent of the potential outcomes (no unmeasured confounding). Ad targeting optimizes exposure toward likely buyers on signals the analyst often cannot see, so that last assumption is exactly what fails. Gordon et al., observational methods versus large Facebook experiments

    The next example is self-contained; it is not the network campaign from Chapter 1, so that network's media budget does not enter the advertiser's return calculation. Randomly split one eligible population into a treatment group, where the campaign may deliver, and a control group (a holdout), where it may not. Net revenue per purchase means sales revenue after refunds and other adjustments but before cost of goods, fulfillment and other variable costs. The pre-advertising contribution rate is the share of net revenue left after those non-advertising variable costs. ROAS (return on ad spend) is revenue divided by ad spend; attributed ROAS uses attributed revenue, and iROAS (incremental ROAS) uses the revenue the campaign actually caused. Assume randomization and event definitions are correct, the window has matured, and there is no interference: one group's treatment does not change the other group's purchases.

    Worked example

    Holdout experiment: from attributed ROAS to a decision

    Given: 100,000 users per group. Over the same matured window, treatment makes 1,200 purchases and control 1,000. Ad spend is $5,000, all in treatment. Attribution credits 500 purchases to the campaign. Net revenue is $50 per purchase and the contribution rate 40%, so each purchase contributes $50×0.40=$20\$50\times0.40=\$20$50×0.40=$20 before ad spend. For the standard error: each user buys at most once and users are independent.

    1. Attributed ROAS: 500×$50÷$5,000=5500\times\$50\div\$5{,}000=5500×$50÷$5,000=5.
    2. Lift (equal group sizes, so counts compare directly): 1,200−1,000=2001{,}200-1{,}000=2001,200−1,000=200 incremental purchases per 100,000 users assigned to treatment.
    3. iROAS: 200×$50÷$5,000=2200\times\$50\div\$5{,}000=2200×$50÷$5,000=2. Each incremental revenue dollar yields $0.40 of contribution, so break-even iROAS is 1÷0.40=2.51\div0.40=2.51÷0.40=2.5.
    4. Incremental contribution after ad spend: 200×$20−$5,000=−$1,000200\times\$20-\$5{,}000=-\$1{,}000200×$20−$5,000=−$1,000. Break-even lift: $5,000÷$20=250\$5{,}000\div\$20=250$5,000÷$20=250 purchases.
    5. Credit that was not incremental: at the point estimate, at least 500−200=300500-200=300500−200=300 credited purchases would have happened without the campaign (assuming the ad never suppresses a purchase).
    6. Standard error of the lift. Each count is binomial with variance np^(1−p^)n\hat p(1-\hat p)np^​(1−p^​): 100,000×0.012×0.988=1,185.6100{,}000\times0.012\times0.988=1{,}185.6100,000×0.012×0.988=1,185.6 for treatment and 100,000×0.010×0.990=990100{,}000\times0.010\times0.990=990100,000×0.010×0.990=990 for control, so SE=1,185.6+990=2,175.6=46.6\text{SE}=\sqrt{1{,}185.6+990}=\sqrt{2{,}175.6}=46.6SE=1,185.6+990​=2,175.6​=46.6. The lift is 200/46.6=4.3200/46.6=4.3200/46.6=4.3 standard errors from zero.
    7. 95% interval: 200±1.96×46.6=200±91.4200\pm1.96\times46.6=200\pm91.4200±1.96×46.6=200±91.4, i.e. [108.6, 291.4]≈[109, 291][108.6,\ 291.4]\approx[109,\ 291][108.6, 291.4]≈[109, 291] purchases.
    8. Map through the linear formulas: iROAS =lift×$50/$5,000=\text{lift}\times\$50/\$5{,}000=lift×$50/$5,000 gives [1.09, 2.91][1.09,\ 2.91][1.09, 2.91]; contribution =$20×lift−$5,000=\$20\times\text{lift}-\$5{,}000=$20×lift−$5,000 gives [−$2,828, +$828]≈[−$2,830, +$830][-\$2{,}828,\ +\$828]\approx[-\$2{,}830,\ +\$830][−$2,828, +$828]≈[−$2,830, +$830].
    9. Decision. Break-even (250) sits (250−200)/46.6=1.07(250-200)/46.6=1.07(250−200)/46.6=1.07 standard errors above the estimate, so this sample cannot sign the profit. To separate a lift of 200 from 250 with 80% power at a two-sided 5% level, you need SE≤50/(1.96+0.84)=17.9\text{SE}\le 50/(1.96+0.84)=17.9SE≤50/(1.96+0.84)=17.9 per 100,000 users, i.e. (46.6/17.9)2≈6.8×(46.6/17.9)^2\approx6.8\times(46.6/17.9)2≈6.8× the sample: about 680,000 users per group at the same spend per user.

    Result: the campaign causes purchases (lift 200, 95% CI [109, 291]); its profit is −$1,000 at the point estimate with 95% CI ≈ [−$2,830, +$830]. Attributed ROAS 5 and a probable loss coexist.

    Check: both ROAS figures equal purchases × $50/$5,000 = purchases/100, so their ratio is 500/200 = 2.5. Contribution also equals $5,000×(0.40×iROAS−1)\$5{,}000\times(0.40\times\text{iROAS}-1)$5,000×(0.40×iROAS−1): at iROAS 1.086 that is −$2,828, matching step 8.

    Repeat purchases, heavy-tailed order values, or cluster randomization widen these intervals. If the two groups differ in size, compare per-person outcomes first, then state the delivery scale you are extrapolating to.

    Assignment to "eligible to see the ad" is not exposure: many treatment users never win an auction slot, never open the app, or scroll past. Use potential-outcome notation. For user iii, Zi∈{0,1}Z_i\in\{0,1\}Zi​∈{0,1} is the randomized assignment (in this section ZZZ is not the competing bid of Chapter 3), Di(z)∈{0,1}D_i(z)\in\{0,1\}Di​(z)∈{0,1} is whether the user would actually be exposed under assignment zzz, and Yi(z)Y_i(z)Yi​(z) is the outcome under assignment zzz. Under the exclusion restriction below, write Yi(d)Y_i(d)Yi​(d) for the outcome under exposure ddd. Because the control group cannot be served the campaign, Di(0)=0D_i(0)=0Di​(0)=0 for everyone (one-sided noncompliance). Let c=P(D=1∣Z=1)c=P(D=1\mid Z=1)c=P(D=1∣Z=1) be the exposure rate in the treatment group.

    Estimand Definition Estimator Requires
    ITT (intent-to-treat effect) τITT=E[Yi(1)−Yi(0)]\tau_{\text{ITT}}=\mathbb{E}[Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)]τITT​=E[Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)], effect of assignment over everyone randomized YˉZ=1−YˉZ=0\bar Y_{Z=1}-\bar Y_{Z=0}YˉZ=1​−YˉZ=0​ Randomization; no interference between users (SUTVA)
    TOT (treatment on the treated) = CACE (complier average causal effect) τTOT=E[Yi(d=1)−Yi(d=0)∣Di(1)=1]\tau_{\text{TOT}}=\mathbb{E}[Y_i(d{=}1)-Y_i(d{=}0)\mid D_i(1)=1]τTOT​=E[Yi​(d=1)−Yi​(d=0)∣Di​(1)=1], effect of exposure on users who would be exposed if assigned (YˉZ=1−YˉZ=0)/c^(\bar Y_{Z=1}-\bar Y_{Z=0})/\hat c(YˉZ=1​−YˉZ=0​)/c^ (Wald / Bloom ratio) ITT assumptions, plus exclusion restriction (assignment affects outcomes only through exposure) and c>0c>0c>0; one-sided noncompliance makes TOT and CACE coincide and makes monotonicity automatic
    Naive exposed-vs-control E[Y∣D=1,Z=1]−E[Y∣Z=0]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid D=1,Z=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z=0]E[Y∣D=1,Z=1]−E[Y∣Z=0] Mean of exposed treatment users minus mean of all control users Nothing valid: it equals τTOT+(E[Yi(0)∣Di(1)=1]−E[Yi(0)])\tau_{\text{TOT}}+\big(\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0)\mid D_i(1)=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0)]\big)τTOT​+(E[Yi​(0)∣Di​(1)=1]−E[Yi​(0)]), and the selection term is positive when delivery targets likely buyers

    Analyze ITT first. Filtering the treatment group down to exposed users and comparing them with all of control reintroduces exactly the selection that randomization removed. Switching the denominator alone identifies nothing; the TOT rescaling is valid only under the stated assumptions. The Wald ratio also adds no precision: it divides the estimate and its standard error by the same c^\hat cc^, so the z-statistic is unchanged. TOT changes the unit (per exposed user instead of per assigned user), not the total effect, the evidence or the profit. Precision needs extra information about who would have been exposed, which is what ghost ads supply.

    Worked example

    ITT, TOT and the naive comparison with exposure logs

    Given: the holdout experiment above, plus hypothetical exposure data. In treatment, 40,000 users were exposed and bought 800 times; the other 60,000 bought 400 times. Ghost-ad logs (described below) flag the 40,000 control users who would have been exposed; they bought 600 times, and the other 60,000 control users bought 400 times.

    1. ITT per assigned user: (1,200−1,000)/100,000=0.002(1{,}200-1{,}000)/100{,}000=0.002(1,200−1,000)/100,000=0.002 purchases, SE 46.64/100,000=0.000466446.64/100{,}000=0.000466446.64/100,000=0.0004664.
    2. Exposure rate c^=40,000/100,000=0.40\hat c=40{,}000/100{,}000=0.40c^=40,000/100,000=0.40. Wald: τTOT=0.002/0.40=0.005\tau_{\text{TOT}}=0.002/0.40=0.005τTOT​=0.002/0.40=0.005 purchases per exposed user, SE ≈0.0004664/0.40=0.001166\approx0.0004664/0.40=0.001166≈0.0004664/0.40=0.001166 (accounting for the sampling error of c^\hat cc^ changes this variance by about 0.1%). z=0.005/0.001166=4.3z=0.005/0.001166=4.3z=0.005/0.001166=4.3, the same as ITT.
    3. Totals agree: 100,000×0.002=40,000×0.005=200100{,}000\times0.002=40{,}000\times0.005=200100,000×0.002=40,000×0.005=200 purchases, so iROAS is still 2.
    4. Naive comparison: 800/40,000−1,000/100,000=0.020−0.010=0.010800/40{,}000-1{,}000/100{,}000=0.020-0.010=0.010800/40,000−1,000/100,000=0.020−0.010=0.010 per exposed user, i.e. 400 "incremental" purchases, twice the truth. The selection term is visible in the ghost logs: would-be-exposed control users buy at 600/40,000=0.015600/40{,}000=0.015600/40,000=0.015 against 0.010 overall, a gap of 0.005, exactly the bias.
    5. Ghost-ad TOT: exposed treatment vs ghost-exposed control, 0.020−0.015=0.0050.020-0.015=0.0050.020−0.015=0.005. Its standard error is 800(0.98)+600(0.985)/40,000\sqrt{800(0.98)+600(0.985)}/40{,}000800(0.98)+600(0.985)​/40,000 =1,375/40,000=0.000927=\sqrt{1{,}375}/40{,}000=0.000927=1,375​/40,000=0.000927, so z=0.005/0.000927=5.4z=0.005/0.000927=5.4z=0.005/0.000927=5.4. The variance ratio (0.001166/0.000927)2=1.58(0.001166/0.000927)^2=1.58(0.001166/0.000927)2=1.58 is worth 58% more users, because the 120,000 never-exposed users only added noise.
    6. Exclusion check: never-exposed users buy 400/60,000 in both groups, consistent with assignment having no effect except through exposure. Without ghost logs this is untestable.

    Result: TOT = 0.005 purchases per exposed user by both methods; the naive estimate (0.010) is 2× too high; ghost ads cut the standard error by 20.5%.

    Check: c^×τTOT=0.40×0.005=0.002=τITT\hat c\times\tau_{\text{TOT}}=0.40\times0.005=0.002=\tau_{\text{ITT}}c^×τTOT​=0.40×0.005=0.002=τITT​, and naive − TOT = 0.010 − 0.005 = 0.005 = selection term.

    The exclusion restriction needs care in an auction. Withholding the campaign from a control user does not leave the slot empty; the next-best ad wins. The estimand is therefore the effect relative to the ad environment the user would otherwise see, not relative to no ad at all. Ghost ads (Johnson, Lewis and Nubbemeyer, 2017) estimate TOT more precisely. For control users the ad server runs the auction with the campaign included, logs a "ghost impression" whenever the campaign would have won and rendered, then serves the runner-up instead. This observes Di(1)D_i(1)Di​(1) in both groups, so you can compare exposed treatment users with ghost-exposed control users directly. It requires the ghost logic to replicate the real delivery decision exactly, with identical code paths in both groups. The older placebo design, which shows control users a public-service ad (PSA), fails under optimized delivery: the optimizer delivers the PSA to different users than it would deliver the real ad, so the two exposed groups are not comparable.

    Model experiments and channel incrementality experiments are not the same question

    A model A/B experiment randomizes traffic between two delivery policies and compares them. A channel incrementality experiment compares advertising with not advertising, with reduced spend, or with different budget levels. The first can show that B beats A; it cannot by itself show that the channel generates positive incremental profit relative to not spending at all. Geo experiments, which randomize geographic regions instead of users, also come in several designs (go dark, heavy-up, budget levels), so choose the question first and the design second. Google GeoX experiment types

    Before launch, fix the primary metric, the minimum detectable effect (MDE: the smallest true effect the design detects with a prespecified power at a prespecified false-positive rate), the duration, the label-maturity period, guardrail metrics (metrics that must not degrade, such as latency, user retention or publisher revenue) and the stopping rule. Several mechanisms couple the arms. A shared budget makes them compete for one quota. Bids from one arm move the prices the other arm pays. Cross-device and cross-region behavior leaks users across assignment boundaries. Whether you randomize by user, region or time block, document how each of these interferences is handled. Deciding to stop whenever a peek shows significance inflates the actual false-positive rate unless the test is designed for sequential monitoring.

    In the running example the network optimizes its gross spread (collections minus media procurement cost; see Chapter 3), while the advertiser cares about incremental contribution. Report both. Otherwise a policy can raise the network's short-term revenue by chasing conversions that are easy to attribute but not incremental, and leave the resulting customer churn to the sales team.

    Privacy and anti-fraud change observability

    On iOS, two separate Apple mechanisms matter. ATT (App Tracking Transparency, iOS 14.5, 2021) requires an app to obtain user permission through a system prompt before it tracks the user across other companies' apps and websites or reads the IDFA (Identifier for Advertisers, the per-device ad identifier that previously enabled deterministic user-level attribution). SKAdNetwork (SKAN), and its successor AdAttributionKit (iOS 17.4), are Apple's privacy-preserving attribution APIs: the device itself decides which ad gets credit for an install and sends the ad network a delayed, aggregated postback with no user identifier. ATT and these attribution APIs are not synonyms. Apple's documentation states that using AdAttributionKit alone does not require the ATT prompt, while tracking as Apple defines it, or reading the IDFA, does. Crowd-anonymity thresholds control which postback fields are populated: with too few installs from a campaign, fields such as the fine-grained conversion value (an app-set integer from 0 to 63 encoding post-install activity) or parts of the source identifier come back coarse or empty. Postbacks are cryptographically signed and carry transaction identifiers so receivers can reject forgeries and replays. Apple ad attribution

    The timing alone reshapes the training pipeline. In SKAdNetwork 4 (AdAttributionKit keeps the same three-window structure), a postback arrives only after its conversion window closes plus a random delay:

    1. day 0
      Engagement and install. The install must follow a StoreKit-rendered ad tap within 30 days or a view-through impression within 24 hours.
    2. days 0–2
      Window 1. The app may raise its conversion value; its postback can carry the fine value (0–63) if the crowd is large enough, otherwise a coarse value (low, medium, high). Postback 1 is sent 24–48 hours after the window closes.
    3. days 3–7
      Window 2. Coarse value only. Postback 24–144 hours after close.
    4. days 8–35
      Window 3. Coarse value only. The last postback can arrive as late as day 41 (35 days + 144 hours).

    The system consequences follow directly. A missing user-level postback cannot be labeled "not converted." Aggregated postbacks cannot be split back into individual users without additional assumptions. A signed event proves authenticity, not incrementality. And missingness is not random, because it depends on consent rates and campaign size. A new platform that subsidizes impression purchases has bought delivery opportunities only. It does not automatically obtain training labels that can be joined across customers and used under long-term consent.

    Examine fraud layer by layer, because each layer is a separate attack surface. Is the supply identity real? Was the impression actually rendered? Was the click made by a human? Is the conversion valid? Was attribution hijacked, for example by click injection, where malware on an Android device detects that an app is being installed and fires a fake click before its first open, winning last-touch credit for an install that was already happening? Was the purchase later refunded? Supply-chain transparency standards address only the first layer. ads.txt (app-ads.txt for apps) is a file the publisher hosts on its own domain listing which ad systems are authorized to sell its inventory. sellers.json is published by each SSP (supply-side platform; see Chapter 2) or exchange and lists the sellers it pays. The SupplyChain object in an OpenRTB bid request (OpenRTB is the IAB's standard bid-request protocol) lists every hop the request passed through. None of these guarantees traffic quality or economic incrementality. IAB ads.txt, IAB sellers.json and SupplyChain FAQ

    The trading analogy applies: positive expected value per trade does not guarantee survival. Correlated fake events, retroactive changes to attribution windows, chargebacks, and a payment-timing mismatch, where the network pays publishers before advertisers pay it, all concentrate risk. A fraud model is one layer. You also need per-source exposure limits, settlement reconciliation, contractual clawback rights, and gradual ramp-up of new sources.

    Real-time advertising systems

    In this chapter

    • Split a 120 ms tmax into network allowance, safety margin and per-stage deadlines, and see why per-stage P99s do not compose into an end-to-end P99.
    • Keep the hard-budget invariant C+R≤BC+R\le BC+R≤B through admit, win notice, billing notice, duplicate notice and timeout, and know which evidence may release a reservation.
    • Choose a deduplication key that turns at-least-once notices into one ledger posting per billable event, and recognize the two ways a wrong key fails.
    • Quantify what the display contract does to the bid (6.666667 vs 6.324555 CPM, $230.93 of spread), and what never releasing reservations costs ($2,743.42 of spread falls to $867.54).

    The accounting examples here use the optional CPA-network case from Chapter 3: a network buys publisher impressions and bills advertisers for attributed conversions. They do not change the main direct-buying advertiser objective. The ledger, timing and reservation principles apply to either arrangement once its payment obligations are specified.

    Organize the system around three pipelines

    An ad network (the intermediary that buys impressions from publishers and sells results to advertisers; see Chapter 1 and Chapter 2) runs three pipelines. The control pipeline manages contracts, campaigns (an advertiser's unit of budget, targeting and goals), creatives (the ad assets themselves), budgets and configuration releases. The online pipeline answers each bid request from an exchange before its deadline: it filters for eligibility, retrieves candidates, predicts responses and computes a bid. The event pipeline records delivery, billing, attribution, training data and reconciliation.

    Terms used in the diagram: eligibility is the set of hard filters a campaign must pass before it is scored (targeting, available budget, approved creative, publisher and advertiser block lists, consent and regulatory rules). Retrieval cheaply narrows the eligible set to a few hundred candidates; ranking orders them by predicted value. Pacing is the online control of spend rate across the budget period (Chapter 3). The online snapshot is a versioned, read-only copy of configuration and features pushed to serving nodes. The diagram is a teaching architecture. It is not the known implementation of Axon or of any other company.

    The hard part of an ad system is not picking a database for each box. It is getting the boxes to agree on a verifiable account of what happened and how much is owed to whom. A successful HTTP response proves neither that an impression was delivered nor that a conversion occurred, let alone that the advertiser benefited.

    One impression spans about nine orders of magnitude of time, from milliseconds to months, and each stage is evidence of something different. The time scales below are illustrative; the integration contract sets the real ones.

    1. 0 ms
      Bid request. The exchange sends the request; the tmax window is measured at the exchange.
    2. ≤ 120 ms
      Bid response. Must reach the exchange inside tmax. The budget reservation is made before the response leaves.
    3. + ms to s
      Auction result. Win notice (nurl) or loss notice (lurl), if the exchange sends them. A win is not a delivered or billable impression.
    4. + seconds
      Render. The creative loads on the device and fires the impression pixel, or fails (probability 1−ρ1-\rho1−ρ below).
    5. + s to hours
      Billing notice. burl fires when the impression becomes billable under the exchange's policy; retries and late arrivals are normal. Reservation becomes confirmed spend.
    6. + days
      Clicks and conversions. Attributed inside the attribution window; create the CPA receivable. Refunds and chargebacks arrive later still.
    7. monthly
      Settlement. The exchange's statement, your log and the advertiser bill are reconciled; corrections are posted as compensating entries.

    Request deadlines and per-stage computation

    OpenRTB is the IAB Tech Lab's protocol family for real-time bidding: the exchange sends a bid request describing one or more impression opportunities (imp objects), and each bidder returns a bid response. The fields this chapter relies on have these OpenRTB 2.x meanings: OpenRTB 2.6 request and bid objects

    • tmax (request): the maximum time, in milliseconds, that the exchange allows for bids to be received, including internet latency.
    • price (bid): the bid price, quoted as CPM (dollars per thousand impressions; see Chapter 3) even though the transaction is for a single impression.
    • nurl (bid): the win notice URL, called if the bid wins. The spec states that a win does not necessarily mean a delivered, viewed or billable ad.
    • burl (bid): the billing notice URL, called when the winning bid becomes billable under the exchange's own business policy.
    • lurl (bid): the loss notice URL, called when the bid is known to have lost.

    All three notice URLs are optional. Exchanges substitute macros into them, notably ${AUCTION_PRICE} (the clearing price, in the same currency and units as the bid, so also CPM; many exchanges encrypt it) and the request and impression ids (${AUCTION_ID}, ${AUCTION_IMP_ID}). ${AUCTION_BID_ID} echoes the response-level BidResponse.bidid, not the per-bid Bid.id; since the bidder writes the notice URLs itself, it should embed its own Bid.id in them. The deadlines and auction types in this chapter's examples are teaching assumptions, not industry facts.

    Suppose a request carries tmax=120. This is a teaching value, not an industry service-level objective. Because the window includes the network round trip and the bidder cannot observe when the exchange sent the request, the bidder has well under 120 ms of compute: it subtracts estimated network time in both directions and a safety margin, then splits the remainder across feature reads, retrieval, inference, budget admission and response encoding. A model whose inference P99 (99th-percentile latency) is 20 ms does not guarantee an on-time end-to-end response. Candidate count, cache misses, fan-out and queueing set the tail, and per-stage P99s neither sum to nor bound the end-to-end P99.

    Worked example

    A 120 ms deadline, split into stage budgets

    Given (all latencies illustrative): tmax = 120 ms; estimated network round-trip P99 of 30 ms for this exchange and region, measured as a round trip from the bidder's own logs (not the sum of two one-way P99s, which per the check below is not a bound); safety margin mmm = 10 ms; feature reads fan out to 20 shards in parallel.

    1. Network allowance: the round-trip P99. tnet=30 mst_{\text{net}} = 30\ \text{ms}tnet​=30 ms
    2. Compute deadline, measured from receipt at the bidder. D=tmax⁡−tnet−m=120−30−10=80 ms\begin{aligned}D &= t_{\max} - t_{\text{net}} - m\\ &= 120 - 30 - 10 = 80\ \text{ms}\end{aligned}D​=tmax​−tnet​−m=120−30−10=80 ms​
    3. Split DDD into stage budgets: decode and eligibility 10, feature reads 15, retrieval 10, inference 30, budget admission 5, pricing and encoding 5, unallocated slack 5 (all in ms). 10+15+10+30+5+5+5=8010+15+10+30+5+5+5 = 8010+15+10+30+5+5+5=80
    4. Fan-out. If each of the 20 feature shards meets 15 ms at its own P99 and shards are independent, the share of requests with at least one slow shard is 1−0.9920≈18.2%.1-0.99^{20} \approx 18.2\%.1−0.9920≈18.2%. For the stage to meet 15 ms on 99% of requests, each shard must meet it at quantile 0.991/20≈0.999500.99^{1/20} \approx 0.999500.991/20≈0.99950, i.e. its P99.95, or the stage needs hedged reads or a default-feature fallback.

    Result: 80 ms of compute after receipt, propagated as absolute deadlines (receipt time + offset) to each stage. A stage that misses its deadline takes its declared degradation path or the request no-bids.

    Check: 30 + 10 + 80 = 120 ms. Stage P99s do not bound the end-to-end P99: let two stages each take 0 ms with probability 0.991 and 100 ms otherwise. Each has P99 = 0 ms, but Pr⁡(sum>0)=1−0.9912≈1.79%>1%\Pr(\text{sum}>0) = 1-0.991^2 \approx 1.79\% > 1\%Pr(sum>0)=1−0.9912≈1.79%>1%, so the end-to-end P99 is 100 ms.

    Every degradation path has an economic meaning. Filling missing features with defaults, switching to a smaller model and not bidding at all bias value estimates differently and carry different risks. If key configuration is stale, the budget has no available quota, or a creative's review status is unknown, bidding anyway can create real spend and breach contracts. Give each degradation path explicit preconditions, a maximum exposure in dollars and a logged reason code. Only then can you tell whether “higher availability” has merely moved losses into the ledger.

    How a single request in the unified example is booked

    Continue the unified example from Chapter 3: a first-price auction (the winner pays its own bid) and the budget-constrained bid of 6.324555 CPM, i.e. at most $0.006324555 of media cost for this one impression, with no fees for now. Assume the upstream contract defines a determinable billing rule and a maximum obligation per bid.

    First the system fixes the bid's business identity, the tuple (exchange, BidRequest.id, Imp.id, Bid.id); the exchange is part of the key because request ids are unique only within one exchange, and Imp.id only within one request (it is often just 1). It also records the campaign, model, feature, configuration and experiment versions. Before the bid response leaves, the budget service must admit the bid and reserve its maximum possible spend.

    Do not accumulate millions of amounts in floating point. Internally, use integers at an explicit scale or fixed-point decimals, and convert and round at protocol boundaries as the contract specifies (price is a float on the wire). Rounding direction matters. In micro-dollars (µ$, millionths of a dollar) the cap here is 6,324.555 µ$, which is not an integer: either use a finer scale (6,324,555 nano-dollars is exact) or round the reservation up to 6,325 µ$. Rounding down to 6,324 µ$ under-reserves by 0.555 µ$ on every bid and silently breaks the hard-cap invariant below.

    The exchange may then call nurl. The spec says this means the bid won the auction; it does not imply that the ad was delivered, viewed or billable. A burl call means the impression became billable under the exchange's business policy (typically on delivery or on view). Whether each notice is sent at all, how late it may arrive and which party's record prevails in a dispute are set by the integration contract. Do not assume every exchange implements every optional field. OpenRTB 2.6 bid notification semantics

    After a win, the network carries an open obligation for that bid. When a contractually recognized billing signal arrives, it books the actual billed amount (for example ${AUCTION_PRICE}/1000 for one impression) as spend and releases the difference between the reserved cap and that amount. This assumes the actual amount does not exceed the cap. If it does, the cost-cap premise is broken: send the case to exception and risk handling, and stop claiming the hard-budget guarantee. A duplicate callback must produce at most one ledger change. A missing impression pixel (the tracking request the rendered ad fires from the device) does not prove there is no external debt, so you cannot wait out a local TTL and spend the amount again. Late notices and settlement discrepancies stay in a pending-reconciliation state until there is enough evidence to discharge the obligation.

    “At most one ledger change per billing event” needs a precise mechanism. Transport is at-least-once: exchanges retry notices and your own queues redeliver. Derive the deduplication key from business identity and event type, e.g. (exchange, auction id, impression id, bid id, billing), not from a transport message id. The uniqueness check and the ledger posting must commit atomically, either in one transaction or by keying the posting row on the dedup key under a uniqueness constraint. Checking a dedup cache and posting in a separate step loses the guarantee on a crash or a race. Dedup state must also live at least as long as the counterparty may redeliver, or a late duplicate posts twice.

    Worked example

    Three billing notices, three candidate dedup keys

    Given: three burl deliveries arrive, each at 6.324555 CPM, posted as 6,325 µ$ (cap and posting both rounded up to whole µ$). D1 is from exchange X for auction 7f3c, impression 1, our bid 9a01, transport message m-101. D2 is X's retry of D1 with a new transport message m-205. D3 is from exchange Y, which happens to mint the same auction id 7f3c and impression id 1, for our bid 9a77, message m-311. Two real billable events exist: D1 (= D2) and D3.

    1. Key = transport message id. All three ids differ, so all three post: 3×6,325=18,9753 \times 6{,}325 = 18{,}9753×6,325=18,975 µ$ against a true 12,650 µ$. CCC is overstated by 6,325 µ$: a double charge that surfaces as a settlement dispute.
    2. Key = (auction id, impression id, event type). D1, D2 and D3 share (7f3c, 1, billing), so only D1 posts: 6,325 µ$. CCC is understated by 6,325 µ$: the payable to Y is missing and bid 9a77's reservation stays open with no billing to discharge it. The budget is still safe, because that cap remains in RRR. It becomes an overspend only if the stuck reservation is later released without authoritative grounds, e.g. by a timer.
    3. Key = (exchange, auction id, impression id, bid id, event type). D1 and D3 have distinct keys; D2 collides with D1 and its insert fails the uniqueness constraint, rolling back its transaction: 2×6,325=12,6502 \times 6{,}325 = 12{,}6502×6,325=12,650 µ$.
    4. A fourth delivery D4 carries D1's key but ${AUCTION_PRICE} = 5.900000. It is not a duplicate: same key, different payload. Store a payload hash with the posting; on a key conflict with a hash mismatch, post nothing and route D4 to exception handling.

    Result: only the full business key posts exactly once per real billable event (2 postings, 12,650 µ$). A key that is too fine double-posts; a key that is too coarse silently drops real debt.

    Check: postings under each key equal the number of distinct key values among D1–D3: 3, 1 and 2. Only the last equals the 2 real events. If every Bid.id you mint is globally unique, (Bid.id, event type) alone would also give 2; the other fields then serve as a consistency check on the notice.

    Clicks and conversions travel through a separate event pipeline. In the default example the publisher is paid per impression and the advertiser pays per billable conversion (CPA, cost per action; Chapter 3), so the event types, attribution windows and payment timing differ. After the media ledger confirms spend, the network may wait days to learn whether that impression produced a collectible conversion, and later still may see a chargeback or refund that reverses it. Store media payables (owed to publishers and exchanges), advertiser receivables and training/attribution events separately; a single “conversion success” field cannot stand in for all three.

    Final reconciliation compares three records: the protocol events you logged, the publisher's or exchange's settlement statement (its periodic invoice of what it says you owe) and the advertiser's bill. Idempotent consumers give you effectively-once application of each event you received. They say nothing about events the counterparty sent that never arrived, or events you recorded that the counterparty did not. There is no end-to-end exactly-once across an organizational boundary. What you can build is a replayable event log, reversal (compensating) entries instead of in-place edits, a defined authority for corrections and an explanation for every discrepancy.

    How delivery probability changes the bid

    This section keeps the first-price auction and the Chapter 3 parameters:

    The contract therefore changes the bid and the returns, not just the event names in reports. If the probability of a successful impression varies with ZZZ, the bid or the quality of the opportunity, you cannot pull a constant ρ\rhoρ out of the expectation; you must model the conditional display probability and the payment function explicitly. On the systems side, the reservation must cover the maximum payment obligation under the contract. In both cases that is bbb per bid: a hard-quota reservation cannot be cut by 10% just because the expected display probability is 90%.

    Division of labor between expected-budget control and hard budgets

    This section switches from expected cost per request to actual ledger quantities, all in dollars for one accounting period. Let CCC be confirmed cumulative media spend (not the per-request expectation CAC_ACA​ or CBC_BCB​ above), RRR the total of maximum possible payment obligations not yet discharged (open reservations), and BBB the hard media budget. RRR here is the reservation total, not the revenue function R(C)R(C)R(C) from Chapter 2. Let cic_ici​ be the cost cap of bid iii (the most it can ever be charged, fees included) and pip_ipi​ its actual billed amount. A hard budget means maintaining the invariant below on every path:

    invariant:C+R≤Badmit bid i only if C+R+ci≤B:R←R+cibill bid i at pi≤ci:C←C+pi,  R←R−ciauthoritative loss or cancellation of i:R←R−ci\begin{aligned} &\text{invariant:} && C+R\le B\\ &\text{admit bid } i \text{ only if } C+R+c_i\le B: && R \leftarrow R+c_i\\ &\text{bill bid } i \text{ at } p_i\le c_i: && C \leftarrow C+p_i,\; R \leftarrow R-c_i\\ &\text{authoritative loss or cancellation of } i: && R \leftarrow R-c_i \end{aligned}​invariant:admit bid i only if C+R+ci​≤B:bill bid i at pi​≤ci​:authoritative loss or cancellation of i:​​C+R≤BR←R+ci​C←C+pi​,R←R−ci​R←R−ci​​

    Billing changes C+RC+RC+R by pi−ci≤0p_i - c_i \le 0pi​−ci​≤0 and a release lowers it, so only admission can raise it, and admission checks the bound. Since R≥0R \ge 0R≥0, C≤BC \le BC≤B follows. This holds under three conditions. Every bid has a reliable cap cic_ici​. Each admission is an atomic check-and-reserve: either a serializable update of a single counter, or escrow, where BBB is split into per-node quotas whose sum is provably at most BBB, each node enforces its own quota, and moving quota between nodes is atomic (or the donor debits before the recipient credits). And each billing or release step applies its two updates atomically, exactly once per bid.

    Worked example

    One bid through the ledger at the last bid's worth of budget

    Given: the Chapter 3 setting (ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1, bid 6.324555 CPM); burl is the contractual billing signal, so a win alone books nothing, and lurl is authoritative for losses. Ledger in whole µ$ (all table amounts); BBB = 2,000,000,000 µ$ ($2,000). Every bid is at 6.324555 CPM with cap ccc = 6,325 µ$ (rounded up), and a billed amount of 6,324.555 µ$ is posted as 6,325 µ$ (rounded up, the conservative direction for a cost; the sub-µ$ residue is trued up at reconciliation). Initial state: CCC = 1,999,987,350 µ$, and one earlier bid jjj is open, so RRR = 6,325 µ$. Headroom B−C−RB-C-RB−C−R = 6,325 µ$: room for exactly one more bid.

Admission (event 1) is the only step that raises C+RC+RC+R: C+R+c=1,999,987,350+6,325+6,325=2,000,000,000≤B.\begin{aligned}&C + R + c\\ &= 1{,}999{,}987{,}350 + 6{,}325 + 6{,}325\\ &= 2{,}000{,}000{,}000 \le B.\end{aligned}​C+R+c=1,999,987,350+6,325+6,325=2,000,000,000≤B.​ The bound is met with equality, so headroom is 0.
    2. Billing (event 3) moves the cap from RRR to CCC: C+RC+RC+R changes by pi−ci=6,325−6,325=0p_i - c_i = 6{,}325 - 6{,}325 = 0pi​−ci​=6,325−6,325=0. With a lower clearing price or a fee rebate, ci−pi>0c_i-p_i>0ci​−pi​>0 would return to headroom here.

    Result: C = 1,999,993,675 µ$ ($1,999.993675), R = 0; C+R≤BC+R\le BC+R≤B held after every event, with equality from event 1 through event 5.

    Check: open reservations = 1 (j) + 1 admitted (i) − 1 billed (i) − 1 released (j) = 0, matching RRR = 0; CCC rose by exactly one posting, 1,999,987,350 + 6,325 = 1,999,993,675 µ$.

    Pitfall: releasing on a timer

    Suppose event 5 had released jjj on its local timeout. Then RRR = 0, bid kkk is admitted (RRR = 6,325), and jjj's late burl posts 6,325 µ$ with no reservation behind it: CCC = 2,000,000,000 and C+RC+RC+R = 2,000,006,325 µ$ > BBB. If kkk also bills, confirmed spend overshoots the hard budget by 6,325 µ$. The amount is small here only because the timeout released one bid; a regional notice outage releases thousands.

    The definitions of cic_ici​ and RRR must cover fees, spend not yet reported, bids whose local timeout expired but that the exchange may still have accepted, and late billing. Reserving expected cost (win probability × bid) instead of cic_ici​ frees capital, but then you have statistical overspend control, not a proof of zero overspend on every path. The overshoot tail depends on correlation between outcomes, and correlated outcomes are exactly what incidents produce. The expiry of a multi-region lease likewise does not discharge obligations already incurred with an external party.

    Worked example

    Reserve the cap or reserve the expected cost?

    Given: remaining headroom HHH = $10 (illustrative, near the end of the period); bid bbb = $0.006324555 per impression, win probability F(b)=b/L=0.31622775F(b) = b/L = 0.31622775F(b)=b/L=0.31622775; ρ = 1; every admitted bid stays in flight until the headroom is used up, then all resolve.
