    Check: the concurrency gain is the reservation ratio, 6,325/2,000≈3.16≈1/F(b)=3.1626{,}325/2{,}000 \approx 3.16 \approx 1/F(b) = 3.1626,325/2,000≈3.16≈1/F(b)=3.162, and 5,000/1,581≈3.165{,}000/1{,}581 \approx 3.165,000/1,581≈3.16. The worst-case overshoot k b (1−F(b))=5,000×0.006324555×0.683772≈$21.62k\,b\,(1-F(b)) = 5{,}000 \times 0.006324555 \times 0.683772 \approx \$21.62kb(1−F(b))=5,000×0.006324555×0.683772≈$21.62 agrees with step 4.

    Keep safety separate from capital availability. Never releasing an undischarged reservation keeps the budget safe but locks up quota. A safe release needs one of: an authoritative final loss (for example a lurl call, where the contract makes it authoritative), a cancellation, a reconciliation result, or a binding contractual cutoff that extinguishes any remaining payment obligation. Such evidence can arrive early, so release need not wait for a deadline. An empirical upper bound on callback delay, or a local TTL, does not terminate a payment obligation. If no confirmable discharge mechanism exists, the system can either hold the reservation indefinitely or accept statistical overspend within an explicit risk limit; the latter is no longer a per-path hard-budget guarantee.

    Prompt discharge makes full-cap reservation cheap. By Little's law, open reservations equal bid rate rrr times mean time to discharge, and losers and winners discharge on different clocks: r [(1−F) Tloss+F Tbill]r\,[(1-F)\,T_{\text{loss}} + F\,T_{\text{bill}}]r[(1−F)Tloss​+FTbill​], where a loser waits for its loss notice and a winner for its billing notice. If the 1,000,000 requests arrive evenly over a day (rrr = 11.57 bids per second), with FFF = 0.316228, a mean loss-notice delay of 2 s and a mean billing delay of 60 s (both illustrative), about 235 reservations are open at once, locking about $1.49 of the $2,000 budget. At a 1-hour mean billing delay it is about 13,192 reservations and $83.44.

    Without any release, the same rule starves delivery. On the exact nano-dollar scale each bid holds 6,324,555 n$, so the $2,000 budget admits ⌊2×1012/6,324,555⌋=316,227\lfloor 2\times10^{12}/6{,}324{,}555 \rfloor = 316{,}227⌊2×1012/6,324,555⌋=316,227 bids before any reservation is released (316,205 at the rounded-up 6,325 µ$), about a third of the 1,000,000 requests. At the same bid and a 31.6% win rate, those yield about 100,000 wins, $632.45 of spend and an $867.54 gross spread, against $2,743.42 when losses are released promptly (Chapter 3, ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1). In general, with no release, B/bB/bB/b bids win B/LB/LB/L impressions in expectation whatever the bid, so gross spread is (B/L)(v−b)(B/L)(v-b)(B/L)(v−b) for b≥B/Nb \ge B/Nb≥B/N. The best response is to bid lower and stretch the budget over all NNN requests: b=B/N=$0.002b = B/N = \$0.002b=B/N=$0.002 (2 CPM) gives N(b/L)(v−b)=$1,300N(b/L)(v-b) = \$1{,}300N(b/L)(v−b)=$1,300, still less than half of $2,743.42.

    So release clearly lost bids promptly, shorten the time to confirm obligations, and allocate quota to regions or shards according to supply quality. Conservative reservation lowers overspend risk but causes under-delivery (spending less than planned). Measure that cost as lost gross spread, not as lock contention or budget-service QPS (queries per second).

    A hard cap on the advertiser's CPA bill is a separate problem. Post-click conversions arrive with a delay and still create receivables, so shutting off new media buying cannot stop impressions already delivered from producing further billable events. Handle this with contract terms, conservative control of the remaining quota and explicit tracking of in-flight conversion obligations. Do not pass off the media ledger as the advertiser ledger.

    Correctness boundaries for data and model releases

    Decision logs must link at least: the bid opportunity's identity; candidate eligibility and the final action; the timestamp or version of the features that were available; predicted probabilities and valuations; bid and budget policy; experiment assignment; win, loss and rejection reasons; impression, click and conversion times; attribution rules; billing status; and later adjustments. Not every field can be kept forever, and access and retention policies must match data permissions.

    Training samples must be reproducible at a specific version. Track the model, the calibrator (the post-hoc map from raw model score to probability), feature definitions, creatives and budget-control parameters together. Train only on matured labels, i.e. examples whose attribution window has closed, so that a missing conversion really is a negative. If one release changes both the model and the attribution window, you cannot tell why online results moved, even if they improved. Rolling back the model without rolling back features or the calibrator may not restore the old behavior either.

    A shadow deployment (the new model scores live traffic, but its outputs drive no decisions) can expose latency and distribution anomalies. Because it does not affect which opportunities are bought, it cannot show that the model makes money online. After a canary rollout (the new model controls a small share of live traffic), check whether the traffic mix and price distribution changed, and evaluate under the same budget constraints with matured labels. A new policy buying different opportunities is part of its effect. You cannot take credit for its traffic selection while analyzing the two arms as if they had bought the same samples.

    A dashboard that drives action

    Good monitoring ties each failure to an economic consequence. On-time response rate and no-bid rate broken down by reason explain lost opportunities. The gap between wins and billable impressions explains delivery and integration risk. The amount and age of open obligations explain budget lock-up. Duplicate billing, settlement discrepancies and the overspend tail measure financial correctness. Per-segment calibration, matured CPA and ROAS (attributed revenue divided by ad spend; Chapter 2) and incremental contribution (Chapter 4) measure policy quality.

    Signal Investigate first Conclusions you cannot draw directly
    Win rate up while profit down Bids, competing prices, traffic mix, fees The model is definitely worse, or definitely better
    Clicks up while conversions down Creatives, landing pages, click authenticity, label maturity CTR (click-through rate) should get more weight
    Sudden drop in spend Eligibility, deadlines, quota, economic constraints All under-delivery is a pacing failure
    Sudden drop in reported CPA Windows, attribution rules, event deduplication, backfill The customer got an equally large incremental lift
    Offline gain, online decline Time leakage, calibration, traffic selection, latency, release versions Just switch to a bigger model
    Open-reservation age rising Missing loss or billing notices, an exchange outage, contract cutoffs The reservations are safe to expire

    Thresholds come from contracts, loss tolerance and business objectives; there is no industry-standard number to copy. Duplicate billing, budget violations and changes to value definitions should each be able to trigger a stop-loss on its own. You cannot wait for conversion reports days later to discover that today's system is already out of control.

    AppLovin and Axon

    In this chapter

    • Trace one MAX auction from ad request to billing, and compute what the publisher, the winning bidder and AppLovin each earn.
    • Separate what MAX tells every bidder (including the final price of every auction it bid in) from what only the auctioneer sees, and state what AppLovin says Axon does not ingest.
    • Compute, in the uniform-threshold model of Chapter 3, how a sharper model and a miscalibrated model change win rate, spend and margin.
    • Name the observable tests that would separate "better model" from "privileged data" from "self-preferencing".
    • Read AppLovin's net revenue correctly, and know which numbers it cannot give you.

    This chapter sorts claims into three bins and labels each one. Public fact: stated in an SEC filing or in AppLovin's own documentation (a company statement, not an independent audit). Inference: our reasoning from those facts. Unknown: not determinable from public sources. Every number in a block marked hypothetical is a teaching assumption, not an AppLovin figure. All pages were retrieved on November 12, 2026.

    What public sources confirm about the products

    Vocabulary first. AppLovin is the ad-tech company under discussion (Chapter 1). A publisher is an app developer that sells ad slots inside its app; an advertiser buys them; an impression is one ad display. An SDK (software development kit) is a library compiled into the app; ad networks reach in-app inventory through SDKs. Mediation software sits in the publisher's app and decides, for each ad request, which of many demand sources fills it (Chapter 2). Under a waterfall, mediation calls ad networks one after another in a configured priority order; under in-app bidding, networks submit real-time bids for the same request and the highest bid wins. A DSP (demand-side platform) is a buyer's system that bids on behalf of advertisers. MAX is AppLovin's mediation product, which the company calls its in-app bidding solution. Axon is AppLovin's ad prediction and bidding engine (the filings call it a "recommendation engine" or "recommendation system"). The advertiser-facing product it powers is called Axon Ads Manager in the 2025 Form 10-K and AppLovin Ads in the Q3 2026 Form 10-Q; this chapter says AppLovin Ads.

    Public fact. AppLovin describes Axon as the AI advertising engine that powers AppLovin Ads. AppLovin bids on each impression according to the value Axon assigns to it for a given advertiser, aiming at that advertiser's return-on-ad-spend (ROAS) goal. The 2025 10-K and the Q3 2026 10-Q both say this product generates substantially all of AppLovin's revenue; the 10-K adds that revenue from other services "was not material". Axon official description, AppLovin 2025 10-K, AppLovin Q3 2026 10-Q

    Public fact. MAX's partner documentation describes a "unified first-price auction" in which the highest bidder wins, and its OpenRTB specification says bidders are expected "to pay the CPM amount they bid in full". DSPs (demand-side platforms) bidding through AppLovin Exchange integrate via OpenRTB 2.5, the IAB Tech Lab's real-time bidding protocol; ad networks bid from inside the app through bid tokens generated by their own SDKs. Non-bidding networks enter the same auction at a CPM price that the publisher types in or that auto-CPM sets daily from the network's reported CPM over the last seven days, weighting recent days more. The documented sequence for one ad request: MAX auction flow, AppLovin OpenRTB specification, bid responses and notices, auto-CPM

    1. Launch
      SDK start-up. When the user opens the app, MAX initializes every eligible network SDK.
    2. Request
      Ad request. The app asks for an ad. MAX collects bid tokens from the SDK bidders and sends the request to the MAX ad server.
    3. ≤ tmax
      Bids. The auction server sends bid requests to SDK bidders and to DSPs in AppLovin Exchange. Only bids returned within the timeout tmax count; the page gives no value.
    4. Resolve
      Unified auction. Bids are merged with the publisher's waterfall networks at their CPM prices; the highest CPM wins. Bidders whose bids are invalid (below the floor, missing or zero) get a loss notice now.
    5. Load
      Win and loss notices. The winner's ad is loaded. If the load fails, the winner gets a loss notice. Other bidders get their loss notice after a different winning ad loads.
    6. Render
      Billing. When the ad renders (video starts, or a graphic is displayed), MAX calls the winner's billing URL. The spec tells DSPs to track impressions and spend on this call.

    The two pages disagree slightly on when the win notice fires: the auction-flow page says after a successful load, the OpenRTB page says when the auction completes and the ad is sent to the device. Both put billing at render.

    Public fact. The notices carry prices. ${AUCTION_PRICE}, the final price, is substituted into both the win URL and the loss URL, "so every bidder (win or loss) sees the final paid price". The winner also receives ${AUCTION_MINIMUM_BID_TO_WIN}, defined as the second-highest bid. A loss notice carries an OpenRTB loss-reason code. MAX notice macros

    Worked example · hypothetical numbers

    One MAX auction: who earns what

    Given, for one ad request (prices in dollars CPM unless marked per impression): publisher floor $3.00; waterfall network W entered at $5.50. Bids: AppLovin Ads $7.50, SDK bidder X $6.80, DSP Y $6.00, DSP Z $2.00. AppLovin Ads bids for an advertiser who pays a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per conversion, with conversion probability q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005 per impression, so value v=qa=$0.015v=qa=\$0.015v=qa=$0.015 per impression; $7.50 CPM is the running example's first-price bid v/2v/2v/2 (Chapter 3). Let φ=5%\varphi=5\%φ=5% be the MAX fee on winning auction spend; MAX's real fee rate is not disclosed.

    1. Filter. Z's $2.00 is below the $3.00 floor, so Z gets a loss notice during the auction.
    2. Rank by CPM: $7.50 (AppLovin Ads) > $6.80 (X) > $6.00 (Y) > $5.50 (W). AppLovin Ads wins and, under first price, pays its bid: b=$7.50 CPM=$7.50/1000=$0.0075 per impression.b=\$7.50\ \text{CPM}=\$7.50/1000=\$0.0075\ \text{per impression}.b=$7.50 CPM=$7.50/1000=$0.0075 per impression.
    3. Notices. The winner learns the second-highest bid, $6.80, so it paid $7.50 − $6.80 = $0.70 CPM more than the minimum needed to win: the cost of bidding without seeing rivals. X and Y each receive AUCTION_PRICE = $7.50 in their loss notices, so each learns exactly the price it would have had to beat.
    4. Render and bill. The billing URL fires at render; the publisher is credited $0.0075 for this impression. Had the load failed, the winner would have received a loss notice and no billing call.
    5. AppLovin's revenue when its own bidder wins. AppLovin is an agent, so it books the advertiser charge minus the publisher payment (see below). Per impression, in expectation over the conversion: v−b=$0.015−$0.0075=$0.0075.v-b=\$0.015-\$0.0075=\$0.0075.v−b=$0.015−$0.0075=$0.0075.
    6. Counterfactual: X wins at the same $7.50. AppLovin earns only the MAX fee: φ b=0.05×$0.0075=$0.000375 per impression.\varphi\,b=0.05\times\$0.0075=\$0.000375\ \text{per impression}.φb=0.05×$0.0075=$0.000375 per impression.

    Result: the publisher earns $7.50 per 1,000 such impressions whoever wins; AppLovin expects $7.50 per 1,000 when its own bidder wins and $0.375 when a third party wins at the same price, a factor of 20.

    Check: (v−b)/(φb)=0.0075/0.000375=20(v-b)/(\varphi b)=0.0075/0.000375=20(v−b)/(φb)=0.0075/0.000375=20. The winning price ($7.50) is at least the second bid ($6.80), as a highest-bid-wins auction requires; a loss notice showing AUCTION_PRICE below the loser's own valid bid would break that rule.

    Inference. The factor of 20 depends on the hypothetical fee and margin, but its direction does not: the auctioneer earns far more when its own bidder wins. That is why the MAX FAQ's claim that every network, "including AppLovin, competes on equal footing" is the claim that matters most, and why the loss-notice price is useful: it lets every losing bidder check the ranking rule on its own traffic. MAX website FAQ

    Do not generalize this sequence. It is MAX's interface semantics. OpenRTB has analogous win, loss and billing callbacks (nurl, lurl, burl), but each exchange decides when they fire and what they commit the buyer to (Chapter 5). MAX's choices do not redefine those terms for other OpenRTB integrations.

    Public fact. The 10-K states that AppLovin is an agent, not a principal, in its advertising arrangements: it does not control the inventory before it passes to the advertiser and is not primarily responsible for delivering it. Under US GAAP an agent reports revenue net, so reported revenue is advertiser payments minus amounts paid or payable to publishers. Revenue is recognized when an impression is delivered (impression-based arrangements) or when a specified action such as a click or install occurs (action-based arrangements). The price is set dynamically from the advertiser's campaign goals, not as a fixed price per impression or per action. Reported revenue was $5,480.7 million in 2025 (up 70.0% from $3,224.1 million in 2024) and $2,184.8 million in Q3 2026 (up 55.5% from $1,405.0 million in Q3 2025); both exclude the divested Apps business. Revenue recognition note, AppLovin 2025 10-K, AppLovin Q3 2026 10-Q

    Inference. Because revenue is net, you cannot recover total advertiser spend, and therefore cannot compute the platform's take rate (amount retained as a share of advertiser spend, Chapter 2), from reported revenue alone. In the worked example the advertiser's expected charge is $15 per 1,000 impressions and AppLovin's revenue is $7.50; a filing shows only the second kind of number. Likewise, "MAX mediation is free for publishers" on the MAX website does not mean MAX is free to everyone in the chain. The same FAQ says bidding networks pay AppLovin a fee on the ad revenue they generate; the 10-K says MAX revenue is "a percentage of client spend", and the Q3 2026 10-Q says "a percentage of winning auction spend". Since revenue outside AppLovin Ads is immaterial, MAX's value to AppLovin lies mainly in the supply and the auction position it provides, not in its fees. MAX website FAQ, AppLovin 2025 10-K, AppLovin Q3 2026 10-Q

    Seeing data is not the same as being allowed to train on it

    Public fact (company statement). AppLovin's Axon page lists the inputs it says Axon uses: device and network information; engagement data about apps, ads and other digital properties, collected by AppLovin or shared by partners; advertisers' own user data, if they choose to share it; and win/loss notices from MAX, which the page says all bidders receive. The page also says the models do not ingest other bidders' bid information or other bidders' user data, nor sensitive personal information or protected characteristics such as age and gender. Axon data description

    Public fact (company statement). The 10-K itself describes a flywheel: as more advertisers use its solutions, AppLovin gains "access to more data regarding users and user engagement", and as distribution grows it gains "better insights for Axon AI". A footnote on that sentence carves out Adjust (below). AppLovin 2025 10-K, Business section

    Put the auction documentation and the Axon page side by side:

    What every MAX bidder learns (public fact)

    The bid request for each auction it is invited to. For each of its own bids: win or loss, a loss-reason code, and the final price AUCTION_PRICE. If it wins, the second-highest bid. A billing call when its ad renders.

    What only the auctioneer sees

    Every bid from every bidder on every request; which requests each bidder skipped; waterfall CPM prices, floors and other publisher settings; load and render outcomes for all networks. AppLovin says Axon does not ingest other bidders' bids or user data; whether the pipeline complies is unknown.

    Inference. Because the final price arrives on every win and loss, a MAX bidder observes, for each auction it entered, the price it had to beat. That is approximately the competitive threshold ZZZ of Chapter 3; the spec does not say how floors and waterfall entries enter these macros. So MAX bidders do not face the censored first-price problem of Chapter 3's last section, and price discovery is not, by itself, an asymmetry in AppLovin's favour. What remains asymmetric is the full bid vector and the traffic a bidder did not bid on.

    Public fact. Adjust is AppLovin's MMP (mobile measurement partner): a third party that advertisers use to attribute installs and in-app events to the ads that drove them (Chapter 2, Chapter 4). The 10-K says Adjust's platform is operated by a wholly owned subsidiary and that data generated by Adjust's services is not shared with AppLovin or used to optimize its recommendation engine unless a customer directs it. Separately, AppLovin sold its Apps business, its own portfolio of mobile games, to Tripledot. The sale closed on June 30, 2025, for $430.6 million in cash plus Tripledot shares valued at $285.0 million, about 22% of Tripledot's ordinary shares (20% fully diluted). AppLovin accounts for the stake under the equity method and treats Tripledot as a related party; Tripledot still buys AppLovin Ads. AppLovin 2025 10-K, AppLovin Q3 2026 10-Q

    These are the company's own statements and disclosures. Nobody outside the company has audited the data pipeline in public. Securities class actions are pending that allege materially false or misleading statements about the advertising solutions and financial growth (class period November 7, 2024 to March 27, 2025) and, in a second case, about matters including the development timeline of an ad-generation tool (February 12 to August 5, 2026); AppLovin says the allegations lack merit. Allegations are not findings. Legal proceedings, Q3 2026 10-Q

    Inference. The phrase "data flywheel" bundles four separate propositions. Each has a different evidentiary status:

    PropositionStatusWhat public sources say
    MAX receives every bid in order to run the auction.Public factFollows from the documented unified auction: the auction server must see the bids to rank them.
    Axon is permitted to use those bids.Company deniesThe Axon page says the models do not ingest other bidders' bid information or user data. Only win/loss notices, which all bidders receive, are listed as inputs.
    The training pipeline actually uses them.UnknownNo public audit either way.
    Only AppLovin has the data that matters for training.UnknownNot established. Final prices go to every participating bidder. The full bid vector stays with MAX, and the company says Axon does not use it. The 10-K says engagement data grows with distribution but gives no measure of its value. Adjust data is excluded by default.

    Owning a measurement company does not mean owning all of its customers' data for training. Merging the four propositions into one "flywheel" assumes the competitive advantage that the argument is supposed to prove.

    Unknown. Public materials do not reveal Axon's current model architecture, parameter count, feature coverage, training frequency, loss function or budget controller. Nor can they separate how much of a given quarter's growth came from the model, the creatives, supply access, customer mix or attribution rules. The architecture diagrams and algorithms elsewhere in this reader are tools for understanding the problem, not a reverse-engineering of Axon.

    How a prediction advantage becomes retained profit

    Start from a standard result: for a single decision-maker, the optimal value of extra information is nonnegative. Let Π(I)\Pi(\mathcal I)Π(I) be the set of feasible policies (same objective, actions and budget constraints) that are measurable with respect to information I\mathcal II. Then

    Iold⊆Inew  ⇒  Π(Iold)⊆Π(Inew)  ⇒  max⁡π∈Π(Inew)E[u(π)] ≥ max⁡π∈Π(Iold)E[u(π)].\mathcal I_{\text{old}}\subseteq\mathcal I_{\text{new}}\;\Rightarrow\;\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{old}})\subseteq\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{new}})\;\Rightarrow\;\max_{\pi\in\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{new}})}\mathbb E[u(\pi)]\ \ge\ \max_{\pi\in\Pi(\mathcal I_{\text{old}})}\mathbb E[u(\pi)].Iold​⊆Inew​⇒Π(Iold​)⊆Π(Inew​)⇒π∈Π(Inew​)max​E[u(π)] ≥ π∈Π(Iold​)max​E[u(π)].

    The new decision-maker can always ignore the extra information and replay the old policy. The result needs every one of these premises:

    • Competitors' strategies and the distribution of clearing prices stay fixed.
    • The objective, the action set and constraints such as budget are unchanged.
    • Acquiring and using the information costs nothing.
    • The new information is available at decision time and refines the old (the old signal can be recovered from the new one).
    • Conditional valuations are accurate, and the policy actually optimizes on them.

    A higher offline AUC (ranking quality on held-out logs) establishes none of this. It does not show that the new information set contains the old one, that probabilities are calibrated, or that decisions are optimal. Still less does it show that the gain survives once the market reacts. The next two examples hold the market fixed and isolate two properties: refinement (telling opportunities apart) and calibration (getting the probability level right).

    Check: $2,812.50×(1−0.22)=$2,700\$2{,}812.50\times(1-0.2^2)=\$2{,}700$2,812.50×(1−0.22)=$2,700 and $2,812.50×1.22=$4,050\$2{,}812.50\times1.2^2=\$4{,}050$2,812.50×1.22=$4,050. Underpredicting by the same amount (r=0.8r=0.8r=0.8) costs the same $112.50 of profit but cuts spend to $1,800.

    Inference. Suppose a new model finds more valuable opportunities. It can stop buying low-value impressions, and it can bid more for high-value ones. Bidding more raises publisher revenue. Competitors and publishers' floor prices (the minimum price a seller accepts, Chapter 3) keep adjusting, and advertisers may push for better pricing. How the resulting rent is split depends on whether the information is exclusive, whether access to it is stable, whether the model generalizes, whether customers have alternatives, and how the platform charges. Both "a model lead turns entirely into profit" and "auctions compete away every advantage" overstate the case.

    To test for a moat, do not ask whether a competitor can build a similar model. Ask whether, on the same supply surface (the inventory one can bid on), with comparable data permissions, label maturity windows (how long one waits before treating a conversion label as final) and budget constraints, new advertisers and additional budget keep producing incremental contribution. Model, measurement, supply access, creatives, execution cost and customer relationships all have to enter the explanation together. Correct for survivorship bias too: a showcase of the surviving high-return customers proves nothing about the rest.

    Inference. Three explanations compete for AppLovin's results: a better model on the same data; privileged data that rivals cannot get; and self-preferencing, meaning MAX lets AppLovin's own bidder win without the highest bid, or lets it bid after seeing rivals' bids. Revenue growth fits all three. These observations would separate them:

    ObservationBetter modelPrivileged dataSelf-preferencingWho can observe it
    Outbid loss notices where the loser's valid bid exceeds AUCTION_PRICENeverNeverOccurEvery losing bidder, from its own logs
    Gap between AUCTION_PRICE and a loser's bid, when AppLovin wins vs when others winSmooth; smaller if AppLovin shades betterSmooth; smaller if it predicts ZZZ betterSpike just above the loser's bid if AppLovin bids lastLosing bidders, pooled across many auctions
    AppLovin Ads' performance on supply MAX does not mediateAdvantage persistsAdvantage shrinks where AppLovin lacks the dataAdvantage disappearsAdvertisers buying across supply sources
    Incremental return per dollar in advertiser holdout tests (Chapter 4)HigherHigherNot higher: AppLovin wins more, advertisers gain nothingAdvertisers running holdouts
    Performance after losing a data sourceSmall changeClear dropNo changeAdvertisers; outsiders only coarsely

    The last row has one public instance: AppLovin sold its own games in June 2025, and revenue from continuing operations, which never included those games, still grew 55.5% year on year in Q3 2026. That weakens the claim that first-party data from those games was essential. It is not decisive: model releases, new advertiser categories such as e-commerce, and pricing changed over the same period, and the filings do not say what data, if any, flows between Tripledot and AppLovin today (unknown). None of the auction-level tests has been published.

    Inference (generic, not a claim about AppLovin's practices). If a platform subsidizes advertisers, for example with credits or discounted pricing, the subsidy buys room for trial and error. It does not buy unbiased labels (the conversion and revenue events used as training targets). Suppose labels come only from subsidized customers, cheap traffic or high-intent retargeting (showing ads to users who have already interacted with the advertiser, and who would often convert anyway). Then the learned relationships may not transfer to the broader market once full pricing applies. The early metrics to check are customer retention after subsidies end, the quality of matured labels the platform is permitted to use, calibration within each segment, and the marginal profit curve. Event counts alone say little.

    Three problems that attractive numbers hide

    Definitions for this section. pCTR is the model's predicted click probability for an impression. Clearing CPM is 1,000 × media cost / impressions: what the buyer actually paid, per thousand impressions. Publisher eCPM is 1,000 × publisher revenue / impressions. A cohort is the set of users acquired by a campaign in a given period. Attributed revenue is revenue that the attribution rule credits to the ad; it is not the same as incremental revenue, the revenue that would not have occurred without the ad (Chapter 4). For a cohort CCC with acquisition spend SCS_CSC​, where user uuu was acquired at time tut_utu​,

    D7 ROAS(C)=∑u∈CRu([tu,  tu+168 h))SC,\text{D7 ROAS}(C)=\frac{\sum_{u\in C}R_u\big([t_u,\;t_u+168\,\text{h})\big)}{S_C},D7 ROAS(C)=SC​∑u∈C​Ru​([tu​,tu​+168h))​,

    where Ru(⋅)R_u(\cdot)Ru​(⋅) is attributed revenue from user uuu in the half-open window. Compute it only after every user's 7-day window has fully elapsed. It remains an attributed return, not an incremental one.

    1. Higher pCTR with flat ROAS. If pCTR rises, clearing CPM rises with it and D7 ROAS stays flat, the model may simply be buying more clickable traffic at a higher price. Decompose the change into price and traffic mix before declaring a win on pCTR or offline AUC.
    2. Higher publisher eCPM. If MAX publisher eCPM rises, publishers earn more per thousand impressions. Total publisher revenue also depends on impression volume. Neither number shows that advertisers gained matching incremental profit; in the miscalibration example above, publisher revenue rises 44% while the bidder's profit falls.
    3. Subsidized growth. If subsidies bring in more advertisers and conversions, but retention falls once full pricing applies, the subsidy may have bought a training distribution that cannot be reproduced.

    For a would-be entrant, technical replicability is only one dimension. The questions that need evidence are: which labels you are permitted to obtain, which supply you can access, how you identify each customer's incrementality, under what constraints marginal returns stay positive, and how long those conditions last.

    Takeaways

    • MAX is a documented first-price, highest-CPM-wins auction; billing fires at render; every bidder whose bid was evaluated receives the final price of the auction in its win or loss notice (whether rejected bids, e.g. below the floor, also receive it is not documented).
    • AppLovin books net revenue, almost all of it from AppLovin Ads. Advertiser spend and take rate are not disclosed, and MAX fees are immaterial to revenue.
    • The auctioneer earns far more when its own bidder wins than from its fee on a rival's win. Neutrality is the claim to test, and loss-notice prices let any bidder test it.
    • Refinement raises profit at a constant win count; miscalibration moves spend to first order and profit only to second order. Neither win rate nor publisher eCPM identifies a better model.

    Comprehensive exercises and answers

    How to use this set

    Time: 50 minutes. Answer all ten questions closed-book in 30, then mark yourself against the collapsed answers in 20. Scoring: 10 points each. Questions 2–6 are calculations, marked on the numbers and on naming the right party, unit and assumption; each answer shows a full worked solution. Questions 1 and 7–10 are conceptual, marked against the listed points a full-marks answer must contain. Pass mark (this reader's own, not an industry standard): 80 or more, with no conceptual error on Questions 3, 4, 6 or 8. Sources: Q1 chapter 2; Q2–Q4 and Q7 chapter 3; Q5 and Q6 chapter 4; Q8 chapter 5; Q9 chapters 3–4; Q10 chapter 6.

    Ten questions, 100 points

    CPA-contract parameters for Questions 2, 5 and 9. The running campaign from “A fictional campaign used throughout” (A one-day learning roadmap), worked through in the optional network-spread appendix. Questions 3–4 separately specify the main advertiser direct-buying contract.

    • Opportunities. N=1,000,000N=1{,}000{,}000N=1,000,000 statistically identical bid opportunities (bid requests from publishers). Every auction win yields exactly one successful impression; display failures are ignored here (Real-time advertising systems relaxes this).
    • Contracts. The ad network sells to the advertiser on CPA terms: it charges a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable attributed conversion, a conversion that the agreed attribution rules credit to the ad and that the contract makes payable. It buys impressions from publishers in first-price auctions: the winner pays its own bid, per impression.
    • Conversion probability. Each impression produces a billable attributed conversion with probability q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005, the same for every opportunity and independent of the bid and of competition. The network's expected collections per impression are v=qa=$0.015v=qa=\$0.015v=qa=$0.015.
    • Advertiser economics. Pre-advertising contribution per order is g=$40g=\$40g=$40: sales revenue minus goods, fulfillment and other per-order variable costs, before ad spend and fixed costs. The true causal lift is Δq=0.0002\Delta q=0.0002Δq=0.0002: for the same opportunity, showing the ad raises the probability of an order by 0.0002 compared with not showing it. Here Δq<q\Delta q<qΔq<q is a property of the given numbers. The two probabilities measure different events and neither bounds the other in general; attribution can both credit nonincremental orders and miss incremental ones.
    • Competition. The competitive threshold ZZZ is the highest competing bid for an opportunity, in dollars per impression, with Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\text{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L), L=$0.02L=\$0.02L=$0.02, independently across opportunities. A bid bbb wins when b≥Zb\ge Zb≥Z, so the win rate is F(b)=b/LF(b)=b/LF(b)=b/L for 0≤b≤L0\le b\le L0≤b≤L.
    • Objective. In the optional network-spread appendix, the network picks one uniform bid bbb for all opportunities to maximize expected media gross spread: expected collections from the advertiser minus expected payments to publishers. That appendix uses a network media budget, which is not the advertiser spend cap in Questions 3–4.
    • Units. “Spend”, “bill” and “collections” mean expected values. CPM is a price per thousand impressions; eCPM (effective CPM) expresses any expected amount per impression as an amount per thousand impressions. Dollars per impression × 1,000 = CPM.
    Question 1: Product dimensions. An ad runs in a mobile game's rewarded video slot (a video the player chooses to watch in exchange for an in-game reward), and the impression is bought in a real-time auction. The publisher charges the buyer per impression. The advertiser has set a target CPA (tCPA) of $30, the average cost per conversion the bidding algorithm aims for (Products and cash flow). Can you conclude that the advertiser pays only when a conversion happens? Which two terms of the advertiser's contract would you need to see to settle it?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Answer: no. A target CPA is an optimization goal for the bidder, not a billing unit. An advertiser can be billed per impression or per click while the bidder steers toward an average of $30 per conversion.

    A full-marks answer contains:

    1. Target ≠ billing event. tCPA says what the algorithm aims for; it says nothing about what triggers a charge.
    2. Missing term 1, the advertiser-side billing basis and price: billed per impression, click, install or conversion, and at what rate.
    3. Missing term 2, the definition of a billable conversion: which event counts, the attribution window, deduplication, and refund and chargeback rules. Even under per-conversion billing, “a conversion happens” means “a conversion the contract makes payable”.
    4. The publisher side is a separate contract. Per-impression buying from the publisher says nothing about how the advertiser is billed. If the advertiser pays per conversion while the network pays per impression, the network carries the conversion risk. Each side's budget must be confirmed separately; neither follows from the tCPA.

    Scoring: 5 points for separating the optimization target from the billing basis; 5 points for naming both missing terms.

    Question 2: Three values. Using the shared parameters above, compute three values, each as an eCPM (dollars per thousand impressions): (a) the network's expected collections; (b) the advertiser's attributed contribution, i.e. attributed conversions valued at ggg each; (c) the advertiser's incremental contribution, i.e. caused orders valued at ggg each. Why can't the network simply replace its own receivables estimate with the advertiser's incremental contribution?
    Reference answers and scoring points
    Worked solution

    Three values per thousand impressions

    Given: q=0.0005q=0.0005q=0.0005 billable attributed conversions per impression, a=$30a=\$30a=$30 per billable conversion, g=$40g=\$40g=$40 contribution per order, Δq=0.0002\Delta q=0.0002Δq=0.0002 caused orders per impression.

    1. (a) Network collections: each impression bills aaa with probability qqq. 1000 q a=1000×0.0005×30=1000×$0.015=$15 eCPM\begin{aligned}1000\,q\,a &= 1000\times 0.0005\times 30\\ &= 1000\times\$0.015 = \$15\ \text{eCPM}\end{aligned}1000qa​=1000×0.0005×30=1000×$0.015=$15 eCPM​
    2. (b) Attributed contribution: the same attributed conversions, valued at ggg. 1000 q g=1000×0.0005×40=1000×$0.020=$20 eCPM\begin{aligned}1000\,q\,g &= 1000\times 0.0005\times 40\\ &= 1000\times\$0.020 = \$20\ \text{eCPM}\end{aligned}1000qg​=1000×0.0005×40=1000×$0.020=$20 eCPM​
    3. (c) Incremental contribution: only caused orders count. 1000 Δq g=1000×0.0002×40=1000×$0.008=$8 eCPM\begin{aligned}1000\,\Delta q\,g &= 1000\times 0.0002\times 40\\ &= 1000\times\$0.008 = \$8\ \text{eCPM}\end{aligned}1000Δqg​=1000×0.0002×40=1000×$0.008=$8 eCPM​

    Result: (a) $15 eCPM, (b) $20 eCPM, (c) $8 eCPM.

    Check: (b)/(a) = g/a=40/30g/a = 40/30g/a=40/30 = 4/3 ✓, and (c)/(b) = Δq/q\Delta q/qΔq/q = 0.4 ✓. The advertiser pays $15 for $8 of incremental contribution, a loss of $7 per thousand impressions; equivalently its true incremental CPA is qa/Δq=0.015/0.0002=$75qa/\Delta q = 0.015/0.0002 = \$75qa/Δq=0.015/0.0002=$75 per caused order against g=$40g=\$40g=$40, matching chapter 3.

    Why not substitute (c) for (a). A full-marks answer makes these points:

    • Receivables are set by the contract. The network collects $30 for every billable attributed conversion, whether or not the ad caused it. Its expected revenue per impression is qaqaqa; bids priced off Δq g\Delta q\,gΔqg would misprice every auction (here they would value an impression at $8 instead of $15 eCPM).
    • Incremental contribution is the advertiser's objective. It measures what the ads are really worth to the advertiser and so its long-run willingness to keep paying.
    • The gap is a separate risk. A $7 loss per thousand impressions is a churn risk. Track it as its own metric or constraint (an incremental-CPA or iROAS guardrail), not by rewriting the receivables forecast.

    Scoring: 2 points for each number; 4 points for distinguishing the two objectives.

    Question 4: An advertiser's budget is a cap. Keep Question 3's direct-buying contract and value. What happens to the optimal first-price bid with a $2,000 expected ad-spend cap? What if the cap is $500? Then find the ideal second-price bid and advertiser outcome under the $2,000 cap. Do these expected-budget solutions guarantee a realized hard spending limit?

    Question 5: Calibration and sampling. A conversion model is trained on downsampled data: every positive example is kept, and each negative is kept independently with probability 10%, regardless of its features (Attribution, experiments, and data). Training applies no weight correction, and the model is calibrated on the sampled distribution. For some feature vector it outputs 0.5. What is the true conversion probability? Separately: a new model has a higher AUC than the current one, but its predicted probabilities are about twice the observed conversion rates across the board. Can it go live as is?
    Reference answers and scoring points
    Worked solution

    Undoing negative downsampling

    Given: negative retention rate s=0.1s=0.1s=0.1, positives all kept, sampled-data prediction ps=0.5p_s=0.5ps​=0.5 (calibrated on the sampled data). Want: true probability ppp for the same feature vector.

    1. For a fixed feature vector, sampling keeps a fraction 1 of positives and sss of negatives, so it multiplies the odds by 1/s1/s1/s: ps1−ps=p(1−p) s.\frac{p_s}{1-p_s}=\frac{p}{(1-p)\,s}.1−ps​ps​​=(1−p)sp​.
    2. True odds: s⋅ps1−ps=0.1×0.50.5=0.1s\cdot\frac{p_s}{1-p_s}=0.1\times\frac{0.5}{0.5}=0.1s⋅1−ps​ps​​=0.1×0.50.5​=0.1.
    3. Back to a probability: p=0.11+0.1=111≈0.0909.p=\frac{0.1}{1+0.1}=\frac{1}{11}\approx 0.0909.p=1+0.10.1​=111​≈0.0909.

    Result: p = 1/11 ≈ 0.0909 (9.09%).

    Check: the closed form p=s ps1−ps+s ps=0.050.5+0.05=0.0909p=\frac{s\,p_s}{1-p_s+s\,p_s}=\frac{0.05}{0.5+0.05}=0.0909p=1−ps​+sps​sps​​=0.5+0.050.05​=0.0909 ✓; at s=1s=1s=1 it returns p=psp=p_sp=ps​, as it must.

    The higher-AUC model cannot go live as is. A full-marks answer contains:

    • AUC is blind to calibration. It depends only on ranking and is unchanged by any strictly increasing transformation of the scores.
    • Bids use absolute probabilities. The network’s expected receipts per impression are v=30qv=30qv=30q, so doubling qqq doubles the value the bidder thinks it buys. In the shared example without a budget, the bid rises from v/2v/2v/2 = $7.50 CPM to (2v)/2=$0.015(2v)/2=\$0.015(2v)/2=$0.015 per impression = $15 CPM, where the true spread (0.015−b) b/L(0.015-b)\,b/L(0.015−b)b/L is zero: the whole $2,812.50 of spread per million requests is lost.
    • Launch checklist. Confirm the sampling correction was applied; recalibrate on matured labels; check calibration by segment (a uniform factor of 2 rarely holds everywhere); evaluate monetary loss, not ranking metrics; then run a limited online experiment.

    Second-order point: under a binding budget a pacing multiplier would absorb a perfectly uniform factor for one campaign (the appendix’s $6.3246 CPM network bid is set by its binding $2,000 media budget, not by vvv), but across campaigns and segments with different errors it misallocates spend. Scoring: number 4 points; calibration and launch logic 6 points.

    Question 6: Incremental profit. This is the experiment from Attribution, experiments, and data. An eligible population is randomly split into a treatment group (the campaign may deliver) and a control group (it may not), 100,000 users each. Over the same matured window, treatment has 1,200 purchases and control 1,000. The attribution system credits 500 of the treatment purchases to the ad. Ad spend is $5,000. Net revenue per purchase is $50 (sales revenue after refunds and other adjustments, before goods, fulfillment and other costs), and the pre-advertising contribution rate is 40% of net revenue. Assume randomization and event definitions are correct and that the groups do not affect each other. Compute attributed ROAS (attributed revenue ÷ ad spend), incremental ROAS (iROAS: incremental revenue ÷ ad spend) and incremental contribution profit (incremental contribution − ad spend). Then explain why you cannot just compare the treatment users who actually saw the ad with the control group.
    Reference answers and scoring points
    Worked solution

    Attributed versus incremental returns

    Given: 100,000 users per arm; purchases 1,200 (treatment) and 1,000 (control); 500 attributed purchases; ad spend $5,000; net revenue $50 per purchase; contribution rate 40%.

    1. Incremental purchases (equal arms, so compare counts directly): 1,200−1,000=2001{,}200-1{,}000=2001,200−1,000=200.
    2. Attributed ROAS: 500×$50$5,000=$25,000$5,000=5.0\frac{500\times\$50}{\$5{,}000}=\frac{\$25{,}000}{\$5{,}000}=5.0$5,000500×$50​=$5,000$25,000​=5.0
    3. iROAS: 200×$50$5,000=$10,000$5,000=2.0\frac{200\times\$50}{\$5{,}000}=\frac{\$10{,}000}{\$5{,}000}=2.0$5,000200×$50​=$5,000$10,000​=2.0
    4. Incremental contribution profit: contribution per purchase $50×0.4=$20\$50\times0.4=\$20$50×0.4=$20, so 200×$20−$5,000=$4,000−$5,000=−$1,000.\begin{aligned}&200\times\$20-\$5{,}000\\ &=\$4{,}000-\$5{,}000\\ &=-\$1{,}000.\end{aligned}​200×$20−$5,000=$4,000−$5,000=−$1,000.​
    5. Break-even: iROAS 1/0.4=2.51/0.4=2.51/0.4=2.5, i.e. $5,000/$20=250\$5{,}000/\$20=250$5,000/$20=250 incremental purchases.
    6. Uncertainty (assuming each user buys at most once and users are independent): SE2=1200(1−0.012)+1000(1−0.010)=1185.6+990=2175.6,SE=2175.6≈46.6.\begin{aligned}\text{SE}^2&=1200(1-0.012)\\ &\quad+1000(1-0.010)\\ &=1185.6+990=2175.6,\\ \text{SE}&=\sqrt{2175.6}\approx 46.6.\end{aligned}SE2SE​=1200(1−0.012)+1000(1−0.010)=1185.6+990=2175.6,=2175.6​≈46.6.​ 95% interval for the lift: 200±1.96×46.6≈[109, 291]200\pm1.96\times46.6\approx[109,\,291]200±1.96×46.6≈[109,291]. Profit is 20⋅lift−5,00020\cdot\text{lift}-5{,}00020⋅lift−5,000, so it lies in about [−$2,830, +$830][-\$2{,}830,\,+\$830][−$2,830,+$830].

    Result: attributed ROAS 5.0, iROAS 2.0, incremental contribution profit −$1,000 (95% interval about −$2,830 to +$830).

    Check: attribution credits 500/200 = 2.5 times the measured lift, and attributed ROAS ÷ iROAS = 5.0/2.0 = 2.5 ✓. The interval matches chapter 4.

    Why not compare exposed treatment users with control. Full-marks points:

    • Exposure is decided after randomization, by targeting, auction wins and how active each user is, all of which correlate with the propensity to buy.
    • Exposed treatment users and the whole control group are therefore no longer comparable populations: the comparison reintroduces selection bias, typically inflating the effect.
    • Analyze the ITT (intent to treat: the effect by original random assignment) first.
    • The effect on exposed users needs extra assumptions or designs: divide the ITT by the exposure rate (assuming no effect on unexposed users), or use ghost ads that record which control users would have been exposed.

    Scoring: numbers 6 points; causal and statistical caveats 4 points.

    Question 7: Price feedback. In a first-price auction you bid $8 CPM, win, and pay $8 CPM. Can you use $8 as a supervised label for that auction's competitive threshold ZZZ (From prediction to bidding and budgets)? In a second-price auction, where the winner pays ZZZ, what bias results if you fit a model of ZZZ only on the prices you paid in auctions you won?
    Reference answers and scoring points

    First price: no. You pay your own bid, so the price carries no information about ZZZ beyond the win itself. Full-marks points:

    • A win says only Z≤8Z\le 8Z≤8 (CPM): a censored observation bounding ZZZ from above, not a label.
    • A loss says only Z>bZ>bZ>b.
    • You learn more only if the exchange returns an extra signal, such as the minimum bid that would have won.

    Second price: downward bias. Full-marks points:

    • A win reveals ZZZ exactly, but only when Z≤bZ\le bZ≤b; training on wins alone drops every auction with Z>bZ>bZ>b, truncating the sample from above.
    • The fitted ZZZ is biased low: it underestimates the threshold and overestimates the win rate at every bid. Cost errors depend on the bid evaluated. Below the logged bid bbb, the predicted cost per win, E[Z∣Z≤b′]E[Z\mid Z\le b']E[Z∣Z≤b′], is correct, but the inflated win rate overstates expected cost per request. Above bbb, the model has no data and understates the cost per win. The bias is worst on contested, high-value inventory, where you lose most often.
    • Fix: keep losses as censored observations at bbb and maximize the censored likelihood (each win contributes the density f(Z)f(Z)f(Z), each loss 1−F(b)1-F(b)1−F(b)), or use a survival-analysis estimator.
    Illustration

    How large the truncation bias is

    Given (for illustration, not stated in the question): Z∼Uniform(0,$20 CPM)Z\sim\text{Uniform}(0,\$20\ \text{CPM})Z∼Uniform(0,$20 CPM), the shared example's LLL, and you always bid $8 CPM in a second-price auction.

    1. Win rate: F(8)=8/20=40%F(8)=8/20=40\%F(8)=8/20=40%. The other 60% of auctions produce no price.
    2. Prices seen on wins: Z∣Z≤8∼Uniform(0,8)Z\mid Z\le 8\sim\text{Uniform}(0,8)Z∣Z≤8∼Uniform(0,8), mean $4 CPM. True mean: 20/2=$1020/2=\$1020/2=$10 CPM.
    3. A model fitted to those prices puts all its mass below $8 and predicts a 100% win rate at an $8 bid; the truth is 40%. Below $8 it gets the cost per win right (b′/2b'/2b′/2), but its win rate b′/8b'/8b′/8 is 2.5 times the true b′/20b'/20b′/20, so it overstates cost per request 2.5-fold. Above $8 it predicts $4 per win against a true b′/2b'/2b′/2.

    Result: the wins-only estimate of mean Z is $4 CPM against a true $10 CPM.

    Check: in general the wins-only mean is b/2b/2b/2, which reaches the true L/2L/2L/2 only at b=Lb=Lb=L, when you win everything and nothing is censored ✓.

    Scoring: 5 points per part.

    Question 8: Ledger states. A bid is placed under Case A in “How delivery probability changes the bid” (Real-time advertising systems): the publisher is paid only after a successful impression, and the contract names the OpenRTB billing notice burl as the signal that confirms billing. Before the bid was sent, the budget system reserved the bid's maximum possible cost. After the bid, a win notice (nurl) arrives but no billing notice; then a duplicate of the same win notice arrives. Can the system book this as confirmed media spend? Can it release the whole reservation? How should it handle the billing notice when it later arrives twice?
    Reference answers and scoring points
    • Confirm spend? No. Under this contract a win creates no payment obligation; only a successful impression does, and burl is what confirms it. The duplicate nurl is deduplicated on the bid's business key (exchange, request, impression and bid IDs) and changes nothing.
    • Release the whole reservation? No. The impression may still render and burl may arrive late, so the external obligation is still open. Releasing the reservation would let the same budget be spent twice. Release it only on authoritative evidence that the obligation is gone: a confirmed loss or cancellation, a reconciliation result, or a binding contractual cutoff. A local timeout is not such evidence.
    • Billing notice twice. The first valid burl moves the actual billed amount from reserved to confirmed spend and releases the difference between the reservation cap and that amount. The duplicate is an idempotent no-op on the ledger, logged for reconciliation. Late, missing or mismatched notices go to a pending-reconciliation state and are settled against the exchange's settlement reports. An amount above the cap means the cost-cap premise has broken: send it to exception handling.

    The ledger, with cap ccc (the reservation) and actual billed amount p≤cp\le cp≤c, starting from confirmed spend CCC and open reservations RRR:

    EventLedger actionConfirmed spendReserved
    Bid admittedReserve cap cccCCCR+cR+cR+c
    nurlMark “won, not billed”; no money movesCCCR+cR+cR+c
    nurl againDeduplicate on business key: no-opCCCR+cR+cR+c
    burlBook ppp; release c−pc-pc−p (one atomic step)C+pC+pC+pRRR
    burl againNo-op; log for reconciliationC+pC+pC+pRRR
    Instead: authoritative “not billable”Release cccCCCRRR

    Only admission raises confirmed + reserved, and admission checks it against the budget; every later step keeps it flat or lowers it. That is what makes the hard budget safe. Scoring: distinguishing the states 4 points; managing the open obligation 3 points; idempotency and reconciliation 3 points.

    Question 9: Offline versus online. A new conversion model beats the current one on offline log loss, but in an online A/B test the network's media gross spread (collections minus media cost, From prediction to bidding and budgets) falls. Give four distinct diagnostic hypotheses, and for two of them name the logs or metrics that would confirm or rule them out.
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Any four distinct mechanisms from this list, each with its causal path to lower spread:

    HypothesisMechanismEvidence
    Miscalibration where it mattersAverage log loss improves while calibration on high-bid traffic worsens. In first price you win precisely where you overestimate, so overbidding concentrates there.Predicted vs matured realized conversion rate by arm, publisher and predicted-score bucket.
    Traffic or price mix shiftOffline data were selected by the old model's wins; the new model bids differently and wins traffic and prices the evaluation set never covered.Per-arm bids, win rate, clearing price, traffic composition, cost and collections per impression.
    Label problemsLabel delay (immature conversions offline) or leakage (features carrying post-impression information) inflates the offline score.Re-score offline on fully matured labels; feature timestamps vs impression time.
    Training–serving skewFeature or model versions differ online, features are missing, or higher latency causes timeouts.Logged online features vs offline recomputation; missing-feature and timeout rates by arm.
    Downstream interactionsBid shading, pacing or budget control tuned to the old score distribution; pacing oscillation.Pacing multiplier and spend-rate traces by arm; bid-shading factor distributions.
    Measurement differencesFees, attribution definitions or label windows differ between arms, or the arms share budgets and interfere.Arm configuration diff; A/A comparison; shared-budget audit.

    A full-marks answer gives four mechanisms that are actually distinct (not four flavors of “the model is worse”) and, for two of them, evidence that would localize the problem rather than merely restate it. Scoring: four mechanisms 6 points in total; two pieces of evidence 4 points in total.

    Question 10: Evidence for a moat. MAX is AppLovin's mediation product, which runs publishers' auctions across demand sources; Adjust is its MMP (mobile measurement partner), which attributes conversions on behalf of advertisers; Axon is its prediction and bidding engine (AppLovin and Axon). Someone claims: “MAX sees all bids and Adjust has all the attribution data, so Axon necessarily trains on all of it, and a competitor that can replicate the technology only needs to subsidize data purchases to catch up.” Identify at least four missing links in this argument, and propose one validation metric better than total conversion volume.
    Reference answers and scoring points

    Missing links (any four, each stated as the specific step that fails):

    1. Seeing is not permission. MAX receives bids to run auctions; contracts and privacy rules govern any other use. MAX also sees only the auctions it mediates, not all bids.
    2. Permission is not use. Data allowed for training does not necessarily enter the training pipeline.
    3. Processing is not ownership. Adjust processes attribution data on advertisers' behalf; owning the MMP is not owning its customers' data.
    4. More data is not unbiased or transferable data. Samples collected under one delivery policy and supply mix are selection-biased for other policies.
    5. Same model, different access. Replicating the technology does not replicate supply access and execution conditions.
    6. Prediction is not incrementality. Predicting short-term responses well is not delivering incremental profit to advertisers.
    7. Subsidies prove nothing about retention. They cannot show that advertisers stay once full pricing starts; and some of the data is not for sale at any price.

    Better metrics (any one, with why it beats volume): advertiser retention and spend after subsidies end; matured incremental contribution from holdout tests under the same budget constraint; or the marginal-return curve of additional budget. Each measures value delivered to the advertiser rather than activity. Scoring: four gaps 8 points; a suitable metric 2 points.

    In this chapter

    • Erratum. The RTB monograph’s budget-constrained second-price bid counts the win rate twice. The correct coefficient is 6LB/N\sqrt{6LB/N}6LB/N​, valid for B/N≤L/6B/N\le L/6B/N≤L/6; the published one overspends the budget by at least 18% wherever the correct one applies (43.6% in the running example).
    • Sources. What to read next, and what each source is good for.
    • Glossary. The reader’s canonical definitions of ad-tech terms, alphabetical.
    • Review record. What was checked in each editorial pass, and what was not.

    An erratum in the RTB monograph’s second-price example

    The monograph “Display Advertising with Real-Time Bidding (RTB) and Behavioural Targeting” by Wang, Zhang and Yuan (arXiv:1610.03013v2, 122 pages; arXiv date July 15, 2017, title page July 18) is a sound end-to-end account of RTB. One worked example in its Section 5.3.4 gets the budget equation wrong: it counts the win probability twice. This section re-derives the example, locates the slip and sizes the error. Equation and page numbers below refer to v2 and were checked against the PDF. arXiv metadata

    Symbols

    Notation follows Prediction and bidding. The monograph’s symbol, where different, is in brackets.

    • ZZZ: the competitive threshold, the highest competing bid on one bid request. We win if our bid is at least ZZZ [market price zzz].
    • L>0L>0L>0: the upper bound of ZZZ, with Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L) [lll].
    • b≥0b\ge 0b≥0: our bid on one request. ZZZ, LLL and bbb are dollars per impression (×1,000 for CPM).
    • F(b)=P(Z≤b)F(b)=P(Z\le b)F(b)=P(Z≤b): the win rate at bid bbb; f=F′f=F'f=F′ [w(b)w(b)w(b), pzp_zpz​].
    • r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1]r∈[0,1]: the request’s predicted click-through rate (pCTR), the probability that a won impression is clicked. Here rrr is a probability, not money. (In the SAM paper cited in Prediction and bidding, rrr is the reward per conversion; that chapter renames it aaa.)
    • b(r)b(r)b(r): the bidding function, mapping pCTR to a bid.
    • NNN: bid requests over the campaign’s life [TTT]. BBB: total media budget in dollars. B/NB/NB/N is the budget per request.
    • C(b)=E[Z 1{Z≤b}]C(b)=E[Z\,\mathbf{1}\{Z\le b\}]C(b)=E[Z1{Z≤b}]: expected payment per request, counting zero on a loss, as in Prediction and bidding. 1{⋅}\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\}1{⋅} is the indicator; EEE is over ZZZ. The monograph’s cost function c(b)c(b)c(b) (Eq. 5.5) is the expected payment given a win, c(b)=E[Z∣Z≤b]c(b)=E[Z\mid Z\le b]c(b)=E[Z∣Z≤b], so C(b)=c(b) F(b)C(b)=c(b)\,F(b)C(b)=c(b)F(b).
    • λ>0\lambda>0λ>0: the Lagrange multiplier on the budget. The objective counts clicks, so λ\lambdaλ is clicks per dollar and 1/λ1/\lambda1/λ is dollars per click.

    Model and correct solution

    The monograph’s special case: an ideal second-price auction (the winner pays ZZZ; no floor, fees or bid increments); every win is one billable impression; r∼Uniform(0,1)r\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)r∼Uniform(0,1), independent of ZZZ; a risk-neutral buyer that maximizes expected clicks subject to expected spend =B=B=B. Nothing assumes the bid is linear in rrr; linearity falls out of the first-order condition.

    Derivation

    Budget-constrained click maximization under second price

    Given: Z∼Uniform(0,L)Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,L)Z∼Uniform(0,L) in dollars per impression; pCTR r∼Uniform(0,1)r\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)r∼Uniform(0,1), independent of ZZZ; NNN requests; budget BBB dollars.

    1. Win rate and costs for 0≤b≤L0\le b\le L0≤b≤L. The per-request cost integrates the payment over winning thresholds only; it already contains the win probability.
      F(b)=bL,c(b)=E[Z∣Z≤b]=b2,C(b)=∫0bz dzL=b22L=c(b) F(b).\begin{aligned} F(b)&=\frac{b}{L},\\ c(b)&=E[Z\mid Z\le b]=\frac{b}{2},\\ C(b)&=\int_0^b z\,\frac{dz}{L}=\frac{b^2}{2L}\\ &=c(b)\,F(b). \end{aligned}F(b)c(b)C(b)​=Lb​,=E[Z∣Z≤b]=2b​,=∫0b​zLdz​=2Lb2​=c(b)F(b).​

      max⁡b(⋅)  N∫01r F(b(r)) drs.t.N∫01C(b(r)) dr=B.\begin{aligned} &\max_{b(\cdot)}\; N\int_0^1 r\,F\bigl(b(r)\bigr)\,dr\\ &\text{s.t.}\quad N\int_0^1 C\bigl(b(r)\bigr)\,dr=B. \end{aligned}​b(⋅)max​N∫01​rF(b(r))drs.t.N∫01​C(b(r))dr=B.​
    3. The Lagrangian separates across rrr. Maximize rF(b)−λC(b)rF(b)-\lambda C(b)rF(b)−λC(b) pointwise. Since C′(b)=b f(b)C'(b)=b\,f(b)C′(b)=bf(b), the derivative is (r−λb) f(b)(r-\lambda b)\,f(b)(r−λb)f(b): positive below r/λr/\lambdar/λ, negative above. So

      N∫01(rc∗)22L dr=N(c∗)26L=B⟹c∗=1λ∗=6LBN.\begin{aligned} N\int_0^1 \frac{(r c^*)^2}{2L}\,dr&=\frac{N (c^*)^2}{6L}=B\\ \Longrightarrow\quad c^*=\frac{1}{\lambda^*}&=\sqrt{\frac{6LB}{N}}. \end{aligned}N∫01​2L(rc∗)2​dr⟹c∗=λ∗1​​=6LN(c∗)2​=B=N6LB​​.​
    6. Validity. The step-5 integral assumed no bid exceeds LLL, i.e. c∗≤Lc^*\le Lc∗≤L, which is 6LB/N≤L26LB/N\le L^26LB/N≤L2, i.e. B/N≤L/6B/N\le L/6B/N≤L/6. For L/6<B/N<L/2L/6<B/N<L/2L/6<B/N<L/2 the bid min⁡(rc,L)\min(rc,L)min(rc,L) costs L/2−L2/(3c)L/2-L^2/(3c)L/2−L2/(3c) per request, so c=L2/(3(L/2−B/N))c=L^2/\bigl(3(L/2-B/N)\bigr)c=L2/(3(L/2−B/N)); it equals LLL at B/N=L/6B/N=L/6B/N=L/6, so the two regimes join continuously. For B/N≥L/2B/N\ge L/2B/N≥L/2 the budget never binds: bidding LLL everywhere costs E[Z]=L/2E[Z]=L/2E[Z]=L/2 per request.

    Result: b∗(r)=r6LB/Nb^*(r)=r\sqrt{6LB/N}b∗(r)=r6LB/N​ for B/N≤L/6B/N\le L/6B/N≤L/6 (dollars per impression; the coefficient is dollars per click).

    Check: (i) Units: LLL and B/NB/NB/N are both dollars, so 6LB/N\sqrt{6LB/N}6LB/N​ is dollars, per click because rrr is clicks per impression. (ii) Marginal cost: spend S=Nc2/(6L)S=N c^2/(6L)S=Nc2/(6L) and clicks K=Nc/(3L)K=N c/(3L)K=Nc/(3L) give dS/dK=cdS/dK=cdS/dK=c, so at the optimum the last click costs exactly 1/λ∗1/\lambda^*1/λ∗, as a shadow price should. (iii) Numerical double integration of E[Z 1{Z≤rc∗}]E[Z\,\mathbf{1}\{Z\le rc^*\}]E[Z1{Z≤rc∗}] over (r,Z)(r,Z)(r,Z), a Monte Carlo run, and a grid search over linear coefficients all reproduce the closed form and the optimum.

    Where the monograph goes wrong

    The monograph’s budget constraint (Eqs. 5.11 and 5.33, PDF pp. 56 and 58) is N∫c(b(r)) F(b(r)) dr=BN\int c(b(r))\,F(b(r))\,dr=BN∫c(b(r))F(b(r))dr=B. That is correct: Eq. 5.5 (p. 54) defines ccc as the conditional payment, so cF=CcF=CcF=C. But Eq. 5.35 (p. 58) evaluates c(b)c(b)c(b) as ∫0bz/L dz=b2/(2L)\int_0^b z/L\,dz=b^2/(2L)∫0b​z/Ldz=b2/(2L), dropping Eq. 5.5’s denominator F(b)F(b)F(b). That is C(b)C(b)C(b), not c(b)c(b)c(b). Eq. 5.36 (p. 59) then multiplies by F(b)=b/LF(b)=b/LF(b)=b/L again, making the per-request cost b3/(2L2)b^3/(2L^2)b3/(2L2). With b=r/λb=r/\lambdab=r/λ:

    ∫01(r/λ)32L2 dr=18λ3L2=BN⟹λpaper=12(NBL2)1/3,cpaper=1λpaper=2(L2BN)1/3.\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\frac{(r/\lambda)^3}{2L^2}\,dr&=\frac{1}{8\lambda^3L^2}=\frac{B}{N}\\ \Longrightarrow\quad \lambda_{\mathrm{paper}}&=\frac12\left(\frac{N}{BL^2}\right)^{1/3},\\ c_{\mathrm{paper}}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{\mathrm{paper}}}&=2\left(\frac{L^2B}{N}\right)^{1/3}. \end{aligned}∫01​2L2(r/λ)3​dr⟹λpaper​cpaper​=λpaper​1​​=8λ3L21​=NB​=21​(BL2N​)1/3,=2(NL2B​)1/3.​

    These are Eqs. 5.37 and 5.38. The linear form b=r/λb=r/\lambdab=r/λ survives; only the coefficient is wrong. The first-price result in the same section, b(r)=r3LB/Nb(r)=r\sqrt{3LB/N}b(r)=r3LB/N​ (Eq. 5.29, p. 58), uses the per-request cost b F(b)=b2/Lb\,F(b)=b^2/LbF(b)=b2/L correctly, so the slip is confined to the second-price case. Page with Eq. 5.5, page with Eq. 5.35, page with Eqs. 5.36–5.38

    Pitfall: conditional vs per-request cost

    “Expected cost” has two meanings: given a win, E[Z∣Z≤b]E[Z\mid Z\le b]E[Z∣Z≤b], and per request, E[Z 1{Z≤b}]E[Z\,\mathbf{1}\{Z\le b\}]E[Z1{Z≤b}]. They differ by a factor F(b)F(b)F(b). A budget constraint needs the per-request one: the win rate enters exactly once. Units will not catch a second factor of FFF, which is dimensionless; scaling will. Under a uniform threshold, per-request second-price spend must grow as b2b^2b2; a formula that grows as b3b^3b3 has counted the win rate twice.

    Size of the error

    Bidding with cpaperc_{\mathrm{paper}}cpaper​, the true expected spend per request is cpaper2/(6L)c_{\mathrm{paper}}^2/(6L)cpaper2​/(6L) as long as cpaper≤Lc_{\mathrm{paper}}\le Lcpaper​≤L. Divided by the budget per request:

    cpaper2/(6L)B/N=4 (L2B/N)2/36L B/N=23(LNB)1/3.\begin{aligned} \frac{c_{\mathrm{paper}}^2/(6L)}{B/N}&=\frac{4\,(L^2B/N)^{2/3}}{6L\,B/N}\\ &=\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{LN}{B}\right)^{1/3}. \end{aligned}B/Ncpaper2​/(6L)​​=6LB/N4(L2B/N)2/3​=32​(BLN​)1/3.​

    The published coefficient keeps every bid at or below LLL exactly when 8L2B/N≤L38L^2B/N\le L^38L2B/N≤L3, i.e. B/N≤L/8B/N\le L/8B/N≤L/8. The factor decreases in B/NB/NB/N, so on that range it is at least 23⋅81/3=43\tfrac23\cdot 8^{1/3}=\tfrac4332​⋅81/3=34​. On L/8<B/N≤L/6L/8<B/N\le L/6L/8<B/N≤L/6 some published bids exceed LLL; true spend is then L/2−L2/(3cpaper)L/2-L^2/(3c_{\mathrm{paper}})L/2−L2/(3cpaper​) per request, and the factor keeps falling to 3−61/3≈1.1833-6^{1/3}\approx1.1833−61/3≈1.183 at B/N=L/6B/N=L/6B/N=L/6. Wherever the correct closed form applies, the published one overspends by at least 18%, and by more as the budget tightens. This is not a boundary effect.

    Where to read next

    For the full RTB picture, read the RTB monograph’s Chapters 2 (how RTB works), 3 (auctions and the bid landscape), 5 (bidding strategies) and 7 (attribution). For how production click models define and calibrate probabilities, read Google’s 2013 click-prediction paper. To build an integration, work from OpenRTB and your counterparties’ contracts. To judge whether advertising creates value for the advertiser, read the randomized experiments. In every paper, write down the explicit assumptions; they matter more than the model names.

    Resource Purpose
    RTB monograph, pinned v2 Main reference for RTB mechanics, auctions, bidding and attribution; see the erratum above
    Optimal Real-Time Bidding Frameworks Discussion Contrasts the true expected second-price cost with using the bid as a cost upper bound
    Google, Ad Click Prediction (2013) Sampling, calibration and other problems of training click models at production scale
    ESMM Joint modeling of impression → click → conversion to reduce selection bias in conversion-rate models
    Delayed-feedback conversion modeling Conversion labels that arrive late, and the trade-off between label completeness and model freshness
    ICML 2023, first-price bidding with budgets Learning to bid under a budget, with guarantees that depend on what feedback the bidder observes
    Statistical Arbitrage Mining (SAM) Risk and optimization for a buyer that sells on CPA and buys on CPM
    Counterfactual risk minimization Logging policies, propensities and offline evaluation of new policies
    Gordon et al., randomized ad experiments at Facebook How far observational ad measurement departs from randomized estimates of causal effect
    OpenRTB 2.6 Response deadlines, price units, request and response objects, and win, billing and loss notices
